stories.Headline: Malaysia partners with Singapore and US to stop AI chip smuggling
stories.Summary:
Malaysia is working with Singapore and the United States to stop chip smuggling, according to a statement released on November 13, 2026. The Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry is checking with local Customs to see if chips brought into Malaysia were re-exported legally. This action follows a 2025 probe by Singapore authorities into several companies, including the cloud computing firm Megaspeed and officer Alice Huang. Alice Huang is a suspected Chinese spy whose affair with Jensen Huang led to the resignation of the Nvidia chief executive. The Malaysian government is now bracing for expected US controls on high-performance artificial intelligence chips and remote compute deals with Chinese firms.

The government has tightened rules since July 2025, requiring permits for US AI chips to leave Malaysia, though importing them remains license-free. Regulations do not require data centres to name end users, but stakeholders estimate half of the 1.4-gigawatt capacity serves the Chinese market. Nvidia requires cloud partners, such as conglomerate YTL, to provide customer information and cap Chinese business at 49 percent of services. YTL Power lost RM5.5 billion, or an eighth of its market value, starting November 10 as investors gauged exposure to Megaspeed. MITI clarified that verification visits at data centres where Speedmatrix, the Malaysian arm of Megaspeed, is a tenant are part of regular monitoring.

Investment, Trade and Industry Minister Johari Ghani said on November 10 that Speedmatrix was not under investigation due to a lack of credible evidence. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim stated on November 13 that Malaysia has not received formal requests from Singapore or the US but will collaborate. He noted that Malaysia is a trading nation that welcomes investments but wants to ensure that all rules are being followed. MITI denied that it has cleared Megaspeed or its local subsidiary of any wrongdoing amid the fallout in the data centre sector. These statements followed revelations over the weekend regarding Jensen Huang's affair, which increased security concerns in Washington over US technology.

Banking executives said that financing deals for about half of upcoming data centre projects in Malaysia have been halted, with delays up to six months. An unnamed investment analyst warned that significant implications for customer concentration and contract enforceability exist if Megaspeed accounts for much of YTL's capacity. David Black of BlackBox Research stated that there will be additional compliance costs, though he warned that a total chip export ban is counterproductive. A digital economy official said the news ruffled feathers, but for now, the situation remains business as usual while they wait. Taylor's University professor Ong Kian Ming suggested that tougher controls could be an opportunity for Malaysia to become a secure AI investment destination.

Data centre investments surged to RM95.8 billion, or 43.9 percent of total approved investments in the first half of 2026, from RM1.25 billion in 2021. This boom is now stalling as lenders avoid companies that might be subject to US probes, according to a local investment bank executive. The executive noted that without graphics processing units, data centre players cannot offer compute, even though demand still outstrips the current supply. Ong Kian Ming, a former deputy minister, suggested that Malaysia should increase MITI's powers to crowd in domestic demand and reduce Chinese dependence. He also mentioned that the upcoming Asean summit in Manila could be a forum for Asean to engage the US on these issues.

The industry is now waiting for clarity from Washington to determine when the stalled financing deals for data centre projects can resume. Malaysia may escalate oversight and implement more progressive policies to shift its AI data centre demand away from Chinese-related sources. Asean may use the unveiling of the Digital Economy Framework Agreement details at the Manila summit to discuss these technology controls. The articles leave open whether the US will launch formal probes into other Malaysian data centre players or implement a total export ban. It remains unclear if the current verification visits by MITI will lead to formal charges against Speedmatrix or other local firms.

stories.Headline: Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon says Anthropic can retrain Mythos with a fraction of the original compute
stories.Summary:
Jacob Coxon, a former researcher at both OpenAI and Anthropic, said on X that Anthropic can already retrain its Mythos model with what he called a fraction of the compute originally needed. He said a slide from Anthropic's IPO roadshow was a major reason he quit the company after only about four months. The chart shows how much compute Anthropic needs over time to train its models, and its axis is compressed so that a 10x and a 100x increase barely look different. Coxon said the curve still climbs steeply, which he argues shows that algorithmic efficiency is improving not just quickly but at an accelerating rate.

Coxon wrote that the plot is insane and that he is surprised Anthropic made it public. He argued that Mythos, which he described as a major capability jump in the spring, was not a one-time deviation but a point on a superexponential trend. The roadshow slide shows a pre-training compute multiplier for code over time, with a logarithmic y-axis, and Coxon said the steep climb from July 2024 to October 2026 points to superexponential algorithmic progress. Anthropic notes that the data points are based on internal estimates and are for illustration only.

Coxon said algorithmic improvements are on the verge of being automated, which is why he wants frontier model development paused next year so competitors can catch up. He wrote that a pause would commoditize human-level intelligence and would only harm OpenAI and Anthropic. He previously trained AI models at OpenAI and, most recently, at Anthropic, and he drew wide attention in September with public warnings about the risks of advanced AI systems. Those warnings were echoed by other protagonists in the industry, and one of their fears is that advanced, self-improving AI could get out of control.

Articles.Title: Anthropic can already retrain Mythos with "a fraction of the compute originally needed," says former researcher Coxon

stories.Headline: Malaysia plans law using data center power consumption to detect AI GPU smuggling
stories.Summary:
Malaysia plans to introduce a new law to catch AI GPU smugglers using data center power consumption. The government intends to prevent the diversion of restricted hardware to countries like China. This plan was reported on November 14, 2026. The law aims to optimize the use of the country's power infrastructure. Authorities want AI accelerators imported into the country to be used domestically.

The law requires operators to disclose the number of GPUs imported and their power consumption. Operators must provide the physical locations of facilities and the identities of operators and hyperscale customers. Data center operators must pay for all reserved electricity capacity, such as paying for 100 MW even if only 50 MW is used. This measure targets capacity reserved for one to three years. The Digital Ministry is reviewing legislation regarding processors subject to U.S. export bans.

Minister of Investment, Trade and Industry Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani spoke on Thursday. He acknowledged that some companies rented Malaysian data center space to import GPUs legally before shipping them abroad. Johari stated that Malaysian authorities are prepared to cooperate with U.S. counterparts. He said they would provide information about facilities housing particular GPUs upon request. The government wants to track data center operations throughout their entire lifetime.

Data center operators are affected by the new requirement to pay for unused electricity capacity. This financial measure is meant to discourage companies from reserving power they do not need. The plan also targets entities that re-export processors to avoid U.S. export bans. Some companies have already used Malaysian facilities as hubs for smuggling operations. The law seeks to stop these entities from pretending hardware is used in Malaysia.

The background involves the use of AI accelerators like Nvidia H100 and H200 SXM GPUs rated at 700W. The B200 SXM accelerators are rated at 1,000W, but actual workloads vary from these ratings. Power consumption estimates are imprecise without knowing server configurations, memory, storage, and networking equipment. Power usage effectiveness of a facility also impacts the accuracy of power data. There is often a considerable delay between the import of GPUs and their deployment.

The government will now determine if local authorities can take action against those who re-export banned processors. Reliable verification of GPU numbers may still require physical inventory audits or other tracking mechanisms. The articles leave open whether the law will require the disclosure of GPU models and serial numbers. It is not specified if authorities will conduct on-site inspections of the facilities. The effectiveness of using power data to spot discrepancies remains a point of concern.

The guide covers tech brands including JBL, Nespresso, Meta, Oakley and Brother. SheKnows noted it may receive an affiliate commission from purchases made through links on its website. The article said Best Buy makes holiday shopping easier with a wide selection of gifts from recognizable tech brands. It said options at different price points let shoppers buy gifts without looking in a dozen different places.

It said the Brother MFC-L2820DW helps home offices and workdays run more smoothly and handles printing, copying, scanning and faxing.

It said the Oakley glasses suit anyone who loves the outdoors, traveling or staying active, with open-ear speakers that do not block out the world around you. It said the Brother HL-L2405W is essential for printing school assignments, shipping labels or work documents. stories.Headline: UK adults spend over $1.3 billion a year on AI tools as paying users reach 5 percent
stories.Summary:
Brits are spending more and more on artificial intelligence, with one in twenty adults in the United Kingdom now paying for AI tools and spending more than $1.3 billion a year in total. That five percent share is still early days, but it is a fast ramp, since it was 1% two years ago and 2.5% a year ago. London is the hotspot, and the professional skew is predictable, with those involved in tech, finance, education and PR most likely to pay. Claude's share of that spending has quadrupled in a year, and the newsletter asks whether the trigger was the improved harness on Claude Cowork.

Agent-based shopping is still early, since Uber says four rides out of 320 million during Halloween week were booked by agents. The writer's Instinct agent secured an iPhone Duo on Tuesday, a job that involved checking Apple's website every few minutes from 7 am. William Gildea made his first purchase using his Instinct agent, sweaters for winter, and Hannah Petrovic's agent booked a squash court for a showdown with Marija Gavrilov. The writer says he would still reach for the app to book an Uber, but finding finicky, complicated products is a perfect job for agents.

On energy, adding wind to solar and batteries cuts the median cost from $105 to $86 per MWh, and north of Milan and Montreal it falls from $164 to $99. Based on hourly modeling over ten years, Kingsmill Bond and Daan Walter reckon that sun and wind mostly cover for each other, except for a difficult combined lull for about a week every four. Ember also finds that 83% of the 750GW of fossil plants being planned sit where reliable renewables, with a bit of gas backup, cost under $100/MWh. The writer's take is that technology costs will keep falling, but redesigning the grid into a largely renewable-based one also requires a better cost of capital and financial instruments that match energy prices to the volatility renewables bring.

stories.Headline: Google threatens to block school search access if New York City bans AI, a reader says
stories.Summary:
The New York Daily News published a “Voice of the People” readers’ letters column on November 15, 2026, at 3:00 AM EST, with the email address voicers@nydailynews.com. A Forest Hills reader wrote that Google threatened to block schools’ search access if the NYC Department of Education bans AI. An Olivebridge, N.Y., reader wrote that Alaska’s Senate race was still too close to call as of Friday. That reader wrote that with 88% of votes recorded, Democrat Mary Peltola led by 3,975 votes. A Western Springs, Ill., reader wrote that Elon Musk spent at least $474 million supporting Republicans in the midterm elections.

The Forest Hills reader wrote that the DOE has over-relied on Google for the classroom, assignments, and grade-tracking and testing by computer. The Western Springs reader wrote that about $224 million was spent on races in Texas, where Musk’s SpaceX and Tesla are headquartered. That reader wrote that SpaceX is dependent on government decisions and contracts, and that Musk wants to build a data center in Texas to support Tesla’s testing for autonomous driving. The Olivebridge reader wrote that Peltola’s opponents are Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan and the Independent Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., who has received 4,199 votes. A Beacon, N.Y., reader wrote that Gov. Hochul’s recent reelection was a mandate, and that the SUNNY Act and the Healthy Homes Right to Know Act have passed the New York State Legislature and await her signature.

The Forest Hills reader wrote that Google’s goal is profit above all and to use our children as guinea pigs to teach its computer system. That reader wrote, “I’d be surprised if the DOE stood up to Google.” The Olivebridge reader wrote that a high-ranking Republican asserts that Dan S. Sullivan should be given the votes that Daniel J. Sullivan received, and identified this Republican as Trump. That reader called the assertion a clear perversion of the election and an insult to every Alaskan, and likened it to the “I just want to find, uh, 11,780 votes” suggestion in the 2020 presidential election. The Manhattan reader wrote that Chuck Schumer may want to ride into the sunset after his term is over, leaving a legacy of regaining his majority leader position.

The Forest Hills reader wrote that AI is quirky at best and wrong 50% of the time, and that students don’t read, want to double check or seek other sources. The Western Springs reader wrote that Musk bought more political speech than millions of ordinary people combined, but that with a strong wave against Republicans his candidates did not do well in this election. That reader wrote that many elections are a lot closer, and in those, huge contributions can be decisive. The Manhattan reader wrote that Schumer snubbed Abdul El-Sayed in favor of Haley Stevens and didn’t direct funding support to Angie Nixon, who came within a hair of defeating the miserable GOP candidate in Florida.

The Manhattan reader wrote that Elissa Slotkin and Bernie Sanders want an open selection process and for prospective candidates to provide a concrete plan for affordability and accountability. The Hamilton Square, N.J., reader wrote that in 1968 two Olympians from the U.S. raised their fists in a Black Power salute and were suspended, and that a few years ago Colin Kaepernick was chastised and punished for taking a knee on a football field. The Bronx reader wrote, “I was once a Trump supporter,” and that the results of the Nov. 3 elections followed a failure to admit and correct mistakes. The Beacon reader cited “World leaders urge stronger and faster action at UN climate talks over inadequate response” (Nov. 11).

The Smithtown, L.I., reader wrote that Ghanaian immigrant Javits Frimpong was murdered for no apparent reason by three thugs, and that Rev. Al Sharpton and civil rights leader Ben Crump held a press conference at Sharpton’s National Action Network. The Staten Island reader wrote that in a TV commercial for his new Broadway show “860” at the Imperial Theatre, Billy Crystal asks the audience to “not wear shorts and tank tops.” The Lakewood, N.J., reader suggested that instead of airing the Jets and Bills game on Sunday, CBS show reruns of the political ads from the midterms.

The Manhattan reader wrote that Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand must see which way the mighty hurricane is blowing and help convince Schumer to not accept an automatic promotion. The Smithtown reader wrote of Sharpton and Crump, “We will know soon.” The Bronx reader wrote, “I am no longer in your corner.” The Forest Hills reader wrote that paper doesn’t lose power and can be read without a headache, but that’s 20th-century thinking, apparently.

stories.Headline: Shanghai police arrest 15 people for using AI to forge a luxury restaurant bill to boost liquor sales
stories.Summary:
Shanghai police arrested fifteen people on November 14, 2026, after discovering a forged restaurant bill. An online liquor seller used artificial intelligence software to alter a genuine receipt from the Peace Hotel. The fake document showed a dinner for six people that totaled 517,127.60 yuan. This forgery included two bottles of 1997 Romanée-Conti priced at 230,000 yuan each.

The scheme required the use of AI to change amounts and substitute the hotel's wine list with products from a private company. To make the image go viral after November 8, the group used batches of accounts and paid for bulk reposting. The investigation involved the Huangpu district police and officers from the suspects' home province. Four individuals, including a boss surnamed Zhao and colleagues surnamed Wang and Dong, now face criminal compulsory measures.

The Huangpu district police stated that Zhao organized his employees to create the fake bill and a staged video. They explained that the goal was to use manufactured virality to increase liquor sales for the company. Authorities noted that the group fabricated false information about a business to deceive the public. The police notice cleared the Peace Hotel of any involvement in the fake luxury dinner.

The forgery was first exposed by internet users who noticed mismatched English names and incorrect service charges. These readers also realized the specific wines listed were not sold by the hotel. This case highlights how generative tools are being used for commercial scams in China. The eleven other suspects involved in the operation received administrative punishments for their roles.

stories.Headline: Sound Ventures holds a $7 billion stake in Anthropic from a $435 million investment
stories.Summary:
Bloomberg reported on November 15, 2026, that Sound Ventures, the firm co-founded by music manager Guy Oseary and actor Ashton Kutcher, holds a stake in Anthropic worth $7 billion based on private market valuations rather than any public share price. The relationship began in spring 2023, when Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei visited Oseary's Beverly Hills home and met with Oseary and Kutcher across the table. Sound Ventures made its first bet on Anthropic that spring with a $35 million investment in the company's Series C round, which valued the AI lab at roughly $4.6 billion before the new money arrived. Google and Spark Capital also participated in that round, giving the deal a mix of Big Tech strategic money and established venture backing.

Over several later rounds, Sound Ventures' total commitment to Anthropic grew to approximately $435 million, and the reported stake works out to roughly 16 times the total cash invested, though those are paper gains rather than realized returns. Sound Ventures was founded in 2015 out of A-Grade Investments, a collaboration between Oseary and Kutcher, and in 2023 it established a dedicated AI fund of nearly $240 million. Anthropic is preparing for an IPO anticipated for late 2026, which would give investors like Sound Ventures a public market for their shares and test the private valuations. Until then, the $7 billion figure is best read as a mark rather than a payout, since lockup periods, share price swings and the timing of any sales would all shape what the firm actually brings home.

The article attributes the reporting to Bloomberg and notes that the $7 billion figure rests on private market valuations, not on a public share price. It describes concentration as a quieter risk for Sound Ventures, because if one holding is worth far more than everything the firm put into it, a lot of the fund's results depend on that single company. The article says a few things are worth tracking from here, including whether Anthropic's IPO plans hold to the anticipated late 2026 timeline and how public markets value the company compared with its last private round. It adds that a third thing to watch is whether Sound Ventures decides to cut its position once there is a market to sell into.

The article notes that Anthropic was a young AI lab started by former OpenAI executives and was still proving it could compete with its old employer when Sound Ventures first invested. It observes that plenty of early backers make one bet and watch later rounds dilute them, while Sound Ventures kept investing, which helps explain how a $35 million opening check became a position measured in billions. It closes by noting that in 2023 Amodei may have been the least famous person in that Beverly Hills living room, and judging by the reported value of the stake, he may also have been the most consequential one for the people sitting across from him. The article carries a disclosure that it was edited by Diego Almada Lopez.

stories.Headline: Marcos signs executive order adopting AI governance framework and creating national AI council
stories.Summary:
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signed Executive Order No. 131 in Manila on November 12, 2026, adopting the AI Governance Framework for the Philippines as the national strategic guide on artificial intelligence. The Order also created the National Artificial Intelligence Council, chaired by the Executive Secretary, to coordinate and monitor how the Framework is carried out. The Order directs government agencies to support the Council. It sets no new license, registration or penalty for businesses. It says existing sector regulators keep their mandates.

Section 1 adopts the Framework as the national strategic guide for policy formulation, regulatory coordination, institutional development, capacity-building and other governance measures. The Framework has four connected elements: ethics and principles, standards and assurance, a risk-based policy toolkit, and enabling resources. The ethics and principles element lists transparency and explainability, security and safety, accountability and integrity, human centricity, fairness and equity, and sustainable development. The risk-based toolkit may include general and sector-specific guidelines, AI impact assessments, regulatory sandboxes, a review of existing laws and regulations, and coordinated complaint and grievance mechanisms. The Order cites the President's power of control under Section 17, Article VII of the Constitution, and recites that the National Artificial Intelligence Strategy for the Philippines was approved in May 2025 and that the National Innovation Council approved the Framework.

The NAIC is an inter-agency body that reports directly to the President under Section 2. The Executive Secretary chairs it, the Secretary of Economy, Planning, and Development is Vice Chairperson, and DEPDev serves as the Secretariat. Members are the Secretaries of Information and Communications Technology, Science and Technology, Trade and Industry, Finance, Education, Labor and Employment, and Budget and Management, the Chairperson of the Commission on Higher Education, and the Director General of the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority. One private sector representative is appointed by the President from nominees of reputable business groups or associations, for three years with one reappointment, and the Council may invite other agencies, local governments, government-owned or -controlled corporations, state universities and colleges, the private sector, academe and civil society as resource persons.

Under Section 3 the Council will keep government AI programs consistent with the Framework, address gaps and remove duplication, oversee the action plans of its technical working groups, strengthen international cooperation and private sector collaboration, help resolve policy, regulatory and other bottlenecks, give policy direction to agencies within their mandates, recommend policy, regulatory, fiscal, institutional and legislative measures to the President, and issue implementing guidelines. Section 4 directs the Council to form five technical working groups: Institutions, Data and Research and Development, Capabilities, Infrastructure, and Demand Generation, the last covering public-private partnerships and financing for AI adoption, including for micro, small and medium enterprises and startups. The Department of Information and Communications Technology will run a digital monitoring and reporting platform, and agencies will update it every quarter. The Council reports to the President within 30 days from the end of each quarter under Section 5 and reviews the Framework at least once every two years under Section 6. Section 7 directs national government agencies, including government-owned or -controlled corporations, to support the Council and encourages local governments, the private sector, academe and civil society to do so.

The Order has no penal clause and sets no license, registration, fee or penalty for companies that build or use AI, and existing sector regulators continue to exercise their mandates under applicable laws under Section 1. The Council may still issue implementing guidelines and recommend legislative measures to the President, and the Framework's toolkit names sector-specific guidelines and AI impact assessments. Laws already in force continue to apply to how a business uses AI, and the Order refers to applicable data privacy laws in Section 4, the main one being the Data Privacy Act of 2012, Republic Act No. 10173. The Order takes effect immediately upon its publication in the Official Gazette or in a newspaper of general circulation under Section 12. Within 30 days from effectivity, DEPDev must form an interim Secretariat under Section 8, and initial funding comes from the current and available appropriations of the Council's members and other sources the Department of Budget and Management may identify under Section 9.

The Order is an executive order, not a statute passed by Congress, and it carries no penalties. One of the Council's functions is to recommend legislative measures to the President. The private sector has one seat on the Council, and it may also be represented in the technical working groups or invited as resource persons. The Council, through DEPDev, leads monitoring and reporting, the Department of Information and Communications Technology maintains the monitoring platform, and agencies update it every quarter. The Framework is reviewed at least once every two years, or earlier when significant technological, regulatory or market developments call for it.

stories.Headline: China's first fully AI-generated feature film flops at the box office
stories.Summary:
China recently released its first fully AI-generated feature film titled Sanxingdui: Future Past, but the project flopped at the box office. The production was created without any human actors or a traditional camera crew to film the scenes. According to data from the tracker Beacon Pro, the movie earned only about 1.8 million yuan, which is roughly 270,000 US dollars. This meager return occurred after the film had spent three weeks playing in theaters across the country. The 100-minute science fiction story requires viewers to imagine a world decades in the future where rogue algorithms cause catastrophe.

To prevent this disaster, the characters must decipher warnings hidden inside bronze artifacts from the ancient Shu kingdom. The film's reported budget was tens of millions of yuan, meaning the final earnings were well below the initial costs. Audiences rejected the movie because of its disjointed plot and visuals that appeared far too stiff. Viewers described the movie as being obviously AI, which contributed to the lack of ticket sales in cinemas.

This failure happened even as short AI dramas continue to boom on smartphones throughout China. The contrast suggests that while small AI clips are popular, full length AI features may struggle. The production attempted to merge ancient history with futuristic technology, but the execution failed to attract a wide audience. More to follow.

Articles.Title: No actors, no crew, no ticket sales: why China’s first AI feature film bombed

stories.Headline: European Commission proposes Digital Fairness Act with AI purchasing agent safeguards
stories.Summary:
The European Commission proposed a Digital Fairness Act on November 11, 2026. The proposal includes safeguards for AI purchasing agents and for digital features that encourage compulsive use. It sits within a broader consumer protection package. The proposal now goes to the European Parliament and Council for discussion, and the safeguards are not yet enacted requirements.

The draft regulation sets out several provisions. Article 17 would require effective controls to disable features that encourage compulsive or excessive use, including persistent automated prompts that simulate relationships, subject to exclusions. Article 26 would require adjustable approval settings for purchasing agents, so consumers could confirm all, selected or no contracts, and paid recommendations or conflicts would always trigger disclosure and confirmation. Articles 12 and 13 would restrict profiling-based advertising using known minors' or sensitive data, with an exclusion for DSA platforms, and restrict personalised pricing likely to harm known minors or vulnerable consumers. Article 17 excludes the education and science categories referenced in Article 2(4)(c) and (e) of the proposed EU KIDS Act, which cover services and systems designed primarily for education and operated by educational establishments, and services and systems developed and operated solely for scientific research and development.

The Commission describes the DFA as a consumer protection safety net complementing the existing digital rulebook. The EU AI Act provides a separate framework based on AI risk, while the DSA addresses platform responsibilities, and the DFA would reach businesses engaged in consumer commercial practices beyond platforms. The Commission also presented a separate revision of the Consumer Protection Cooperation Regulation, which would give it powers to investigate and fine businesses in large cases affecting consumers across the Single Market. The Commission says the proposals will now be discussed by Parliament and Council, and its announcement supplies no adoption deadline.

For university product teams, the immediate significance is a published legislative proposal to assess and follow as negotiations proceed, rather than a new implementation date for a compliance calendar. The comparison suggests concrete additions to a model evaluation suite, such as examining whether users can disengage, whether purchasing limits hold, and whether commercial incentives are visible. Research offices and technology transfer teams are advised to examine a project's purpose, operator and commercial use before assuming an exclusion applies. A consumer-facing spinout merits its own scope assessment, because university origins alone do not establish that the specific Article 17 categories fit.

stories.Headline: AI Lawsuit Jersey 2026: Settlements, Eligibility and Filing
stories.Summary:
New Jersey faces three major AI class actions in 2026, according to lawfold.com, with the largest, Martinez v. TechHire Solutions, covering over 15,000 job applicants in the Newark metro area who claim an AI tool scored them lower based on zip code. The second, Doe v. SocialAI Corp, involves 8,000 New Jersey residents whose likenesses were used without consent to generate synthetic media. The third targets automated lending platforms and alleges AI loan denials disproportionately affected Black and Latino borrowers, with a class estimated at 12,000 applicants.

The Martinez case was certified by Essex County court in January 2026, the SocialAI Corp motion to dismiss was denied in February 2026, and the lending case began discovery in March 2026. The state attorney general filed two enforcement actions this year, both targeting AI vendors selling untested hiring tools to New Jersey employers. The cases invoke the 2025 AEDT Act, which gives workers a private right of action and requires a bias audit within 12 months of use, annual re-audits every 12 months, public disclosure, and candidate notification before AI use. Penalties run $500 per day for a missed initial audit, $1,000 per day for a missed re-audit, $500 per violation for non-disclosure, and $250 per applicant for missing notification. Deepfake victims can sue for statutory damages of $1,000 per incident under the 2025 privacy expansion, and the updated privacy framework took effect in January 2026, requiring explicit opt-in consent for AI data use.

Damages range from $500 to $2,500 for unauthorized data scraping under the NJ Consumer Fraud Act, $1,000 per violation for hidden AI data use, $1,000 to $5,000 for biometric misuse, and $5,000 per child for children's data harvesting. A 2025 state study found a 34% disparity in AI-driven loan approvals, against a 9% gap for human loan officers. The articles attribute the claims to New Jersey workers who say automated systems denied them jobs unfairly, and to plaintiffs who argue that non-compliance with the AEDT Act itself proves negligence. The articles state that employers must now prove their AI tools are bias-free and that companies that fail face penalties under the 2025 AEDT Act. The articles say the state attorney general filed the two enforcement actions, that penalties could exceed $10 million per case, and that the NJ Division on Civil Rights is actively investigating.

The articles state that the EEOC has referenced New Jersey cases in its own guidance. The articles say staffing agencies are the biggest targets and are named as co-defendants in multiple suits, and that at least four Fortune 500 firms paid undisclosed sums to New Jersey applicants. The articles state that over 20,000 workers have reported suspicious rejections since 2024, that over 40,000 New Jersey workers may be owed compensation, and that most claimants can expect between $200 and $5,000. The articles say the combined class size exceeds 35,000 people, that tech, finance, and staffing face the most exposure, and that the lead court is Essex County Superior Court. The articles state that retail chains face class actions over facial recognition data collected in New Jersey stores and offices.

The articles state that New Jersey passed the AEDT Act in 2025, that it was the first law of its kind in the state, and that the state leads the nation in AI regulation enforcement. The articles say New Jersey expanded its privacy laws in 2025 to cover synthetic media and that the updated privacy framework took effect in January 2026. The articles state that the claims fall under the NJ Law Against Discrimination, the NJ Consumer Fraud Act, the NJ Fair Housing Act, the NJ Biometric Privacy Act, and a NJ COPPA Extension. The articles say the law does not require proof of intentional discrimination and that disparate impact alone is enough under New Jersey law. The articles state that many employers missed the first audit deadline, creating a wave of new claims in early 2026.

The articles state that filing deadlines are approaching fast for several claims and advise workers rejected by AI systems to keep all emails, and deepfake victims to document screenshots, URLs, and timestamps. The articles do not name the defendants in the lending case, the employers or agencies named as co-defendants, the four Fortune 500 firms, or the retail chains facing biometric claims. The articles do not give the filing deadlines, the amounts paid in the undisclosed settlements, or the outcomes of the two enforcement actions. The articles do not state when the three class actions will next be heard or how the 34% disparity study was conducted.

stories.Headline: Lai Mohammed urges media literacy and ethical AI regulation at Caleb University lecture
stories.Summary:
Alhaji Lai Mohammed spoke at a public lecture on November 14, 2026, in Imota, Lagos. The former Minister of Information and Culture urged citizens to embrace media literacy and verify information. He also called for the ethical regulation of Artificial Intelligence to protect the public interest. This event marked the maiden edition of the Caleb University Public Lecture series. The lecture focused on defending truth against disinformation and fake news in the digital age.

The lecture took place at Caleb University in Imota, Lagos, on November 14, 2026. It addressed the theme of fake news, disinformation, and Artificial Intelligence in the digital age. Mohammed warned that uncontrolled deepfakes could lead to information nihilism where truth is no longer believed. He stated that AI creates convincing falsehoods and causes people to dismiss authentic evidence as fake. These changes require citizens to verify all information before they choose to share it.

Alhaji Lai Mohammed is responsible for calling for the ethical regulation of Artificial Intelligence. He explained that the greatest danger of AI is the tendency to dismiss authentic evidence. Vice-Chancellor Professor Olalekan Asikhia said universities must be strongholds of ethical fact-checking and intellectual integrity. Registrar Mr. Mayokun Olumeru reaffirmed that the university will produce graduates who are custodians of truth. Principal Information and Media Expert Olawale Adekoya said the university was honoured to host Mohammed.

The event attracted various students, media executives, and leading scholars who attended the lecture. These groups are affected by the spread of deepfakes and the rise of information nihilism. The attendees witnessed the presentation of a commemorative plaque to Alhaji Lai Mohammed during the event. This plaque recognized his contributions to national communication and public policy in Nigeria. The university aims to ensure its graduates can identify and combat digital disinformation.

The articles provide background on the role of universities in maintaining intellectual integrity. They highlight the specific dangers posed by the uncontrolled spread of Artificial Intelligence and deepfakes. The text establishes Alhaji Lai Mohammed as a distinguished figure in media and public relations. It describes the university's goal to produce credible graduates who can defend the truth. The lecture series was inaugurated to address these modern challenges in the digital age.

The university will continue its commitment to producing graduates who serve as custodians of truth. Scholars and media executives will likely continue discussing the regulation of Artificial Intelligence. The articles leave open how the government will implement ethical AI regulations in Nigeria. They do not state if other universities will adopt similar ethical fact-checking strongholds. No further details are provided regarding the specific laws needed for AI regulation.

stories.Headline: Foreign investors withdraw nearly US$50 billion from Asian equities over AI and cash burn concerns
stories.Summary:
Foreign investors withdrew nearly US$50 billion from Asian equities during October, marking the largest monthly outflow since June. This sell-off targeted tech-linked stocks in South Korea, Taiwan, India, Indonesia, Thailand, Vietnam, and the Philippines. The retreat was driven by concerns over the cash burn of hyperscalers and fears that US midterm elections would bring tougher artificial intelligence regulations. These worries persisted after Democrats won elections in states where opposition to new data centers has increased.

The net withdrawal totaled US$49.8 billion, with Taiwanese stocks seeing a net loss of US$30.7 billion, the highest since January 2008. South Korean shares experienced a net outflow of US$14.6 billion, while Indian stocks lost US$3.6 billion for a second straight month. Indonesian and Thai markets saw outflows of US$938 million and US$199 million, though Vietnam and the Philippines gained US$122 million and US$109 million. In early November, foreigners offloaded another US$22.6 billion, including US$19.8 billion from Taiwan and US$8.3 billion from South Korea.

Wael Makarem of Exness stated that the outflows showed a retreat from AI positions due to doubts about profitability and infrastructure spending. He noted that tighter environmental reviews and regulations were expected to hinder chip demand and data center construction. Scarlett Liu from BNP Paribas suggested that investors were drawn to the resilience of the S&P 500 compared to the MSCI Asia ex-Japan index, which fell 6.9 per cent in October. She also mentioned that some investors moved money into US Treasuries as the 10-year yield reached 5.3 per cent in early October.

Herald van der Linde of HSBC upgraded India to overweight on Monday, citing reasonable valuations and resilient earnings. This positive outlook is reflected in the fact that cross-border investors have put a net US$5.7 billion into Indian equities so far this month. Other analysts believe investors are reallocating capital from Asia toward developed markets. This shift follows a period where the MSCI All Country World Index declined by only 1.7 per cent during October.

stories.Headline: Lawyers see AI take over research and drafting while human judgment stays essential
stories.Summary:
The article, published by LLM GUIDE on November 14, 2026 and updated November 15, 2026, was written by Mubin S. Khan, a Canadian-Bangladeshi journalist and Columbia Journalism School graduate based in Montreal. It examines which areas of law will be most resilient to artificial intelligence for lawyers pursuing an LL.M. in 2026. Khan reports that AI is taking over tasks once central to lawyers' work, from research and document review to drafting contracts and legal memoranda. The article draws on interviews with Shikha Shukla of Osuji & Smith Lawyers in Calgary, Anna Gorodetsky of Major, Lindsey & Africa, and Andrew Perlman, dean of Suffolk University Law School. Khan has more than two decades of experience in journalism, policy research and higher education, and has written for The Guardian, The Sunday Times and The Daily Beast.

Shukla holds an LL.M. from Canada's University of Calgary and leads the employment law practice at Osuji & Smith Lawyers in Calgary. Gorodetsky is a UC Berkeley-trained lawyer and partner specializing in in-house counsel recruiting and board services at Major, Lindsey & Africa. Perlman is dean of Suffolk University Law School, and Shukla is a founding member and board member of the Foot In The Door Initiative, which helps internationally trained lawyers gain Canadian legal experience. The article names the University of California, Berkeley Law, the University of Calgary Faculty of Law and Suffolk University Law School in Boston, Massachusetts. It also lists Suffolk's LL.M. in Global Law and Technology and its Master of Laws in Legal Innovation & Technology.

Shukla says AI is already useful for summarizing documents, constructing timelines from emails, comparing contract clauses and drafting routine correspondence, but she warns against relying on it where mistakes are costly. She says there are many horror stories of AI hallucinating case citations that look real, which lawyers have carelessly used in court without verifying, and that this can be fatal to a case. Gorodetsky says employers increasingly expect lawyers to use AI to work faster, and that producing a polished document is less of a differentiator when the first draft is easier to generate. Perlman points to new positions emerging within law firms and legal departments, AI-native firms and legal technology companies serving people who previously could not afford legal services. Perlman says we have to ask not just what legal jobs will be preserved but which jobs will be created as a result of AI.

Shukla says trial advocacy, negotiation and conciliation all depend on reading the room, judging credibility, understanding emotions and knowing when someone is psychologically ready to settle. She says clients facing dismissal are often dealing with lost income and professional identity, not merely a legal dispute, and she identifies personal accountability and applying existing employment and human rights laws to AI-driven decisions as areas requiring lawyers. Perlman says lawyers are called counselors for a reason and that people will still want human counsel on important issues, even if that counsel is enhanced and informed by AI. He says society may choose to reserve certain responsibilities for humans even if AI becomes technically capable, including judicial decisions affecting civil liberties, prosecution, public defense and aspects of lawmaking. Gorodetsky identifies situations involving incomplete facts, high stakes and competing interests as particularly dependent on human expertise, saying AI can contribute to the analysis but someone still has to ask the right questions, weigh the trade-offs, earn trust and take responsibility for the recommendation.

Perlman says traditional legal skills, including sound judgment, problem-solving, advocacy, negotiation and client counseling, remain essential, and that lawyers need to know the law well enough to realize when AI is wrong. Shukla says someone asking about severance is often really asking whether they were treated fairly and what happens next, and that AI doesn't pick up on how they feel, only what they say. Gorodetsky says she would be cautious about calling any practice area AI-proof, because resilience depends heavily on the responsibilities within a role, and she contrasts a commercial lawyer negotiating a strategically important partnership with one primarily processing standardized agreements. She expects complex negotiations, investigations, disputes, board counseling and regulatory strategy to remain particularly dependent on lawyers, and says product counseling, privacy, cybersecurity and AI governance also present opportunities. Perlman says future lawyers must combine traditional expertise with the ability to deliver legal services more efficiently using AI, and that we need future lawyers to understand how to use AI to deliver services better, faster and cheaper.

Gorodetsky advises LL.M. graduates to develop substantive expertise, understand the industries they serve and seek practical experience under experienced lawyers, and says cross-border experience and language skills can be valuable for internationally trained lawyers when aligned with employers' needs. Shukla emphasizes learning the fundamentals before relying heavily on technology, saying that if you outsource your learning, you lose the ability to catch its mistakes. She recommends gaining courtroom, negotiation and client-facing experience early, becoming proficient at supervising AI tools and exploring fields where law and technology intersect. Shukla says your personality, communication skills and a reputation for good judgment are ultimately what get clients to hire you again. The article also links to related LLM GUIDE pieces, including one from June 23, 2026 on how law schools are teaching LL.M. students to work alongside AI and one from October 19, 2026, a student blog by Addys Rojas Villegas on a University of Houston LL.M. student's journey from Venezuela to the U.S.

Articles.Title: What Areas of Law Will Be Most AI-Resilient After Your LL.M.?

stories.Headline: Professor Hoang Van Kiem proposes a three-tiered model to develop talent in gifted schools in the AI era
stories.Summary:
Professor Hoang Van Kiem, former Chairman of the State Council for Professor Titles in Information Technology, wrote in Thanh Nien Newspaper that talent development in specialized and gifted schools needs to change in the age of AI. The article was published on 15/11/2026, in commemoration of the 30th anniversary of the High School for the Gifted, Vietnam National University, Ho Chi Minh City. For decades, specialized schools and gifted schools have contributed to training many scientists, mathematicians, engineers, artists, and others who have made significant contributions to society. The article appeared amid ongoing debates surrounding admissions and training in specialized schools. The piece was presented by Thanh Nien Newspaper and carried by Vietnam.vn.

The article says talent is the result of the interaction of individual potential and biological characteristics, family and social environment, quality of education and teachers, opportunities to access knowledge and technology, training, experience, and creativity, and motivation, passion, and perseverance. It proposes a three-tiered talent development model: Tier 1 foundational competencies including mathematics, language, science, technology, arts, physical education, emotional intelligence, and humanities. Tier 2 is development of specialized talents in mathematics, computer science, natural sciences, languages, arts, social sciences, and emerging fields. Tier 3 is interdisciplinary creativity with scientific research, technological innovation, AI projects, digital art, entrepreneurship, and practical problem-solving. It proposes a model of Gifted High School, Youth Research Center, Creative Space, and Open Academic Community, with five components.

The article says teachers need to discover hidden potential that grades don't reflect, ignite passion and a desire for exploration, and guide students to think independently without relying on AI. It says they should impart research experience and scientific standards and educate students on character, ethics, responsibility, and compassion. It says the philosophy should shift from selecting the elite to unleashing talent, from selecting gifted students, intensive training, student competitions, and achievement to discovering potential, unleashing abilities, research and innovation, talent development, and contribution to society. It says competitions and Olympiads still play an important role in identifying and nurturing exceptionally talented students but should not be the sole objective of gifted education. It says achievement is a milestone, not the ultimate goal of gifted education.

The article says a student who doesn't win an Olympic medal can still become an outstanding scientist, a technological innovator, a talented artist, or an innovative entrepreneur. It says a student who wins numerous awards also needs to continue developing independent thinking, creativity, and adaptability to new problems. It says a student who excels in mathematics shouldn't just study math but needs exposure to computer science, physics, music, art, data science, and practical applications. It says a student who excels in literature shouldn't be judged solely on writing ability but needs philosophical thinking, social observation skills, artistic creativity, and communication skills. It says specialized schools will have to compile statistics on what jobs their graduates are doing after graduation.

The article says the Imperial Academy, established in 1076, is a symbol of Vietnam's tradition of training talent for the nation. It says the modern system of specialized high schools in Vietnam mainly emerged in the 1960s, and specialized mathematics education began in 1965 with a specialized mathematics class at Hanoi University, the predecessor of the specialized school model at the University of Science, Vietnam National University, Hanoi. It says Hanoi ,  Amsterdam High School for the Gifted commenced its first academic year on September 5, 1985, formed by consolidating the specialized classes of several high schools in Hanoi. It says that on July 14, 1993, Deputy Minister of Education and Training Tran Chi Dao signed a decision to establish the specialized high school system for mathematics and computer science at the University of Ho Chi Minh City. It says that on July 4, 1996, Minister of Education and Training Tran Hong Quan signed Decision No. 2693/GD-ĐT establishing the High School for the Gifted, Vietnam National University Ho Chi Minh City.

The article says future gifted high schools should develop according to the model of Gifted High School, Youth Research Center, Creative Space, and Open Academic Community. It says connecting with universities and research institutes is a key advantage that should be strongly promoted at the High School for the Gifted under Vietnam National University Ho Chi Minh City, where students can receive guidance from university lecturers, scientists, and business experts and participate in seminars, research projects, and academic activities appropriate to their age. It says student laboratories should provide opportunities for research projects on AI, robotics, biology, materials, environment, energy, music, and digital art. It says the article also covers proposals for admission to specialized schools based on subject groups and subject combinations and proposed changes to the entrance exam for specialized 10th-grade classes. It leaves open what students, parents, and teachers say about those proposed changes.

Articles.Title: Talent development in specialized schools and gifted schools needs to change in the age of AI. - Vietnam.vn

stories.Headline: Burbank council bans generative AI art in city content after artists urge local work
stories.Summary:
The Burbank City Council adopted a ban on Tuesday night, November 10, 2026, that prohibits generative AI artwork in any public-facing content the city produces or displays, according to Hey SoCal. The move was brought forward by Councilwoman Nikki Perez, who said the council chose an outright prohibition over the professional standards that city staff had recommended. The decision followed more than an hour of deliberation and public comment, in which artists and residents argued that AI-generated imagery is built on stolen creative work. One speaker called AI art theft that is ugly, lazy and lame and urged the council to pay local artists instead, while another compared the practice to having a car stolen.

The ban applies to all content the city produces, while graphics shared from nonprofit partners and outside organizations will carry a tagline identifying the original source. The only carve-out allows staff to use generative AI as a very last resort in an emergency, such as when no graphic designer or cartographer is available. Staff had cautioned that a broad ban could restrict common AI-assisted editing tools already built into software such as Adobe Photoshop and complicate the sharing of third-party content. The council ultimately distinguished between AI-assisted tools embedded in everyday design software and generative AI art, which Perez described as the stolen content of creative people worldwide.

Perez told the council that saying the city is banning this speaks much louder than a softer standard would. Public Information Specialist Mariam Movsesian said the city does not use AI-generated art in graphics or social media, and that staff had recommended professional standards rather than a complete ban. Another speaker noted that Burbank is home to Disney Animation and other studios whose artists' work has been taken. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the adoption of the ban.

Articles.Title: Burbank council bans generative AI art in city’s published content - Hey SoCal. Change is our intention.

stories.Headline: UAE lawyer says companies face liability for harm from AI-generated advice under civil law
stories.Summary:
Under UAE law, liability for AI-generated advice or decisions that cause financial loss, legal violations or harm may be considered under general principles of civil liability, contractual obligations and any applicable sector-specific legislation, according to Ashish Mehta, founder and managing partner of Ashish Mehta & Associates, writing in Khaleej Times on 15 November 2026. The UAE Civil Transactions Law does not establish a separate liability regime specifically for AI-generated outputs or advice or work rendered on the basis of AI-generated advice, he wrote. Article 245(1) of Federal Decree-Law No. 25 of 2025 promulgating the Civil Transactions Law provides that, subject to special legislations, the chapter applies to liability arising from a harmful act committed by a natural or legal person. Article 246 provides that every act causing harm to another obligates its perpetrator to compensate for the damage, even if the perpetrator lacks discernment. Article 247 distinguishes harm caused directly, where a guarantee is due without any condition, from harm caused by causation, where no guarantee is due unless the perpetrator was a transgressor or acted intentionally, or the act led to the harm.

Liability may depend on the role each person played in the development, deployment or use of the AI system, the nature of the act or omission involved, and whether a sufficient connection can be established between that conduct and the damage suffered. Using AI as a tool would not by itself necessarily exclude liability on the part of the person or entity responsible for its use. A company may be liable where an AI system is used in its business operations and the resulting harm can be attributed to the company's acts or omissions, including inadequate assessment of the system, insufficient safeguards or a failure to appropriately monitor its use. Article 645 of the Civil Transactions Law defines a professional company as a company established by one or more persons licensed to practice a liberal profession, or thereby with others, whose purpose is to practice that profession, unless the law or the agreement provides otherwise. Article 651 provides that each partner is personally liable for their professional faults towards the professional company and the rest of the partners, and the professional company is liable for the faults of the partners vis-à-vis third parties.

Article 651 also provides that the professional company is liable for any act or conduct carried out by the manager or managers in the ordinary course of management, and for any act carried out by one of its employees or agents whenever such person has the authority to act on its behalf and the third party has relied on such authorization in dealing with it. Any provision in the articles of association of a professional company permitting approval of the exemption of any person from any personal liability borne thereby in their capacity as a current or former manager shall be void. Professional companies remain liable under UAE law for professional services they provide, regardless of whether rendered by a manager acting in the ordinary course of business or an authorised employee, and regardless of whether the service deliverables relied on advice generated by artificial intelligence. Such liability may not be expelled by the professional company's constitutional documents or other agreements. Article 3.2.1 of the AI Ethics: Principles and Guidelines (December 2022), issued by the UAE Ministry of State for Artificial Intelligence, Digital Economy and Remote Work Applications, provides that accountability for the outcomes of an AI system lies not with the system itself but is apportioned between those who design, develop and deploy it.

Article 3.2.2.1 of the AI Ethics Guidelines states that AI operators and AI developers should consider designating individuals to be responsible for investigating and rectifying the cause of loss or damage arising from the deployment of AI systems. Article 3.5.1 provides that AI developers should ensure AI systems will not cause any unintentional harm and adverse impacts. The AI Ethics Guidelines also provide procedures through which individuals affected by significant AI-assisted decisions may challenge those decisions and seek human review, but the Guidelines expressly describe themselves as non-binding and should be read as policy guidance rather than as a standalone basis for imposing legal liability. Where AI-generated advice or decisions by a company result in financial loss, legal violations or harm to an individual, the individual shall have a right of recourse against the company itself, and if the service was rendered by a partner, the partner remains personally liable to the company for any loss suffered as a result of such third-party claim or action. As to a manager who was not acting in the ordinary course of business or an unauthorised employee acting in bad faith, the company may subsequently take action against such partner, manager or employee, including termination of employment.

Article 614 clause 3 of the Civil Transactions Law provides that if the manager of the company exceeds the powers specified in the contract, he shall be liable for any damage that befalls the company as a result of such act. Clauses 2, 3, 4 and 9 of Article 44 of Decree Law No. 33 of 2021 on the Regulations of Employment Relations allow an employer to dismiss an employee without prior notice, after a written investigation and by a written and reasoned decision, in specified events. These include an employee committing an error resulting in gross material losses to the employer, or deliberately causing harm to the employer's property and admitting the same, provided the employer notifies the Ministry of Human Resources and Emiratisation within 7 working days of being aware of the occurrence. They also include violation of the establishment's bylaws on work and workers safety, where such instructions are in writing and posted in a visible place and the employee has been advised thereof, and failure to perform main duties under the employment contract despite a written investigation and two warnings of dismissal in case of recidivism. Clause 9 covers an employee abusing his position with the aim of obtaining personal gains and profits.

Any claims by a company against an AI developer shall be subject to the contractual terms governing their relations. The applicable provisions cited are Federal Decree-Law No. 25 of 2025 promulgating the Civil Transactions Law and the AI Ethics: Principles and Guidelines (December 2022). Ashish Mehta is qualified to practise law in Dubai, the United Kingdom and India, and full details of his firm are on www.amalawyers.com. Readers may e-mail their questions to news@khaleejtimes.com or send them to Legal View, Khaleej Times, PO Box 11243, Dubai. The article states that the information provided is intended for general guidance and does not constitute legal advice, and recommends seeking formal legal counsel.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: California education department urges teachers to responsibly incorporate AI as Thurmond warns against misuse
stories.Summary:
California's Department of Education encouraged teachers and school leaders to responsibly incorporate artificial intelligence into their classrooms, as schools continue to grapple with the technology's role, at a Monday summit hosted by the state education department. State Superintendent of Public Instruction Tony Thurmond told the summit that striking the balance of use versus abuse is the ultimate responsibility, and that the conversation must cover how to get all the main benefits and tools AI can provide. He said the technology should not be a reason that students stop thinking, stop writing or stop researching, and he noted that in some cases students have used it to circumvent learning. Educators and policymakers, he said, need to learn how to responsibly incorporate AI into their teaching to students' benefit.

During the summit, education technology leaders and school officials offered examples of how AI can support student learning and how districts can provide students with equitable access to AI tools. Casey Cuny, who was selected as the California Teacher of the Year in 2024 and is founder and CEO of the Whit.ai app, said his biggest worry is that schools will gatekeep their most vulnerable students from using the technology while kids in the suburbs master it. Thurmond, who will leave at the end of the year after serving two terms as state superintendent, said AI will never replace a teacher. The department has released guidance to schools on the safe and effective use of AI in classrooms, but he said state officials and school leaders must ensure the tools are not misused or abused.

Sonal Patel, the program director for digital learning at the San Bernardino County Superintendent of Schools, said some districts are already incorporating AI in K-12 classrooms, and at Fontana Unified School District students have used AI tools to support peer education in math. She said districts are in the process of having serious conversations about whether to keep Google AI tools accessible to students after the company announced last week that it would shut off access to its popular search feature if schools opt out of artificial intelligence. Patel said those conversations are happening through a data privacy lens, about whether districts should enable the tools under the new circumstances and how to ensure guided learning builds the student's thinking rather than simply delivering answers. The article, written by staff at the nonprofit newsroom EdSource, was republished by The Mendocino Voice in partnership with EdSource.

stories.Headline: AI drafts legal briefs but lawyers still hold responsibility for judgment
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence now drafts legal briefs and organizes case law in minutes. This technological shift occurred by November 15, 2026, according to Seoul Economic Daily. Junior lawyers previously spent entire nights reading records and revising drafts manually. Now, these colleagues receive completed drafts before their morning coffee even cools. The technology replaces the long hours once required for building basic legal skills.

The system can sort through tens of thousands of emails overnight without pay. It can also instantly pull together manuals for handling Fair Trade Commission inspections. In cartel cases, the first leniency applicant has its fine waived entirely. The second applicant to come forward receives a 50 percent reduction in fines. These specific rules mean a single order can change a company's fate.

Lee Chang-hoon is an attorney at the law firm Shin and Kim. He says that responsibility for brief contents cannot be handed to machines. Lee believes lawyers now sell professional judgment rather than just providing information. He notes that AI delivers wrong answers with composure and fabricates rulings. He argues that AI cannot take the blame for a lawyer's mistakes.

Some lawyers in the United States were sanctioned for citing invented case law. These fabricated rulings are described as plausible but are disasters for clients. Flustered employees may try to delete emails during on-site inspections by investigators. Commissioners at plenary hearings do not read AI prepared answers before asking questions. Clients are affected because they need advice on which options to choose.

Lawyers used to believe that working longer hours helped them build more skill. AI can now write opinion letters and prepare anticipated questions for hearings. However, it cannot stop an employee from deleting evidence during a raid. It cannot grasp the true intent of a commissioner's question during a hearing. AI cannot walk a chief executive through reputational damage or employee fallout.

Lawyers must still recommend decisions amid uncertainty and take responsibility for outcomes. They must guide executives on whether to rush into a leniency application now. The articles leave open whether the lawyer's job will disappear with late nights. They do not state if more lawyers will be sanctioned in America. The future of the profession depends on the value of human judgment.

Articles.Title: AI Can Draft Legal Briefs, But Lawyers Still Carry the Judgment - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Progress Software's Ed Keisling says AI token costs now come out of salaries and bonuses
stories.Summary:
Ed Keisling, chief AI officer at Progress Software, said in a November 15, 2026 CDOTrends article by Winston Thomas that the era of nearly free tokens ended as little as nine to 12 months earlier. He said that money must now come from somewhere, such as employee salaries, bonuses or travel. He described the gap between expectations and reality in AI deployment as far more complicated than executives expect. He compared it to his early career, when his team shipped finished Sun hardware and Oracle software stacks to banks instead of letting each bank install them. He said that work was much more difficult in practice than on paper.

Accenture surveyed 750 executives in 17 countries and found they expect per-token prices to fall 19% over two years while consumption grows 78%. GitHub moved every Copilot plan to token-based billing on June 1, 2026. Accenture found only about one dollar in five of token spend can be tied to a financial return. One in three organizations ran out of its annual token budget before year-end, and fewer than one in 12 use chargeback. By April 2026 Uber had used its full-year budget for AI coding tools and now limits each employee to USD1,500 a month in token spending per agentic coding tool.

Keisling said employees should see their own spend and managers their team's, with budget thresholds that force a conversation about whether work justifies the money. He said nothing should be deployed to a production or even test environment without cost controls in place. He said Progress wired cost telemetry into every agent before release and shut down internal agents after comparing spend with output, saying there was no ROI there. He called dumping everything into a growing context window probably the most expensive route and pointed to retrieval-augmented generation instead. He said getting data ready for a small language model takes months and that governance and observability tooling simply does not exist as a complete package.

The FinOps Foundation notes provider bills show spend by API key or project, not by business unit or cost center, and tooling around a production agent can make up 40% to 60% of feature spend. Gartner predicts companies will use small, task-specific models at least three times as much as general-purpose LLMs next year. IBM found high levels of shadow AI added USD670,000 to the average breach cost, and Ramp data reported by Axios showed 28% of corporate OpenAI chat spending in February flowed through personal consumer plans. Keisling said there is a good chance some data sent to frontier models ends up training them, while OpenAI states it does not train on API or enterprise data by default. Accenture's research suggests only about one-third of workloads must stay sovereign.

Progress describes itself as providing context and control for AI, including control over cost, and bought agentic RAG startup Nuclia in 2025. Progress sells agentic RAG as a service starting at USD700 a month. TypeSafe AI's Jev launched with USD5 in starter credit, which the company says buys about 120 million tokens. Keisling said newer small models are orders of magnitude cheaper than mid-tier ones, and he pins cheap models to routine tasks while saving frontier models for hard ones. He also points to a new class of decision models that classify and choose rather than write.

Keisling scores agents that act on four dials: the access the agent holds, the financial impact of its decisions, how fast a bad change can be reversed and the damage to reputation. He said companies should put a dollar on it and test the agent before it ships. He said what matters is how big a box you were able to put the agent in, in terms of tools, skills and budget. The article says most companies are still drawing theirs. The article ends by saying tokens got cheaper but ready did not.

stories.Headline: Nearly 70% of aides and lobbyists expect AI safety rules to pass in the 120th Congress
stories.Summary:
A Canvass survey published by Punchbowl News on November 15, 2026 found that nearly 70% of respondents expect artificial intelligence safety rules to pass in the next Congress, which will be the 120th. The survey combined senior congressional aides with leaders of the wider lobbying world, drawing on top Capitol Hill staff and K Street professionals. Those respondents see the next Congress as the time for action on artificial intelligence safety. The article presenting the survey was dated November 15, 2026, and appeared in Punchbowl News.

The survey result points to a shift in expectations for AI guardrails, with nearly 70% of those polled saying they view safety rules as likely to pass in the next Congress. The 120th Congress is the body the respondents identified as the one that would take up the issue. The article did not give a specific date for when a vote might occur or what the rules would contain. It also did not say how many people took part in the survey beyond describing them as senior congressional aides and leaders of the wider lobbying world.

Democrats have rallied behind the idea that artificial intelligence needs legal guardrails, according to the same article, but they are divided on how to tax the tech. That division is the only detail the article offered on the substance of the debate, and it did not say where Republicans stand. The article also linked to separate coverage on Florida asking a court to stop OpenAI development and on what the Trump-Xi meeting means for tech. No lawmaker or staffer was named as responsible for the push, and the article carried no direct comment from any official.

The article did not say what happens next beyond the survey finding, and it did not give a timeline for when AI safety legislation might be introduced or voted on. It presented the 120th Congress as the window respondents expect, without naming a committee, a sponsor or a draft bill. The piece was a preview of premium tech coverage, and the full story was available only to subscribers.

stories.Headline: Punjab bans camera-equipped smart glasses for 30 days from October 2026
stories.Summary:
Punjab province in Pakistan imposed a 30-day ban beginning in October 2026 on the use and sale of camera-equipped smart glasses with hidden recording ability, and the order also covers miniature cameras disguised as pens or keychains. Retailers cannot evade the ban by selling the affected devices online, and authorities said they received complaints of spying devices being used for illegal surveillance, harassment and blackmail. The articles do not name which models are included, and the ban is limited only to Punjab. No country has a permanent, outright ban on AI glasses, but courts, schools and other public places are increasingly restricting them for safety and privacy reasons.

New York has banned smart glasses with cameras, microphones or computers in all 1,240 state and local courts since July 20, 2026, and the devices must be turned over to uniformed court officers for safekeeping, so turning them off will not help. Prescription Ray-Ban Meta glasses are also prohibited, and court officials urge visitors to pack a traditional pair. England and Wales have banned the glasses in courts and tribunals, where security personnel can hold them until visitors leave, and Western Australia has banned them from public schools since October 12, 2026, for students, staff and visitors, with exemptions for approved medical, accessibility and educational reasons. Victoria has announced similar restrictions that take effect on January 27, 2027, and smart glasses are prohibited from SAT test sites even during breaks unless an accommodation is granted, with scores possibly canceled for violations.

Marine Corps policy at Camp Lejeune and other bases does not allow smart glasses, and Canterbury-Bankstown Council in Australia has banned them at its leisure and aquatic centers. UK cinemas are rolling out measures citing privacy and film piracy, and Royal Caribbean permits the glasses on board but prohibits their use in casinos, medical facilities or youth areas. Norway's government is considering temporary restrictions that could cover parks, beaches, shopping centers and gyms, though the proposals have not been enacted and officials have not settled on which types would be covered. That distinction matters because the Even Realities G2 has no camera, while Ray-Ban Meta and Oakley Meta glasses can take photos and videos.

In September 2026, Paris prosecutors opened investigations following complaints about women being filmed without consent using smart glasses, with the footage posted online, and prosecutors did not identify which brands were involved. Meta claims the white recording LED on its glasses lights up when photos or videos are taken and that the camera is disabled if the system detects tampering with the light. Ray-Ban's documentation states that some camera-based AI functions on newer models can work without the LED being activated, since they are not saving shareable photos or videos, which is not the same as taking a stealth video but means bystanders might not know when the camera is being used for AI. At Mark Zuckerberg's testimony in Los Angeles in February 2026, Judge Carolyn Kuhl warned that recording glasses must be taken off, though no recording of the proceedings was confirmed.

Articles.Title: Some Places Have Already Banned AI Glasses, And The List Just Keeps Growing - Engadget

Various governments and organizations restricted camera-equipped AI glasses in public places on November 15, 2026. These restrictions target devices that can record video or photos while looking like ordinary eyewear. Authorities implemented these rules to address growing concerns regarding safety and personal privacy. The measures range from temporary bans to specific venue restrictions across several different countries. No single country has yet imposed a permanent and outright ban on all AI glasses.

Punjab province in Pakistan started a 30-day ban in October 2026 on sales and use. This order covers smart glasses with hidden recording abilities and cameras disguised as pens or keychains. New York barred smart glasses from 1,240 state and local courts starting on July 20, 2026. Western Australia banned AI glasses in public schools on October 12, 2026, for students and staff. Norway is considering temporary restrictions for gyms, shopping centers, beaches, and public parks.
