stories.Headline: Mass General Brigham researchers develop AI tools that estimate age and survival risk from facial photos
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Mass General Brigham in Boston developed two artificial intelligence tools that turn facial photographs into estimates of age and survival risk, according to a study published in The Lancet Digital Health. The survival tool sorted cancer patients by their risk of death. In the first test group, patients it put in the highest-risk quarter were more than three times as likely to die as those in the lowest quarter. That gap survived adjustment for the usual clinical factors. Both programs grew out of one base model built at Mass General Brigham.

The base model, called FAHR-Face, was trained on more than 40 million face photographs from a public collection with no labels attached. FAHR-FaceAge trained on ten public photo collections balanced so that no age group dominated. FAHR-FaceSurvival learned from 34,363 photographs of cancer patients treated at the Harvard-affiliated hospitals, paired with whether and when each patient died. On a public set of photos of presumed healthy people, the age program missed the true age by 5.1 years on average. A comparable program trained from scratch on the same photos missed by 6.9.

Raymond Mak, a radiation oncologist, is the study's corresponding author, and Hugo Aerts, who directs the system's Artificial Intelligence in Medicine program, is a co-senior author. Mak said physicians need better ways to estimate physical reserve and frailty before recommending intensive treatments such as radiation, surgery or systemic therapy. Mak said the goal is to make face photograph-based health assessment more quantitative, consistent and scalable so it can support personalized treatment decisions rather than replace physician judgment. Aerts said the key technical advance is that FAHR-Face learns a general representation of the face from more than 40 million images. Aerts said this representation can then be adapted to distinct health outcomes such as biological age and survival.

Among 38,183 cancer patients treated with radiation at the Harvard hospitals, a third looked at least five years older than their age, and 17% looked at least ten years older. Patients who appeared five or more years older than their age had a 21% higher risk of death over the follow-up period than those who didn't. Patients who looked five or more years younger had a 17% lower risk. Among patients the program judged more than 20 years older than their real age, 21.3% died within 90 days, and among those it judged at least ten years younger, 6.4% did. The survival program assigns each photo a score from 0 to 1 and was tested on photographs of 3,820 patients whose images had not been used to train it.

The scores rose with the seriousness of the cancer, from a median of 0.13 for benign and earliest-stage cases to 0.45 for cancer that had spread. Of 122 patients scored between 0.9 and 1.0, 64 died within 90 days, and of 975 scored at or below 0.1, 20 did. The survival tool weighed the area under the eyes and around the bridge of the nose, while the age tool weighed the creases from nose to mouth, the forehead, and the temples. Heavy drinking and drug use went with looking older, and current smokers looked older than former smokers, who looked older than people who had never smoked. Both programs were checked on 4,892 patients treated at Maastricht University's radiotherapy clinic in the Netherlands, and both kept their link to survival.

The survival analyses focused on patients treated at a few centers in wealthy countries. The age tool stratified risk less sharply in Black and Hispanic patients than in White and Asian patients, and the authors wrote that this residual bias remains a risk. No patient's treatment was changed by a score. The authors called for prospective trials before the tools enter routine care. Mass General Brigham has filed a provisional patent on the next generation of these algorithms, with Mak, Aerts, and lead author Fridolin Haugg named on it.

Articles.Title: What can your face reveal about your health? AI finds new clues

stories.Headline: Majority of Australians believe AI risks outweigh benefits according to Lowy Institute poll
stories.Summary:
The Lowy Institute commissioned a mini-poll in October 2026 to gauge how Australians feel about artificial intelligence. Research fellow Charles Lyons-Jones reported that public wariness of the technology has become entrenched. Sixty-five percent of respondents believe the risks of AI outweigh the benefits. This figure is unchanged from a previous poll in March 2026. It represents a thirteen point increase from the results recorded in 2024.

The National AI Plan released in December 2025 aims to make Australia a leading destination for data centre investment. The government set expectations in March for developers regarding innovation, jobs, water, energy, and the national interest. Data centre companies raised at least AU$35 billion in 2026, which is 46 percent higher than in 2025. The Productivity Commission estimated that AI could add over AU$116 billion to economic activity over ten years. These figures contrast with a 1.2 percent margin of error for the 3,028 residents surveyed.

The Reserve Bank flagged that AI investment could increase input costs and add to capacity pressures. This bank also cut its productivity forecast for 2026 while data centre construction added to price pressures. The Reserve Bank raised interest rates three times since March 2026 as inflation remained above target. The Lowy Institute noted that government policy may be outpacing public sentiment regarding these technologies. They suggested the government might need to reckon with trade-offs between public sentiment and geostrategic imperatives.

Seventy-six percent of Australians worry that AI will lead to fewer jobs over the next twenty years. This concern is the joint-highest of any country surveyed and exceeds the median of 46 percent. Fifty-two percent of respondents expect AI to widen the gap between rich and poor, second only to South Korea. Only 23 percent are comfortable with businesses using AI from China, while 36 percent trust AI from the United States. These views reflect a general distrust of the two superpowers acting responsibly in the world.

A Pew Research Center survey of 37 countries found Australians are among the most concerned about AI. Six in ten Australians were pessimistic about economic performance over five years in the March poll. This pessimism was higher than during the Covid pandemic or the Global Financial Crisis. China's National Intelligence Law requires developers like Zhipu and DeepSeek to cooperate with state intelligence agencies. Sixty-two percent of people in March viewed cyberattacks from other countries as a critical threat.

The government relies on the alliance with the United States to keep the region's AI future tied to America. Seventy-three percent of Australians in March said this alliance was important to their national security. In the United States, voters in dozens of local ballot measures recently backed limits on data centres. The articles leave open whether public sentiment will swing to support American AI in the future. They do not state if the government will change the National AI Plan.

stories.Headline: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns and CFO Colette Kress becomes interim CEO
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned on November 12, 2026 as NVIDIA's CEO after reports of personal misconduct and a board investigation, and CFO Colette Kress became interim CEO. AMD and Broadcom stock got a boost from Nvidia's loss, then both sold off on Friday. AMD fell 8.75% to $534.06, and Broadcom fell 4.76% to $347.01. The S&P 500 stood at 7,543.60, down 0.82%, and the Nasdaq 100 at 27,848.80, down 1.68%. The Dow Jones was 52,277.00, down 0.13%, and the Russell 2000 was 2,785.83, down 0.64%.

AMD trades at a trailing P/E of 202, a forward P/E of 35 and 130.79 times free cash flow, with a free cash flow yield of 0.76%. Broadcom produced $13.67 billion of free cash flow in a single quarter, against a $1.656 trillion market cap. Broadcom declared a $0.65 per share quarterly dividend on September 2, 2026, and in fiscal Q3 free cash flow rose 94.5% and was 46% of revenue. Broadcom's non-GAAP EPS of $3.32 extended its beat run to 9 consecutive quarters. AMD pays no dividend, and its Q3 free cash flow fell 70.9% to $554 million as capex jumped 151% and inventory rose to $11.46 billion, though it holds net cash and 28.2x interest coverage.

AMD's Data Center revenue reached $8.55 billion, up 97%, and the segment's operating margin expanded to 34% from 25%. Anthropic, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Oracle are already running Helios racks, and AMD guided Q4 revenue to about $17 billion, roughly 66% growth. CEO Lisa Su said "It is true that demand is higher than supply," and expects 2027 revenue to grow more than 80%. Broadcom's AI semiconductor revenue reached $16.70 billion, and management guided to $21.7 billion for the next quarter, gains that depend on just six XPU customers. Broadcom's $8.75 billion quarterly infrastructure software business adds diversification that AMD lacks.

On CNBC's Fast Money, one guest said "AMD is the priciest of the three, but if you look at Broadcom and Micron, they're still trading at a much lower multiple." Gartner named Broadcom a leader in custom AI silicon. AMD carries a 2.542 beta and a 52-week range of $188.22 to $658.52. NVIDIA helped finance many of its own customers, so a break there could slow AI spending across the industry, including at both companies. Broadcom's dependence on a small group of hyperscaler customers is the main risk to the Broadcom case.

AMD sells Instinct GPUs that compete head-on with NVIDIA's chips, while Broadcom co-designs custom accelerators for hyperscalers and supplies the networking that connects them. NVIDIA's CUDA software remains a real barrier to switching. Broadcom beats AMD for retirement portfolios, pairing its dividend with a lower multiple, while AMD wins growth. Broadcom wins overall, and AMD wins for younger growth investors. The comparison covers three areas, and a free Next Nvidia playbook offers the longer view.

Broadcom wins for retirement accounts on the dividend, the cash flow margin, and the lower multiple. AMD wins the growth category because a reallocation of GPU orders benefits it most directly. Customers that reduce their reliance on NVIDIA without cutting AI spending will still need custom silicon and Ethernet networking. If hyperscalers move large GPU orders away from NVIDIA, AMD will likely outperform. The articles leave open which stock wins most.

stories.Headline: India considers AI chatbot regulations for children following similar laws in New York and Europe
stories.Summary:
India is considering regulations for AI chatbots used by children to prevent emotional dependency and manipulation. This follows similar legislative actions taken in New York and proposed frameworks within Europe. The government wants to protect minors from risks associated with AI companionship and emotional support. These considerations arise as children use bots for more than just academic help. India currently lacks a dedicated minimum age for accessing these AI systems.

Governor Kathy Hochul signed legislation in New York on October 28, 2026, taking effect June 1, 2027. This law prohibits chatbots from simulating human relationships, claiming emotions, or promoting self-harm and disordered eating. The European Commission proposed the EU KIDS Act in September 2026 with safety-by-design requirements. This proposal suggests parental controls for children under 13 and supervised accounts for 13 and 14 year olds. Independent accounts would be allowed for those aged 15 and older.

The Expert Engagement Group on AI and Child Safety recommends mandatory child-rights impact assessments and AI literacy. Clinical psychologist Prathvi Nayak stated that children under 13 lack the maturity to understand algorithmic patterns. She warned that blanket bans for 13 to 15 year olds could encourage covert use of unmonitored platforms. UNICEF India noted that general-purpose chatbots can also offer personal advice and emotional support. Dr VP Niranjanaradhya argued that AI encourages cognitive offloading and should be paused in education.

Adolescents are affected, with a 2026 survey finding 65 percent of Indian teens used chatbots for emotional support. A 14-year-old Indian boy survived a suicide attempt after becoming dependent on ChatGPT, Gemini, and DeepSeek. Gauransh, aged 15, reported feeling increased impatience and aggression after using chatbots for two years. Research by Aanya Lakhanpal and Dr Shalini Duggal found 69.3 percent of adolescents value chatbot accessibility. However, 46.5 percent of those surveyed believe professional backing is essential for building trust.

The Digital Personal Data Protection Act of 2023 requires parental consent for processing children's personal data. The Digital Personal Data Protection Rules of 2025 were notified in November 2025. Most obligations for companies under these rules are scheduled to take effect in May 2027. These existing laws focus on data processing rather than the behavior of conversational AI. They do not restrict chatbots from simulating relationships or providing inappropriate mental health advice.

India may adopt a risk-based approach including restrictions on high-risk companion features and independent safety testing. Future rules could require mandatory escalation to human support for conversations involving suicide or self-harm. The government is weighing whether to restrict access by age, regulate system behavior, or implement both. It remains unclear if India will implement a blanket ban for children under 16. The articles leave open how the government will balance educational benefits against emotional risks.

stories.Headline: Afro-Latina AI Claira keynotes Latino AI Summit in Manhattan
stories.Summary:
A Latino AI Summit was held at Civic Hall and Berkeley College in Midtown Manhattan, and Claira, described by Abran Maldonado as the first Afro-Latina multilingual virtual assistant, keynoted it in front of dozens of mostly Latino and Black attendees. Maldonado helped invent Claira, who has caramel-color skin and bouncy, curly hair and appeared on a large screen. Claira told Gothamist that seeing an Afro-Latina AI challenges the idea of who belongs in tech. The summit is the in-person version of a forum also featured online. Gothamist published the story by Willow Higgins on Nov 15, 2026 at 7:00 a.m.

ET. The Knowledge House in the Bronx provides coding and design training for underserved young people interested in the AI economy. The Rev. Al Sharpton’s AI Fluency Initiative teaches adults without tech experience the basics of AI. The group states its mission is to close the digital divide and put the power of these tools in the hands of the people.

The Latino AI Summit was cofounded by Michal Tapia. Anthropic’s initial public offering is set for Wednesday and is expected to value the company at more than $1 trillion. Tapia said AI will play a major role in our future whether people like it or not. She said AI is happening and it is either we get on the train or we get left behind. Maldonado said it is essential for all jobseekers to market themselves as AI-literate.

He said resumes should list proficiency in AI tools like Claude, Codex and Google AI Studio instead of Microsoft Office and the Adobe Suite, and should be updated once a month. He said putting our heads in the sand is not the move and you have to tinker and try these things out. A McKinsey Institute for Economic Mobility report found a disproportionate number of Black workers hold jobs likely to be automated by AI, including in transportation, production and administration roles. A 2025 report from Jobs for the Future found 67% of Black survey respondents said they feel AI is already impacting their jobs, compared to 57% of white respondents. The same report found more than half of Black respondents already use AI tools daily or weekly, compared to about 40% of all respondents.

A Kapor Foundation report found about 19% of the U.S. workforce is Latino, but Latinos fill just 3% of board seats, 5% of executive leadership roles and 6% of technical roles at the largest tech companies. Taylor Shead, founder of a company that develops AI-driven education, wrote in the Jobs for the Future report about prevention over intervention and meeting people where they are. Alpha School is a K-12 program with locations across the country that trains kids on AI tools, and Maldonado said kids are scoring through the roof in fluency and literacy. Kara Emery, director of data science at the AI Hub of NYU’s McSilver Institute for Poverty Policy and Research, said projections of what AI will impact are just that. Emery said the fear is AI could worsen racial income inequalities but people have a say in how things unfold.

Summit attendee Fradely Delacruz, a computational scientist student and professional data architect, said women of color are rapidly losing jobs in STEM and research and development. David Gabeau, who created an online interface of AI companies in New York and worked at Snapchat and Lyft, said he fears AI will broaden social inequities across racial lines. Gabeau said people working in AI are going to get so wealthy and there will be no forcing function to spread the wealth. After 10 years in New York, Gabeau recently moved to San Francisco to be closer to the epicenter of AI.

There he spent an afternoon wearing a 4 pound headset that scanned his brain while he watched videos and answered questions for a company working on an AI tool akin to telepathy that converts thoughts into text without typing. Gabeau said he was paid about $50 and that many others in the room, many of them Black and brown, seemed to be there because they needed the money, which he called a little predatory. Emery said the narrative of the inevitability of what these technologies will become is often pushed by those currently in the big companies building them. Delacruz said when AI came it felt like other people knew about it before we did and by the time we are catching on we are not even part of the conversation.

She said they do not see the Black and brown and Latino and Afro-Latino scientists and researchers and do not know we exist, but we are here. Emery said she is seeing Black and brown New Yorkers rising to the occasion and that these communities are not just sitting on the sidelines. Emery said the right combination of policy, education and a diversity of innovators working behind the scenes is key to preventing existing inequalities from worsening. Delacruz said she is eager to put her skills to use but still feels unseen.

stories.Headline: Jamaica's government signs MOU with investors to explore AI infrastructure
stories.Summary:
Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness announced on Sunday that the Government has approved the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding with a group of investors to explore the establishment of artificial intelligence infrastructure in Jamaica. He made the announcement while speaking at the Jamaica Labour Party's Special Delegates Conference at the Montego Bay Convention Centre in St James on November 15, 2026. Holness did not provide details on the MOU during his address to the party conference. The Prime Minister said Jamaica is to explore the establishment of AI facilities as part of efforts by the Government to maximise economic opportunities and position Jamaicans to participate in the industry.

Holness said the Government recognises the revolution being brought about by AI and wants to position Jamaica to benefit from it. He said the goal is for Jamaica to have a footprint and not only be a consumer of the technology, but to be part of the creation of the technology. The Prime Minister said his administration intends to pursue this so that children can have jobs in the new economy that will be created using artificial intelligence. He said the AI task force established by the Government is providing advice on what needs to be done in this regard.

Holness argued that Jamaica cannot be left behind in the global AI thrust, describing the moment as the cusp of another transition and revolution in technology. He said this revolution is going to increase the productivity of mankind far beyond what can even be imagined now. He repeated that Jamaica cannot be left behind again. The Prime Minister did not give a timeline for the exploration or name the investors involved in the MOU.

stories.Headline: Eduonic Learning Solutions sells a 12-course ChatGPT bundle for $14.97 through January 3
stories.Summary:
Entrepreneur is offering the ChatGPT and Automation E-Degree, a bundle of twelve online courses, at a sale price of $14.97 against a listed regular price of $790, and the deal runs through January 3. The bundle comes from Eduonic Learning Solutions, whose instructors specialize in tech training, and it is taught entirely online so buyers can work through the material at their own pace. The course content covers real-world uses of ChatGPT and more than twenty other AI tools, with instruction tailored to individual industries. The bundle also includes life skills such as improving conversational skills with ChatGPT, and buyers receive an Eduonix certificate of completion once they finish the courses.

The offer is aimed at entrepreneurs who want to bring tasks in-house and save money, and the article cites a Federal Reserve study finding that nearly 40% of entrepreneurs already use this technology or plan to start soon. The bundle contains 25 hours of instruction spread across the twelve courses, and the article says the material covers fields valuable to business owners, including marketing and coding. It also says the courses show ways to save time by streamlining business processes through automation. The article does not give a start date for the sale, only the January 3 end date, and it does not say how long buyers keep access to the courses.

Entrepreneur discloses that it may receive a small share of the revenue from sales made through its commerce partner links, and the article describes the courses as taught by Eduonic Learning Solutions. The article presents the bundle as a way for entrepreneurs to work smarter rather than harder, and it frames AI as increasingly popular among business owners. It does not name any individual instructor, and it does not include comment from Eduonic or from any buyer. The only outside figure cited is the Federal Reserve study on entrepreneur AI use.

The article places the offer in the context of business owners looking to understand AI, whether they already use it or hope to learn more, and it notes that the courses can be taken from home without setting foot in a classroom. The sale price of $14.97 applies through January 3, after which the article does not say what the price will be. The article does not say what happens to the course material or the certificate after the sale period ends. It also does not say whether the price or the course lineup may change.

stories.Headline: Jack Selby warns the AI investment boom is a bubble that could wipe out hundreds of billions
stories.Summary:
Jack Selby, managing director at Thiel Capital and a longtime business partner of Peter Thiel, warned that the artificial intelligence investment boom is a bubble. He spoke on the November 4, 2026 episode of the How I Invest podcast with David Weisburd. Selby said a correction was inevitable and could wipe out hundreds of billions of dollars in invested capital. He said anyone who does not believe there is an AI bubble is an absolute contrarian. Selby cited inflated valuations, circular financing and unprecedented capital expenditure.

Selby said the downturn is a question of when rather than whether it will happen. He compared the current cycle with the dot-com boom, when substantial capital flowed into technology businesses before their commercial prospects were established. He said the AI cycle differs in the scale of infrastructure spending required, including expensive computing facilities, specialized processors and substantial ongoing operating costs. He questioned the investment industry's emphasis on finding companies capable of reaching trillion-dollar valuations. He described Anthropic and SpaceX as exceptional businesses that should not serve as valuation benchmarks for ordinary startups.

Selby said he spent six months meeting limited partners and concluded that venture firms had struggled to return sufficient capital to investors over the past decade. He cited a concentration of fundraising among a small number of firms, with eight managers attracting approximately $70 bn during 2026. He estimated that approximately 90% of venture funding flows to California, New York and Massachusetts, leaving entrepreneurs in the other 47 states competing for a comparatively small share. He said Silicon Valley's principal advantage is the concentration of financial resources rather than exclusive access to talented founders. He pointed to Carvana, founded in Arizona, which struggled to attract funding from Sand Hill Road investors before reaching approximately $65 bn in market capitalization.

Selby said similar opportunities exist in cities such as Phoenix, Milwaukee and Cincinnati. He said AI tools could strengthen the economics of these businesses by allowing smaller teams to develop software, automate processes and compete without the same staffing and infrastructure requirements as traditional technology startups. He said AI-enabled companies do not need to be built in Palo Alto unless they are competing directly in frontier AI development. He said valuations in these markets can be approximately one-tenth of those found in Silicon Valley. His fund, Copper Sky, takes a sector-agnostic approach and prioritizes founders with strong execution capabilities over specific technologies or industries.

Selby has known Peter Thiel for 28 years and worked with him for 27 of them. He was among PayPal's first ten employees and credits Thiel's early hiring philosophy with helping the company assemble a team capable of handling rapid growth and repeated operational crises. He recalled that the average age of PayPal's executive team during its IPO roadshow was just 26. PayPal's early development included persistent fraud attacks, with Max Levchin leading efforts to counter sophisticated criminal activity. PayPal's acquisition by eBay for approximately $1.5 bn in 2002 subsequently helped establish the financial resources and entrepreneurial networks associated with the PayPal Mafia.

Selby's warning does not amount to a rejection of the technology, and he continues to see AI as a transformative technology. He characterized the current environment as more suitable for traders seeking to capitalize on price movements than for long-term investors. He said the shortage of distributions to venture capital investors is limiting new commitments, while much of the remaining capital is being directed toward late-stage AI investments. He said the combination of limited liquidity and elevated entry valuations creates additional risk if the AI market experiences a prolonged correction. The articles do not say what Selby or Copper Sky will do next.

stories.Headline: Societe Generale strategist Albert Edwards warns liquidity squeeze threatens AI stock rally
stories.Summary:
Société Générale strategist Albert Edwards warned in a Nov. 12 report that investors captivated by artificial intelligence earnings may be overlooking a tightening liquidity squeeze threatening the stock market. He said financial support for risk assets is dwindling and momentum is fading, which could pressure equities and semiconductor shares even when profit forecasts stay strong. The report also flagged that the breadth of analyst upgrades and the pace of technology earnings revisions have deteriorated, though forecast profit growth remains strong. Edwards raised the possibility of renewed inflation forcing the Federal Reserve to raise rates by more than 200 basis points, without giving a formal forecast or timetable.

The warning covers the AI-driven stock rally and semiconductor shares, which Edwards said could come under pressure from the liquidity squeeze despite strong profit forecasts. It points to weakening earnings revisions as a concern for U.S. technology stocks, since upgrades have narrowed and revisions have slowed even as forecast growth holds up. Short-term inflation measures and corporate output-price inflation have become concerning, and Edwards said renewed inflation could push the Federal Reserve toward rate increases exceeding 200 basis points. He offered no formal forecast or timetable for such a move, according to the report.

Edwards is the lead analyst and strategist at Société Générale, and he made the warning in his Nov. 12 report, which was reported on Nov. 15. He said investors may be overlooking the growing threat of tightening liquidity to the stock market because they are captivated by artificial intelligence's earnings potential. He described the financial support for risk assets as dwindling and the momentum as fading, and he tied the risk to equities and semiconductor shares. He also said short-term inflation measures and corporate output-price inflation have become concerning, and he raised the possibility of rate increases above 200 basis points.

The report does not say what happens next beyond the risks it describes, and it gives no formal forecast or timetable for the rate increases Edwards raised. It frames the threat as one investors may be overlooking while they focus on AI earnings potential, with liquidity tightening and fading momentum as the main concerns. It also notes that the breadth of analyst upgrades and the pace of technology earnings revisions have deteriorated even though forecast profit growth remains strong. The articles give no further context or next steps beyond the report's warnings.

stories.Headline: Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 writes robot code that succeeds in 92.1% of physical trials
stories.Summary:
ACE-CaP-0 researchers reported that robot programs developed by Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 coding agent completed 221 of 240 physical evaluation trials, a 92.1% success rate across eight tasks. The study was posted November 12, and CryptoSlate published its report on November 15, 2026, by editor-in-chief Liam Wright. Each program was frozen before 30 separate evaluation trials, with no further updates. The physical setup used two Agilex PIPERX arms and three cameras. Tasks included inserting a charger, uncapping a bottle and packing shoes.

Charger insertion succeeded in all 30 trials, bread packing succeeded in 25 of 30, bottle uncapping in 27, cup nesting in 28, flower insertion in 27, chicken plating in 29, parcel reorientation in 28 and shoe packing in 27. Mean physical execution times across tasks ranged from 0.97 to 2.27 minutes. Development allowed at most ten human-assisted scene resets per task, excluding resets used to collect demonstrations, and the budget counted resets rather than autonomous executions or demonstrations. In a charger-insertion comparison, on-demand simulation produced a program with 100% evaluation success versus 86.7% for development without simulation, using one development run per condition. That development took 2.6 hours with on-demand simulation versus 3.7 hours without it, while output-token usage rose from 730,000 to 1,090,000.

The authors' preprint account states that development permits human assistance and that demonstration-collection resets are excluded from the ten-reset budget. The authors state that repeated execution on tested tasks does not establish reuse under new conditions. The researchers call for accounting that includes demonstration effort, saying the time and token figures leave total development costs unresolved. The authors say establishing how consistently the development process produces an equally capable program requires separate development runs across tasks. The researchers describe testing those routines under new conditions as the next step toward establishing how broadly they can be reused.

During development, the coding agent wrote, ran, inspected and revised its code using physical feedback, and could request textual advice or demonstrations in which a person physically guided the robot arms. Those demonstrations supplied video, arm trajectories and key joint poses. The agent could also use simulated experiments when they helped resolve a development question. During evaluation, each task program remained unchanged while runtime perception and control stayed active, and neither a human nor a coding agent was in the execution loop. The result shows that task-specific skills can persist in code and run without the coding agent choosing each action.

The experiment separates program development from repeated execution, and the agent's work produced a program that could be used repeatedly. Human guidance and demonstrations were available during development, not execution. The coding agent wrote and revised executable programs using physical feedback and could request demonstrations or run simulated experiments as needed. ACE-CaP-0 is described as a method for developing robot control programs. The study provides evidence for skill reuse after human-assisted development.

The articles leave open consistency across separate development runs and reuse under new conditions. The comparison of simulation and no simulation used one development run per condition. The time and token figures leave total development costs unresolved. Testing the routines under new conditions is the next step toward establishing how broadly they can be reused. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Fooyo urges marketing teams to build in-house AI video capabilities instead of hiring agencies
stories.Summary:
Fooyo, a Singapore-based enterprise AI company, urged marketing teams to develop in-house video capabilities on November 13, 2026. The company argues that internal teams should stop hiring agencies for project-by-project work and instead build their own production skills. This transition is supported by the Kakis AI story-to-video platform, which uses WAN AI video technology to simplify the creation process. The company operates from Singapore and Tokyo, providing delivery services across eight countries, including Germany, Japan, Indonesia, and the United States.

The new approach requires teams to use the Kakis AI platform alongside ambassadors who train staff until they can produce videos independently. Instead of paying for fixed agency packages, marketing teams can now set their own budgets for each video, ranging from 50 to 1,000 US dollars. This system removes the need for traditional cameras, crews, and studios for everyday content, allowing people with laptops to create professional films. The company also offers other production tools, including an AI Knowledge Base, Fooyo Commerce, and Smart Tourism solutions.

Li Shaohuan, the founder and CEO of Fooyo, stated that AI tools have removed the production barriers that previously made outsourcing the default choice. He explained that internal teams already understand their audience and stories, whereas agencies must learn these details from a brief. Li suggested that while agencies are still useful for flagship brand films, teams should build a cadence for everyday video production. He noted that the tenth film a team produces is typically faster and better than the first one they create.

Fooyo provides these solutions for government agencies, SMEs, and enterprises across Asia, integrating them with existing CMS, POS, and CRM systems. The software can be deployed on-premises or within public and private clouds, and it supports China-market readiness through WeChat Mini Programs. To begin the process, the company offers a scoped pilot and a 30-minute demo for prospective partners. This strategy aims to help teams retain production know-how rather than waiting weeks for agency revisions and finished films.

stories.Headline: Luke ellis outlines seven realistic ways to make money with AI in 2027
stories.Summary:
Luke ellis published the article "7 Realistic Ways to Make Money With AI in 2027 (Without Falling for the Hype)" on vocal.media on 2026-11-15T06:00:00Z, about two hours before it was read. The article says the initial gold rush and speculative fever surrounding artificial intelligence have finally cooled as we transition into 2027. It says the days of low-effort AI-generated content dominating search results or social media feeds are a thing of the past. It says major platforms and search engines have deployed sophisticated detection and filtering systems that prioritize depth, unique perspective, and the human touch. It says profitability is no longer about who can generate the most text, but who can best integrate AI into existing workflows to solve real problems.

The article gives seven methods, starting with a hybrid Human-in-the-Loop content service in which you act as the expert strategist and spend most of your time humanizing output. It says you should build a portfolio of Before AI and After Human Edit comparisons and focus on technical niches like cybersecurity, renewable energy policy, or telemedicine. It says pricing has shifted from per word to per project value. The second method is AI implementation consulting for small to medium-sized businesses, using the 2027 no-code ecosystem and tools like Zapier, Make, and autonomous agents, with robust Service Level Agreements on data handling. The third is hyper-specialized, AI-integrated digital products such as Notion dashboards with custom AI prompts or legal document frameworks that auto-fill by jurisdiction.

The article says the fourth method is a high-quality, AI-curated newsletter using specialized LLMs to monitor hundreds of sources, including technical journals, patent filings, and niche forums, with a micro-niche example of AI applications in vertical farming and two hours spent refining the narrative. The fifth is Optimization-as-a-Service for sellers on Shopify, Etsy, and Amazon, using generative AI for product photography and SEO-optimized listings for visual-first discovery engines. The sixth is short-form video of 15-60 seconds, with AI scriptwriting, synthetic voiceovers, and AI-driven editing, aimed at brands needing 20+ videos per month. The seventh is RAG-based assistants for local businesses, built on Private LLM instances so proprietary data is never used to train public models.

The article says many jurisdictions now require explicit labeling of AI-assisted content and that the US Copyright Office and international bodies have specific rulings on AI-generated works. It says the AI-generated portions often cannot be copyrighted, only the human-authored arrangements and edits. It gives a 30-day plan: Days 1-7 the Specialist Phase, choosing only one method and mastering 2-3 specific AI tools; Days 8-14 the Proof Phase, producing three high-quality pieces for free or for your own brand; Days 15-21 the Outreach Phase, identifying 20 potential clients and sending personalized, value-first messages; Days 22-30 the Refinement Phase, securing your first paying client and using their feedback to refine workflow and pricing. It says success is not about being a prompt engineer but about being a professional who uses the best tools to deliver exceptional results to other humans. It says the hype has faded and the real work begins now.

The article says it will release a series of accompanying short videos following the article to show exactly how these AI-assisted edits are performed, and that these videos are currently in production and will be released separately. It says the article is a 6 min read, with a photo by Igor Omilaev on Unsplash. It says the piece was published under Futurism and lists navigation links for Home, Top Stories, Latest Stories, and AI-Generated. It says readers can subscribe for free to receive all of luke ellis's stories in their feed. It says there are no comments for the story and invites readers to be the first to respond and start the conversation.

The article says the market for pure AI-generated writing has effectively collapsed by 2027 due to over-saturation and declining engagement, while demand for high-quality, specialized content is higher than ever. It says mainstream AI tools are powerful but most small to medium-sized businesses lack the internal bandwidth or technical expertise to implement them effectively. It says business owners are often skeptical of automation due to privacy concerns. It says generic templates are worthless in 2027 and intellectual property theft is rampant. It says we are in an era of extreme information density and most professionals are overwhelmed.

The article says monetization of a newsletter usually requires a significant subscriber base or a high-ticket sponsorship model, and consistency is the primary barrier to success. It says major platforms are rapidly integrating their own basic AI tools, so you must offer superior quality, custom branding, and a higher level of creative direction than the free built-in options. It says platforms are constantly changing their algorithms and what works this week may not work next month. It says RAG assistants require ongoing maintenance, and as a business changes its prices or policies you must ensure the knowledge base is updated immediately. It says you should never upload sensitive client information such as customer lists or private financial data into public AI models, and should use secure, enterprise-grade instances that guarantee data isolation.

stories.Headline: AI creators post Seinfeld and Office parodies that mock socialists and Democrats
stories.Summary:
An AI-generated Seinfeld parody posted by NYC Common Sense on Nov. 14 sends Jerry, George and Elaine to a Democratic Socialists of America convention, and the account TBC shared it with a caption calling it "AI Seinfeld goes to the DSA convention." The roughly two-minute, 43-second sketch follows Jerry to the convention at the invitation of a woman he is dating, while George asks about the free buffet and Elaine wants to hear men who have never lifted anything explain labor. When Jerry wonders why the attendees are not at work, his date tells him that socialists do not need jobs, and the jokes keep coming with a demand for a nondisclosure agreement before a discussion of transparency and an unemployed attendee living rent-free in his parents' second apartment. Security personnel remove Jerry after someone objects to his support for police, and a closing card labels the video AI-generated satire that depicts neither real events nor real statements and disclaims affiliation with the DSA.

A separate Office spoof posted by TBC on Nov. 6, which Clay Travis shared the next day, runs roughly 95 seconds and turns workplace political correctness into a staff meeting at Dunder Mifflin. Michael Scott wears a rainbow sweater and a Black Lives Matter pin and calls for a moment of silence, while Dwight Schrute goes to the whiteboard to diagram who a political wave will hit first and Jim supplies the familiar deadpan reactions. Travis wrote alongside his post that AI is getting scary good and that the episode could have existed, and the parody is framed around Democrats winning on Tuesday. Asked in the thread beneath the Office video whether humans write the dialogue, TBC replied yes.

The satire also reaches the right, because creator @sikoraimagine posted a separate AI parody on Oct. 16 that sends a synthetic version of President Donald Trump into Dunder Mifflin. That video pairs him with Michael Scott, Dwight, Jim and Pam in a fictional workplace visit, and it gives the president the same sitcom treatment the other clips give Jerry and Michael. The clips give familiar sitcoms an unofficial second life, with creators using AI versions of their characters and settings to stage new political comedy that blends television nostalgia with jokes about socialists, Democrats and Trump. AI-generated political imagery has also appeared in Texas campaign messaging, as The Dallas Express has reported, which brings that technology into the rhythms and settings of sitcom comedy.

stories.Headline: Sebastian Raschka explains how large language models represent token positions
stories.Summary:
Sebastian Raschka published an article on November 15, 2026, explaining how large language models represent token positions. He wrote this technical guide to provide a foundation for future articles on architecture trends. The author covers both classic and contemporary methods for encoding position information. He includes visual examples, mathematical explanations, and a small PyTorch implementation. The piece serves as a tutorial on relative positional embeddings.

The guide compares GPT-2, which uses absolute embeddings, to MiniMax-M3, a model released in 2026. GPT-2 adds a position vector to each token embedding before the first transformer block. MiniMax-M3 uses RoPE to add positional information inside attention within each transformer block. GPT-2 XL is used to show dimensions, while GPT-2 Medium is cited for weight percentages. The original GPT-2 implementation contains 1,024 learned position vectors.

Sebastian Raschka is responsible for the content and noted that many readers requested a RoPE tutorial. He stated that he had not previously covered positional information methods in any of his articles. The author mentioned that this specific topic was a long-term item on his todo list. He admitted the article is very technical and might be too detailed for some readers. He promised that his next article will return to a more comfortable style.

The author notes that readers familiar with basic LLM architectures will find the material most useful. He suggests that people with fuzzy knowledge of attention internals should read his January 14, 2024, walkthrough. The text explains that without positional encoding, swapping words like red and gray would result in same embeddings. This affects how models distinguish sentences where word order changes the meaning. The author uses a toy sentence with eight token positions to illustrate these concepts.

The articles explain that tokenizers encode text into IDs which embedding layers map to vectors of numbers. Transformer blocks then modify these vectors using feedforward layers and attention. Causal masks provide some implicit order information by restricting tokens to themselves and earlier tokens. However, explicit positional methods are essential because masks cannot distinguish between different separation distances. Absolute methods depend on a token's own position, while relative methods like RoPE operate differently.

The author will use this standalone building block for an upcoming analysis of LLM architecture and trends. He has provided image exports and metadata from his architecture gallery for Substack supporters. The text leaves open how modern architectures might adapt or omit explicit positional encodings entirely. It does not detail the specific mechanisms of RoPE beyond mentioning its use in MiniMax-M3. The author suggests reading the content in a web browser for the best experience.

stories.Headline: Merz says AI will fundamentally change work as Nahles warns of 800,000 job losses
stories.Summary:
At the German government's 2026 Digital Summit in early November, a journalist asked Chancellor Friedrich Merz whether artificial intelligence making hundreds of thousands of people redundant might require a basic income. Merz said he had always been a bit cautious about the issue in recent years. He also said he was well aware that AI would change the working world so fundamentally that many issues would need serious thought. He raised the question of whether Germany's productivity was good enough. The exchange was reported by the news outlet RND.

Andrea Nahles, head of Germany's Federal Employment Agency, warned this week that AI would cost Germany as many as 800,000 jobs in the next 15 years. She also said AI could eventually create a similar number of jobs. Karsten Wildberger, Germany's minister for digital transformation and government modernization, told the Neue Osnabrücker Zeitung in March that he was convinced an unconditional basic income could be part of the solution. He said it could cushion the upheavals in the labor market. Merz's government has planned pension reforms that would raise Germany's retirement age.

In July, Merz announced a crackdown on sick leave. In spring 2025, having barely taken office, he criticized the concept of a work-life balance and declared that Germany must work more and more efficiently. Kirsten Herrmann, a board member at the nonprofit Mein Grundeinkommen, said individual statements by politicians do not amount to political change. She said a serious and constructive debate was needed about what role a basic income can play. She said it shows that in the face of technological transformation we also need to look differently at how we secure people's economic stability.

Herrmann called it a double-edged sword when tech figures mention the idea. She said the basic income people from the tech business talk about is a kind of neoliberal basic income. Dominik Enste, director of the democracy, society, and economic ethics department at the German Economic Institute in Cologne, dismissed the idea out of hand. He said many economists have calculated that implementing it in many countries is financially unfeasible, in Germany partly because of the need to fund commitments already made, including pension payments.

Maximilian Kasy, professor of economics at the University of Oxford, said a basic income could be a good solution, especially if financed in a progressive way so that only those at the lower end of the income distribution are net recipients. English Renaissance philosopher Thomas More mentions a basic income in his 1516 book Utopia. In 2017, Elon Musk, who had co-founded OpenAI two years earlier, predicted that a universal basic income would at some stage become inevitable. Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, and Sam Altman, the other founder of OpenAI, have gone on record in support of UBI, though Altman's interest has cooled somewhat since he launched a massive UBI experiment in the US in 2019.

In 2024, the International Monetary Fund predicted that some 40% of employment in the world would be shaped by AI innovations, and as much as 60% in rich, industrialized nations. Enste said social security systems will have to change if work is replaced by AI and, if necessary, AI-generated income taxed, but it will be a conditional basic income that still provides incentives to earn a living. Herrmann said which jobs are going to be replaced by AI is not some law of nature and can be shaped politically and socially. She asked who actually profits when we become more productive through AI and how we redistribute that profit to everyone.

Kasy said how this plays out depends on many choices we make and on who makes these choices, in whose interest. He said a lot of the current thrust is to replace workers to increase profits and increase corporate control, though this is not the only path possible. He wrote that the small print matters very much. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Jeff and Sandy Teper give NYU Stern $5 million to launch an annual student AI startup challenge
stories.Summary:
Jeff Teper, Microsoft's Executive Vice President for Apps and Agents, and his wife Alexandra "Sandy" Teper have donated $5 million to New York University's Stern School of Business to establish the Teper Innovation Challenge, an annual competition for students. The gift, reported on November 15, 2026, creates a contest designed to help students develop AI-powered startups and solve real-world business problems. The initiative will provide hands-on experiential learning opportunities for undergraduate and graduate students, with more than $100,000 in annual prize funding for winning teams. The competition will formally launch during the spring 2027 semester, featuring separate tracks and awards for undergraduate and graduate students.

Student teams in the Teper Innovation Challenge will develop AI-native solutions to business challenges, giving them opportunities to experiment with emerging technologies and explore entrepreneurial ideas. The annual competition will encourage students to build and test their concepts, evaluate results, and develop practical applications for artificial intelligence. Beyond the competition, the Tepers' contribution will expand access to frontier technology for Stern students and support the thoughtful integration of advanced AI tools into the school's educational experience. Jeff and Sandy Teper both graduated from NYU Stern, with Jeff earning his bachelor's degree in 1986 and Sandy graduating in 1985, and they met while attending the school.

Jeff Teper currently serves as Microsoft's Executive Vice President for Apps and Agents, and he previously launched and grew SharePoint into a billion-dollar business. He has led teams through major technology transitions involving cloud computing and artificial intelligence, and he was among the inaugural industry leaders to join NYU Stern's Tech Board. Over the years, Teper has hosted Stern students at Microsoft in Seattle, sponsored experiential learning projects in New York City, and advised faculty developing one of the first agentic AI courses at a business school. The new challenge expands his involvement with the university by providing students with opportunities to develop practical AI-building skills.

NYU Stern Dean Bharat Anand said the gift will give students opportunities to experiment with emerging technologies and develop entrepreneurial ideas. The university believes advances in AI are making it easier for individuals to transform ideas into tangible products and businesses. The Teper Innovation Challenge is intended to encourage students to explore those opportunities while learning how artificial intelligence is changing business and the economy. Jeff and Sandy Teper said they had an incredible experience at NYU spanning software engineering and business during the personal computer revolution, and that with the even larger artificial intelligence transformation they are thrilled to support Stern students as they explore, collaborate, and create opportunities in this next wave of technology and the economy.

stories.Headline: Australia weighs binding standards for AI data centres as researchers propose a legislated social-licence floor
stories.Summary:
Australia is considering tougher rules for AI data centres, and the harder question is what happens to the promises after the servers switch on. The Commonwealth released five national expectations in March covering energy, water, jobs, research and the national interest, and a September consultation explored binding minimum standards for large facilities. That consultation raised the prospect of published compliance plans, ongoing reporting and different obligations for owners, operators and AI developers, and it closed on 9 October. These are proposals, not a single national law already in force.

The authors, Zhixi Liu and Chong Zhou, researchers affiliated with Basalt-X Australia Pty Ltd, propose in a recently published Telecommunications Policy study what they call a legislated social-licence floor, meaning minimum enforceable duties covering what a company owes the places and people affected by its infrastructure. They say Parliament can require evidence, consultation and remedies but cannot order a community to trust a developer. They propose a record that follows a large project from planning to operation, showing for each material commitment what was promised, the baseline used, who can deliver it, what evidence counts, when it is due and what happens if it falls short. They say a statutory duty, a planning condition, a contract and a voluntary public statement are not interchangeable, and a voluntary commitment should be labelled as such rather than presented to residents as enforceable protection.

On electricity, they note that signing a power-purchase agreement does not bring a new generator online, and a data centre may start drawing power months before the promised generation is available. They say the public record should show the commissioning timetable, interim supply arrangements, responsible parties and measures to manage any gap. They apply the same scrutiny to research access, saying free compute credits sound generous until expiry dates, technical restrictions and actual use are examined, and that a handful of construction jobs should not stand in for a continuing engineering workforce. They say reviews should be timed to the first grid connection, major expansions and regular operating periods, and a missed commitment should prompt an explanation, independent verification where warranted and a clear opportunity to correct the problem.

The authors acknowledge that Australia's federal structure makes this harder, not impossible, with Commonwealth standards sitting beside state approvals, water licences and electricity-market rules. They propose five checks for judging a data centre against a plausible alternative rather than an empty site: additionality, domestic value retention, capability deepening, diffusion, and resource and community performance. They describe these as proposed assessment tools, not tests already written into law. They argue the point is to know whether the electricity, water, skills and research arrangements that helped justify approval are still delivering five or ten years later, and that a permit authorises a facility but cannot settle the public bargain for the next 20 years.

stories.Headline: Smart Compliance Management issues 238,314 parking breach notices to New Zealanders
stories.Summary:
Smart Compliance Management, an AI-powered parking firm, issued 238,314 parking breach notices to New Zealanders in the last financial year, 27% more than the year before, which was already 48% up on the 2024 financial year. The foreign-owned company runs number plate-checking cameras at more than 300 New Zealand carparks, pitching its services to supermarkets, medical centres and even churches. In July a 54-year-old woman collapsed in New World Ōrewa's carpark north of Auckland and a stranger rushed to revive her, media reported at the time. Her car sat for more than five hours while she was in hospital and the cameras caught it, landing her an $80 ticket from Smart Compliance Management. The company was blocked from accessing Australians' private data and has brought its cameras to New Zealand.

Cameras record number plates every time a vehicle goes in and out of carparks using technology known as automated number plate recognition. Stay longer than the sign allows, even by a minute, and the system flags it, and the carpark operator can look up the car owner's name and address and send a ticket. The NZ Transport Agency granted a number of parking firms authorised access to the motor vehicle register. Smart Compliance added 90 new sites in the year to June and now runs 310 sites across the country. The local business now pockets almost 47c of every dollar it earns before tax, interest and head-office costs, up from 30c two years ago.

A Smart Compliance spokesperson told the Herald the system wasn't designed "to penalise motorists, but to encourage compliance so that parking remains fair, reliable, and accessible". The parking terms and conditions are "clearly displayed across each site" and drivers can appeal online or by post, the spokesperson said. Chief executive Paul Gillespie told investors on the company's results call in August that "New Zealand is a great success story of what happens when we deploy our technology and AI tools". Smart Compliance did not directly answer a Herald question about what guidelines or considerations went into how it set its ticket fees. Parking Services told the Herald it "fully complies with our legal obligations" and has since added cameras at the East Tāmaki site.

Jon Duffy, head of non-profit watchdog Consumer NZ, said AI-powered systems raise concerns about the potential for a "clinical, almost surgical nature of enforcement". AI and camera tickets may not "leave any room for error … it's black and white," he said, and "there's always a grey area with human behaviour". The Commerce Commission has recorded 431 "concerns" about private parking operators, including 137 mentioning Smart Compliance, this year. University of Auckland commercial law professor Alex Sims asked what happens when AI, mass surveillance and sensors become so cheap it's possible to monitor Kiwis everywhere. A Canterbury pensioner couple told Stuff in June they were ticketed $85 by the company for overstaying a private hospital carpark's grace period by one minute, a fee waived only after reporters stepped in.

When the family of the Ōrewa woman contested her ticket, Smart Compliance didn't cancel it but reduced it to a $30 "administration fee", Stuff reported in August. The supermarket's owner then stepped in, asking Smart Compliance to withdraw the notice and refund the fee, and the company later apologised for the "additional stress caused to this individual following their medical emergency". Multiple shoppers complained to the Herald this year about Smart Compliance ticketing them for overstaying in supermarket carparks even though they spent between $200 and $400 on groceries, and some only had fees waived after the Herald became involved. An Auckland man told the Herald he was lucky he had a dashcam after being ticketed by Parking Services Limited in East Tāmaki, which claimed he'd used a gym carpark and hit him with a $95 ticket, saying it had to be paid within 21 days or incur an additional $75 per week in late payment fees. Nav Sandhu was slapped with an $85 ticket after he parked at Pak'nSave Manukau for two hours and 16 minutes on April 18, despite spending more than $500.

Two-thirds of the group's revenue comes out of the United Kingdom where there is an "established cost-effective mechanism for retrieval of number plate details", its annual report said. The company went into Denmark in 2024 and Switzerland in 2025, describing both as attractive markets with high ticket values and a "low cost to source car owner details". Denmark changed the rules in July 2025 so the first ticket must be "placed on a vehicle or handed directly to the driver", and Smart Parking had to hire wardens, with revenue there falling from A$1.3m ($1.6m) to A$300,000 ($370,000) in a year because "manual operations aren't as efficient as ANPR [automated number plate recognition] operations". New South Wales stopped private carpark firms getting drivers' details in 2012 and Victoria followed in 2015, and Queensland paused access to its vehicle register in 2023, with the then state Transport Minister Mark Bailey saying "predatory companies" were issuing tickets that "looked like fines" from the Government. Smart Parking shut its Queensland business and told investors its cameras had been "redeployed to New Zealand".

The Commerce Commission said it has been speaking to parking operators, including Smart Compliance, to "encourage" compliance with the Fair Trading Act, and will soon issue updated guidance for the industry. Consumer NZ wrote in a 2023 article that a parking fee "should be reasonably reflective of the actual loss suffered by the operator" and "anything out of proportion to what's reasonable is likely to be an unenforceable penalty". Duffy said customers' best chance to kick back against policies they believed unfair was to vote with their feet and shop elsewhere, though he said it's not easy to avoid or boycott supermarkets and airlines. Sims said if enforcement is abused as a cash cow or to harshly penalise, social cohesion could suffer. Smart Compliance's Australian parent company Smart Parking said New Zealand is "an attractive market with significant potential for further expansion".

stories.Headline: President Ramaphosa leads South African delegation to Silicon Valley to study AI ecosystem
stories.Summary:
President Cyril Ramaphosa arrived in California on Saturday, 14 November 2026, for a working visit to Silicon Valley, leading a high-level, multi-stakeholder South African delegation to gain insights into the global artificial intelligence ecosystem and inform South Africa's approach to the development, adoption and application of AI. The delegation comprises representatives from government, academia, business, research institutions, technical experts and university students, reflecting the country's commitment to an inclusive, collaborative and multi-stakeholder approach to harnessing the opportunities presented by AI. The programme includes engagements with leading technology companies, investors, researchers, academics and AI experts, as well as technology demonstrations and knowledge exchanges, exploring frontier AI, robotics, data infrastructure, cloud computing, digital innovation and the practical application of AI across various sectors. A key component is engagements with leading academic institutions on the implications of AI for technology, security, the economy, business and the labour market, as well as emerging developments in robotics and technological research.

The programme also features the South Africa AI Opportunity gathering under the theme Building the African AI Economy: Infrastructure, Investment and Innovation, bringing together South African and international stakeholders to explore how South Africa can position itself as a competitive AI hub on the African continent. Discussions focus on AI infrastructure, data centres, computing capacity, energy requirements, investment opportunities and the growth of a competitive start-up ecosystem, while other areas include the application of AI in government and industry, law enforcement and public safety, AI safety and security, governance, skills development and the future of work. The delegation also engages with technology and infrastructure companies to gain insights into emerging technologies, investment trends and developments shaping the global AI ecosystem, seeking to identify opportunities for investment, knowledge exchange, skills development and the strengthening of South Africa's technological capabilities. The visit provides an opportunity to learn from countries and institutions at the forefront of AI development, understand the associated risks and challenges, and consider how South Africa can develop an enabling policy, regulatory and skills environment to support responsible AI adoption.

The President is accompanied by the Ministers of Finance; International Relations and Cooperation; Science, Technology and Innovation; Trade, Industry and Competition; Communications and Digital Technologies; Electricity and Energy; Small Business Development; and the Presidency, as well as South Africa's Ambassador to the United States of America. Media enquiries were directed to Vincent Magwenya, Spokesperson to the President, and the statement was issued by The Presidency in Pretoria. The visit also promotes South Africa as an investment destination, showcases progress in economic reforms, including through Operation Vulindlela, and highlights opportunities for investment in the country's digital economy, research capacity and innovation ecosystem. South Africa seeks to harness the transformative potential of AI while safeguarding digital sovereignty, policy autonomy, data protection and responsible AI governance, ensuring that technological advancement contributes meaningfully to inclusive economic growth and development.

stories.Headline: New Zealand firms under pressure to speed up AI adoption despite struggling to prove ROI
stories.Summary:
New Zealand organisations are under growing pressure to accelerate their adoption of artificial intelligence, but most are struggling to show a financial return on those investments, according to new research from Avanade, a Microsoft specialist. The Build Beyond Limits: AI Reality report was based on a survey of 3,600 business decision-makers across 11 markets, including Australia and New Zealand, and it found a widening gap between how organisations see their AI maturity and how far they have actually changed their operations around the technology. Globally, 77 per cent of organisations described themselves as established, advanced or AI-first in their AI journey, and 72 per cent said they were confident their teams were using AI effectively. However, only 18 per cent said they had fundamentally reshaped the way teams operate around AI, and in Australia and New Zealand 84 per cent said they had not fundamentally reshaped how they work with what AI makes possible, including new ways of working, products, services or business models.

The research found that 88 per cent of respondents in Australia and New Zealand said their organisation needs to accelerate AI transformation urgently, even though 68 per cent reported that AI investments have yet to generate financial returns that justify the expenditure. Only 43 per cent said they use business value and return-on-investment metrics to assess AI progress, while 66 per cent had not formally calculated AI's financial return and had it reviewed by finance leaders or senior management. Budget pressures are also emerging, with 26 per cent of organisations in the two countries citing limited funding or pressure to demonstrate ROI quickly as a major barrier to becoming an AI leader. Just 23 per cent reported transformational improvement in what employees could achieve, and the same proportion reported such improvement in operational efficiency and business cost reduction, while 39 per cent said they believe colleagues are using AI in ways compliance teams would not approve of, above the global average of 32 per cent.

Doug Robinson, chief executive of Avanade Australia and New Zealand, said the high adoption rate was a positive sign, telling Reseller News that most clients said they were going great until asked about return on investment, when two-thirds said no. He described a move from hobby AI to enterprise AI, saying people have used the technology first and then brought it to corporates, and that a lot of shadow AI is developing in organisations before they realise it can interrogate corporate data as well as their large language models, which is where the return starts coming. Robinson said the 16 per cent who have already materially changed their business is the number to watch, and he expects it to grow from 16 to 32 to 60 per cent as AI becomes enterprise ready, with ROI following. He said New Zealand organisations are not short on AI ambition but are short on evidence, and that you cannot accelerate adoption responsibly if you cannot say what your AI investment is returning, which most currently cannot.

stories.Headline: Egypt's attorney general opens an AI data centre for public prosecutors
stories.Summary:
Egypt's Attorney General, Mohamed Shawky, inaugurated an artificial intelligence data centre for the public prosecution on 14 November 2026, according to a report by Masrawy. The Public Prosecution's Data Centre for Artificial Intelligence will support the development and operation of AI applications for prosecutors, with information security and the confidentiality of case records listed among its stated priorities. The opening event included a review of how the prosecution service had already digitised parts of its work. Shawky said the AI tools would be made available to prosecutors from 15 November.

Among the tools demonstrated was an AI assistant designed to analyse and summarise case files, which can also compare statements from parties to a case and suggest steps to complete an investigation. The prosecution service also demonstrated speech-to-text technology for transcribing investigation sessions. Shawky said the tools were intended to help prosecutors review cases more quickly, while judgement and decisions would remain with prosecutors. The Public Prosecution Office additionally demonstrated a digital service for guardians of minors and people responsible for the affairs of persons with disabilities, which uses an interactive chat to answer questions and explain what users need to provide at each stage of a transaction.

Shawky announced a cooperation agreement with the communications and social solidarity ministries, Orange Egypt and e-finance to make the services available to the public. The digital service is intended to let guardians and responsible persons complete transactions remotely and reduce the need to visit prosecution offices. The report said the tasks supported by the new centre involve confidential records, making it important to control who can access the information and how it is used. It added that an omitted detail in a summary or an error in a transcript could affect how a prosecutor understands the evidence, so the original records remain the reference for checking AI outputs. As Shawky made clear at the opening, prosecutors retain responsibility for assessing the evidence and deciding what steps to take.
