stories.Headline: IIIT-B to showcase AI, DPI innovations at Bengaluru Tech Summit
stories.Summary:
The International Institute of Information Technology-Bangalore will showcase its research in artificial intelligence, digital public infrastructure, healthcare, telecommunications and smart manufacturing at the Bengaluru Tech Summit 2026, which runs from Tuesday to Thursday. The institute will present projects ranging from digital identity systems used around the world to AI-based tools for healthcare monitoring, smart manufacturing and autonomous vehicles. It will also highlight its work on AI skilling and technology startups during the three-day event. The summit display brings together several strands of the institute's research under one roof.

The institute will showcase five digital public infrastructure initiatives, namely MOSIP, OpenG2P, CDPI, COSS and INJI, which together support more than 45 countries. MOSIP helps countries build national digital identity systems and is being rolled out in more than 30 nations, while OpenG2P assists governments in providing welfare benefits. CDPI and COSS support countries in developing digital public infrastructure, and INJI provides an open-source platform to issue, store and verify digital credentials. Healthcare research from the institute's Electronics and Health Research Centre will cover public health, surgery, assistive devices, self-care tools and Tele-MANAS. AI-based tools for remote health monitoring will be on display, including projects to predict sepsis risk, FatigueShield for fatigue and heat-stress forecasting, and ArogyaSense for identifying clinically relevant health information.

The IIIT-B COMET Foundation will showcase a prototype of Reconfigurable Intelligent Surfaces, a technology that uses electronically controlled surfaces to direct wireless signals, reduce interference and improve network coverage. The technology is particularly useful indoors and in private 5G networks, and the project was developed with support from the institute's Technology Innovation Hub under the Department of Science and Technology's NM-ICPS programme. The Karnataka AI Hub, supported by the State government and anchored at IIIT-B, will showcase initiatives to build AI capabilities for students, professionals, researchers and entrepreneurs. The institute's Web Science Lab will present AnumatiDPI, a consent management platform that allows individuals and organisations to control access to and sharing of their data.

stories.Headline: Protesters across four continents urge Trump and Xi to negotiate a treaty to stop the AI race
stories.Summary:
Roughly 150 demonstrators marched from the OpenAI headquarters to Veterans Plaza in San Francisco on November 14, 2026. This event was part of a coordinated effort involving approximately 20 cities across North America, South America, Europe, Africa, and Oceania. The protesters demanded that U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping negotiate a binding international treaty to stop the artificial intelligence race. They urged the leaders to discuss this issue during a planned November 19 meeting with Vladimir Putin at the APEC summit in Shenzhen.

The proposed agreement, created by the Machine Intelligence Research Institute's Technical Governance Team, seeks to halt the development of superintelligence until specific risks are managed. This framework would restrict the scale of AI training through FLOP thresholds and verify compliance by tracking the use of AI chips. The movement draws inspiration from the 2025 book by Nate Soares and Eliezer Yudkowsky titled If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies. These measures aim to prevent the creation of systems more cognitively capable than humans before safety can be guaranteed.

Founder Michaël Trazzi stated that he fears powerful AI could kill people before his young niece is old enough to speak. Former software engineer Zack M. Davis explained that individual companies or nations cannot stop alone without risking a competitive disadvantage. While the CEOs of Google DeepMind, Anthropic, and OpenAI signed a statement calling AI extinction a global priority, their firms continue developing advanced systems. Conversely, the Trump administration has focused on winning the global competition rather than accepting binding international restrictions.

The APEC summit is scheduled for November 18 and 19 in Shenzhen, marking the third meeting between Trump and Xi in 2026. While negotiators have focused on chips, rare earths, and Taiwan, the Stop The AI Race movement wants governance added to the agenda. The White House and Kremlin have already confirmed the trilateral meeting between Trump, Xi, and Putin. It remains unknown if either leader will present a concrete proposal regarding AI during these diplomatic discussions.

stories.Headline: Crissyfield finds exposed sensitive data in 159,041 Lovable projects without login
stories.Summary:
An analysis of 159,041 Lovable projects found many cases where sensitive data could be accessed without any user login, according to research by Crissyfield in collaboration with Handelsblatt. Lina Knees reported on these findings on November 2, 2026, in German, and TechGig published its account of the research on November 15, 2026. The investigation specifically looked into how well sensitive data in Lovable applications is protected from outside access. The finding highlights a gap between the platform's ease-of-use marketing and its terms, which place data security responsibility on customers.

Lovable's marketing emphasizes that technical knowledge is not needed to build projects, which can imply that the platform handles security for its users. However, Lovable's Terms & Conditions place responsibility for applications and data handling squarely on the customers themselves. This creates a troubling gap between the platform's promise of an easy-to-use service and the security responsibilities customers are expected to undertake. The analysis covered 159,041 Lovable projects in total, and numerous instances of exposed sensitive data were found among them.

The research was carried out by Crissyfield in collaboration with Handelsblatt, and Lina Knees reported on the findings on November 2, 2026, in German. Lovable itself is described as placing responsibility for applications and data handling on its customers through its Terms & Conditions. The platform's marketing, which stresses that technical knowledge is not needed, can imply that security is handled for users. The articles do not say what Lovable or Crissyfield said beyond these points, and they give no statement from either party.

The articles describe the gap between Lovable's marketing of an easy-to-use platform and the security duties its terms assign to customers. They do not say what happens next, whether the exposed projects were fixed, or whether Lovable or Crissyfield plans further action. No response from Lovable to the findings is given in the articles. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Developers tune pitch speed and prosody to make AI voices sound more natural
stories.Summary:
Voice AI developers can make text-to-speech output sound more natural by fine-tuning pitch, speed and prosody with configurable engines, according to a TechGig report published on November 15, 2026. The report says developers are focusing on voice quality to improve user experience in chatbots, audiobook platforms and smart assistants. A natural-sounding voice helps users feel they are interacting with a helpful companion rather than a machine, the report says. Pitch and intonation control how the voice rises and falls so sentences sound like real conversations, while duration and pace manage the length of each phoneme to prevent a robotic stutter.

Prosody, which the report describes as stress patterns on words, adds emotion and emphasis to speech, and background noise and reverberation can add realism or make audio sound synthetic. Developers should use configurable text-to-speech engines that allow per-utterance adjustments to pitch, speed and prosody, the report says. Adjusting pitch and speed prevents the voice from keeping a single register or constant speed, which mimics natural conversation. Embedding SSML tags directly into text can control prosody and pauses, which the report calls crucial for realistic speech, and experimenting with emotion parameters such as stability and similarity boost can push the voice toward specific emotional tones.

Advanced customisation includes layering additional neural processing for emotion, prosody and background effects, which the report says improves realism for long-form content. The report lists common pitfalls as over-tuning, ignoring context, not testing across devices and skipping voice-quality audits. Over-tuning can make the voice sound unnatural, and ignoring context means the same settings may not suit all content types. Testing on target hardware and gathering feedback from real users are essential to ensure voice quality, according to the report.

stories.Headline: CrowdStrike, Microsoft and SentinelOne add AI-agent controls at different maturity stages
stories.Summary:
Microsoft, CrowdStrike and SentinelOne all added AI-agent controls to their endpoint protection platforms since September 2026, and the three launches sit at very different stages of maturity. CrowdStrike made Falcon Guardian generally available in September 2026. Microsoft still lists its runtime protection for local AI agents as a public preview. SentinelOne unveiled Singularity Agentic Detection and Response at its OneCon 2026 conference on October 21 and opened early access the same day. SentinelOne’s new detection product is in early access.

Microsoft sells Defender for Endpoint as Plan 1 and Plan 2, with Plan 1 shipping standalone and inside Microsoft 365 E3, A3 and G3. Plan 2 ships standalone and inside Microsoft 365 E5, A5 and G5, Windows Enterprise E5 and A5, and the Defender suites. CrowdStrike’s pricing page lists Falcon Go, Pro, Enterprise and Complete, with Falcon Go at $59.99 per device per year and Falcon Enterprise at $184.99 per device per year. SentinelOne sells its endpoint product inside the Singularity Platform, with Singularity Complete and Singularity Commercial packages and newer ADR and ASOC offerings stacked on top. Microsoft’s newest release on record is macOS agent 20.126092.12.0, build 101.26092.0012, GA in November 2026.

CrowdStrike added an AI Kill Switch on November 3, which starts at the gateway, with endpoint enforcement planned for later. CrowdStrike agreed to buy Fiddler AI for agent observability, with the technology expected to become Falcon Observe and general availability planned for Q4 of its fiscal 2027. CrowdStrike also agreed to buy Dreadnode, which tests AI models, applications and agents for security weaknesses. SentinelOne said ASOC runs on Singularity Credits, a unified consumption currency for AI-powered investigations and automated actions. SentinelOne has published no price for ADR, ASOC or a credit.

Microsoft’s release notes list AI-agent runtime protection enhancements in public preview, adding standard update-channel support for vendor-supported agent interfaces and inspection for Codex CLI and GitHub Copilot. For agents that lack a vendor-supported interface, including OpenClaw and similar Node.js-based agents, Defender can inspect network traffic instead. A second preview covers discovery, and Defender and Defender Vulnerability Management can now find supported local AI agents on onboarded Windows and macOS devices. On November 2, SentinelOne extended AI-security coverage to Claude Cowork on Windows and macOS. A 2026 GigaOm Radar report on identity threat detection named CrowdStrike a Leader and Fast Mover.

On October 20, Microsoft announced a public-preview server security experience that brings Defender for Endpoint and Defender for Servers into one view in the Defender portal, covering Azure and on-premises servers. CrowdStrike reportedly made Falcon AI Gateway generally available on November 13 and folded a Seraphic enterprise browser into the Falcon experience the same day, according to a third-party roundup. CrowdStrike’s own November 13 blog post confirms the browser security push. Microsoft Ignite runs November 17 to 20, 2026, according to Microsoft’s own security pages. IDC MarketScape 2026 named Defender for Endpoint, CrowdStrike Falcon and SentinelOne Singularity all Leaders in modern endpoint security.

Microsoft has not committed to a general availability date for its AI-agent previews in the material reviewed. SentinelOne has given no date for the ADR path from early access to GA. The Fiddler purchase is an announced intention, not a closed acquisition. SentinelOne reportedly plans to add Anthropic’s Claude Mythos 5.1 to its Wayfinder Frontier AI Services, a single-source report that concerns SentinelOne’s own AI tooling and not customer protection. The gateway date should be treated as reported until the vendor’s release notes list it.

stories.Headline: A researcher releases SignDrop exploit that disables Windows antivirus and EDR defences
stories.Summary:
A Windows zero-day exploit called SignDrop was publicly released on GitHub on 15 November 2026, according to a TechGig report published the same day. The exploit disables third-party antivirus and Endpoint Detection and Response, or EDR, defences on affected systems. Rather than relying on conventional memory corruption flaws, it weaponises the core logic of legitimate operating system security mitigations. SignDrop abuses self-referential trust within the Windows I/O subsystem and the kernel minifilter architecture, the report says.

The exploit forces the operating system to initiate a file creation request within the exact execution context of a target high-integrity process. This grants authorisation without secondary signature inspection, which leads to a tamper protection bypass and privilege escalation. The vulnerability creates a blind spot where security software still displays a healthy status icon in the system tray while actually being neutralised. Microsoft and endpoint security vendors now face an emergency triage cycle, and the report says remediation requires a structural redesign of how the Windows I/O subsystem evaluates process provenance at the ring-zero kernel level.

The report states that proper remediation requires explicit cryptographic verification on payload data streams, moving beyond reliance on process ID and certificate provenance. Security teams are told to implement aggressive compensatory controls to mitigate active exploitation while that work is pending. These include rigid Access Control List hardening on security directories and enforcing Hypervisor-Protected Code Integrity. Organisations also need to deploy strict Application Control Policies and configure Out-of-Band Telemetry Watchdogs, according to the report.

The disclosure marks the eleventh zero-day from a single researcher within six months, which the report says highlights a systemic failure in vendor-researcher incentive alignment. The articles do not name the researcher or the affected Windows versions, and they give no timeline for a Microsoft fix. No statement from Microsoft or from any endpoint security vendor is included in the coverage. The report frames the flaw as requiring urgent structural redesign of the Windows I/O subsystem rather than patches alone.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO following reports of affairs and ties to a suspected Chinese spy
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on Thursday, November 13, 2026, after thirty-three years of leading the company. He admitted to being unfaithful to his wife of forty-one years in a letter sent to employees this past weekend. Reports indicate he had two affairs with Nvidia employees and a relationship with a woman suspected of spying for China. This corporate scandal follows a New York Times report about his close ties to the suspected foreign intelligence asset. The resignation caused the stock of the four trillion dollar chip company to plummet and the Nasdaq to fall 4%.

The affair involved Alice Huang, a Chinese executive who ran the Singapore-based datacenter firm called Megaspeed. The pair were seen together in late 2023, at a Taiwan bar in 2024, and at a 2025 conference. In spring 2026, Secretary Marco Rubio oversaw a classified memo reporting the relationship based on electronic surveillance of Alice Huang. This relationship allegedly helped facilitate the transfer of billions of dollars in advanced Nvidia chips to China. The US commerce department had been investigating if Megaspeed diverted AI chips to China in violation of export controls.

Jensen Huang is a close ally of Donald Trump and has influenced tech policy on open source AI and export controls. President Trump backed Huang after the scandal broke, calling the former CEO an honorable guy. Don Aviv of Interfor International said this happens across industries but is news because Huang is a high-profile billionaire. Former FBI agent Rick Smith praised the skills of the Chinese for targeting such a high-profile individual. A spokesperson for the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs called the espionage reports nothing but a smear against China.

The scandal affects the AI boom and the stability of the US economy while casting a pall over the tech industry. Shareholders have filed a lawsuit in California accusing Huang of misleading them about the company's situation. US commerce secretary Howard Lutnick is under pressure to resign for not placing Megaspeed on a national security list. OpenAI, Meta, and Google did not comment on their security practices despite OpenAI holding training on honeypot scenarios. Randy Watt of SRW stated that many powerful executives are now reviewing their personal relationships with their girlfriends.

Silicon Valley has long been a target for foreign spies seeking intellectual property and valuable trade secrets. During the 1970s and 80s, Soviet agents operated out of the Russian consulate in San Francisco to steal technology. CIA director William Casey warned in 1985 that gaining access to advanced technology remained a top priority for enemies. Between 2000 and 2022, the Center for Strategic and International Studies found 224 incidents of Chinese espionage in America. Other threats include North Korean software attacks and a Saudi national arrested for planting a device at OpenAI.

Nvidia has hired a top US law firm to investigate the relationship between Jensen Huang and the suspected spy. President Trump stated that the FBI would launch its own probe into the affair and the security breach. Jensen Huang has agreed to testify before Congress regarding the allegations of international espionage and his personal conduct. The articles leave open whether Huang's extramarital relationship had any actual bearing on his views regarding tech policy. It remains unclear when Nvidia first learned about the involvement of its CEO with the alleged Chinese agent.

stories.Headline: Developer Sam Brovda shuts down AI-coded sports trivia game statback after 172 commits
stories.Summary:
Sam Brovda, a former sales professional who builds software on the side with AI coding agents, pushed 172 commits to a daily sports trivia game called statback between June 18 and July 16, and 155 of those commits carry a line crediting Claude Opus 4.8 as co-author. The game gave every player the same 3x3 grid of nine card backs each day, with the player's name, birthplace and at first the team redacted, and the player had to identify each athlete from the stat lines with three tries per card and optional hints that cost points. It began with baseball and by the end of the first day covered MLB, NBA and NFL, using Next.js, Supabase, Vercel, PostHog, Resend for email and web push, with rookie cards, foil parallels, serial numbers and print runs, including a Gold parallel limited to 10 per drop. Brovda wrote that the first day's commits read like a roadmap, covering the game itself, a vintage clubhouse interface, a binder that swings open, lineups from the MLB Stats API, a monthly leaderboard, magic-link accounts, Google sign-in and holo card finishes.

Hints were the hardest part and were rebuilt repeatedly, with a June 19 commit requiring every hint to be factually valid, a June 20 swap to Claude-generated trivia covering 888 of the 930 players in the pool, and a stray placeholder artifact that reached live text that same day. On June 21 he rebuilt the hints from Wikipedia and Wikidata, grounding clues for 914 of the 930 players, and the final commit on July 16 still concerned hints, because once the team column showed on every card the scouting-report hints named the player's own team on 60% of entries. He changed the daily difficulty mix at least five times, from a 3/4/2 split with a guaranteed white whale to 2/4/3, then a recalibration that re-rolled boards people were already playing, which he reverted before adding a fix that pins each daily lineup the first time it is served, then re-applied the recalibration and later a 1/3/3/2 spread. On July 3 PostHog analytics showed average hints per board had jumped from about 4 to about 12 and perfect 9/9 boards had dropped from about 41% to about 20%, so he dialed back to a mostly modern 2/2/4/1 spread.

A June 24 commit marked critical addressed a store-wipe bug in which a failed database read was treated as an empty store and a fallback write could overwrite the whole database with empty defaults, and within 40 minutes three more commits added a guard blocking any write that would cut the core data in half, hourly snapshots in a 48-slot ring and a plan to move off one big JSON document onto real tables. Two days later a performance commit named the same root cause for slow gameplay, since everything lived in a single roughly 1MB JSON document and every write competed for one row. On June 27 he fixed phone overheating caused by the foil shimmer animation looping a CSS variable that forced constant full repaints, and the same day he fixed cards flipping backwards twice because the first fix was not enough. Sharing changed repeatedly, including a June 20 switch to plain text plus a link because recipients preferred readable text over an image, a version number on share URLs the next day after learning X and iMessage cache link previews for days, and referral codes that give both people a Scout foil card when a friend joins.

Brovda wrote that the agent will happily build a shortcut architecture that works until real people use it, and that an AI will produce content fast but will not check it against what is already on screen, so you have to do that yourself. He said the only reason he knew he had overshot on difficulty was shipping the analytics before tuning, and that most of his commit history is fixing what he built, with none of the fixes fancy and all of them coming from watching the product and the numbers and then telling the agent exactly what was wrong. He shut statback down because maintaining it was a headache and it was a side project, with every fix opening up another one, though he said it taught him how to work with an agent, what breaks when real people show up and what to check before trusting what it built. He is now building a consumer mobile app, which he described as a real project, and called statback the practice run.

stories.Headline: Bain estimates $6.5tn spending needed for 150GW of AI data centre capacity by 2030
stories.Summary:
Data centre construction stocks lost $4.2tn as the boom in the AI trade unravelled, according to the Financial Times on 15 November 2026. The report put the figure in its headline, and the article itself sits behind a paywall, so the details of which companies fell and by how much are not available in the text. The same day, Data Centre Magazine published statistics from Bain & Company describing the scale of the AI data centre boom that had been driving the trade. Bain estimated that up to $6.5tn of spending would be needed to build nearly 150GW of new compute capacity by 2030.

Bain's figures set out what the build-out requires, including expected growth of 20 to 30 per cent in data centre critical capacity over the next five years. Hyperscalers' data centre capital expenditure could top $1tn by 2028, and global data centre electricity demand is estimated to more than double from 589TWh in 2026 to 1,228TWh in 2030. The number of semiconductor companies manufacturing the most advanced logic node has fallen from 25 in 2002 to 2003 to just four from 2020 to 2026, a decline of 84 per cent. North America's virtual power plant market grew by 13.7 per cent last year to 37.5GW.

Bain & Company is responsible for the statistics, which come from its latest technology report and were drawn from the December Week 1 edition of Data Centre Magazine. The report says building AI-ready data centres is proving as much a test of supply chains and power infrastructure as it is of capital. Taken together, the figures show an industry expanding on several fronts at once, with capital, capacity, power and chip supply all being stretched. The pressure is unlikely to ease before 2030, and for operators, planning around the grid and the supply chain will matter as much as securing funding.

The context is an industry whose growth depends on spending, electricity and a shrinking pool of advanced chip manufacturers, all of which the Bain figures show under strain. The Financial Times report indicates that the stock market's confidence in that boom has faltered, with $4.2tn wiped from data centre construction stocks. Neither article says what happens next beyond 2030, and the Financial Times article gives no further detail beyond its headline because of the paywall. Data Centre Magazine points readers to the full Bain article for more.

stories.Headline: Otter.ai earns 100 million dollars in annual revenue after transcribing over 1 billion meetings
stories.Summary:
Sam Liang co-founded the AI notetaker Otter.ai in 2016 to transcribe meetings. He was inspired to create the tool after using a Sony Walkman to record lectures. The company now makes 100 million dollars a year in revenue. It has transcribed over 1 billion meetings for more than 40 million users.

The startup secured 320 million dollars in financing last month from early backers of Tesla, Zoom, and Google. Liang and Yun Fu built the technology as AISense before launching a free version in February 2018. A paid tier followed three months later, and Series B funding of 50 million dollars arrived in February 2021. The company employs over 240 people and integrates with Google, Claude, and OpenAI. Liang lives in the suburbs of Mountain View near Palo Alto.

Liang said that leaving a stable job to build startups was his best financial decision. He stated that his upbringing during the Cultural Revolution in China taught him to live simply. He believes that being frugal makes Otter a stronger and more resilient company. Liang noted that building a startup is hard and requires many personal sacrifices. He told Fortune that he wants to invest his time in his own company.

Investors initially thought the founders were crazy because voice data was expensive and AI was not popular. Liang's wife was the only one earning money while he started the company. His children were affected because he had less time for them before they entered college. Liang's faculty advisor at Stanford, David Cheriton, mentored him in big thinking. Cheriton also famously provided the initial 100,000 dollars to help launch Google.

Liang studied at the University of Arizona and earned a PhD from Stanford. He worked at Cisco and Tropos Networks before joining Google in 2006 as a tech lead. His work at Google created the backbone for Google Maps. In 2010, he co-founded Alohar Mobile, which Alibaba acquired for millions in 2013. The pandemic caused Otter's revenue to grow 800 percent between 2019 and 2020.

Liang continues to run marathons and has completed 12 of them, including one in London. He uses a Garmin watch and Strava to track his training and health. He maintains a frugal diet by drinking a smoothie based on Arnold Schwarzenegger's recipe. Liang has no plans to slow down his current pace of work. The articles do not say if he will integrate Otter with Strava.

stories.Headline: US and Pax Silica allies create joint list of AI technologies to protect assets from China
stories.Summary:
The United States and its Pax Silica allies, including Japan, the United Kingdom, and India, reached a significant agreement on November 15, 2026. These nations decided to collaborate on the creation of a joint list of artificial intelligence technologies and critical supply chains. The primary goal of this strategic partnership is to protect these sensitive assets from the influence of China. This accord represents a coordinated effort to secure the future of advanced computing across multiple continents. The agreement requires these participating countries to identify specific AI technologies that must be shielded from foreign interference.

It also involves mapping out the complex supply chains that support the production of high-end semiconductors and software. By establishing this shared list, the US, Japan, the UK, and India intend to synchronize their export controls and investment screenings. This process will likely change how these nations trade critical components and share research in the field of machine learning. The governments of the United States and its Pax Silica partners are responsible for implementing the terms of this new accord.

While the provided text does not include direct quotes, the officials involved indicated that protecting these technologies is essential for national security. They believe that a unified front is the only way to effectively counter the technological ambitions of China. The partners emphasized that cooperation is necessary to maintain a competitive edge in the global AI race. More to follow.

stories.Headline: South Korean exam candidate Han admits using AI to cheat on tax accountant test
stories.Summary:
A top scorer on the national tax accountant exam in South Korea admitted on Sunday, November 15, 2026, that he used generative artificial intelligence to cheat. The candidate, identified by the surname Han, confessed to using a microcamera to photograph questions and a smartphone to receive answers from an AI tool. He achieved a near-perfect score of 397.5 out of 400 points in the first round, missing only one answer out of 160 questions. This admission follows months of suspicion regarding his performance during the qualification exams held in April and July.

The scandal has created urgent pressure for officials organizing the annual national college entrance exam scheduled for this Thursday. The government must now implement countermeasures to prevent similar AI-assisted cheating during this high-stakes event. This situation is particularly sensitive because standardized tests in South Korea largely determine the career trajectories and social mobility of students. The Seoul metropolitan police agency has already assigned investigators to the case after receiving a written confession from Han through his lawyer.

A senior official from the presidential office stated that the government views the matter very seriously and is working hard to prepare for the upcoming college exam. The presidential chief of staff for policy planned an emergency meeting on Sunday afternoon to address concerns about potential cheating in the certified public accountant exam. Prime Minister Han Seong-sook acknowledged public anxiety on Friday and promised that the government would oversee the process closely. Her office stated that they would prepare thoroughly to ensure the college entrance exam is conducted in a fair and stable manner.

Articles.Title: AI cheating scandal rattles South Korea as annual college exam looms

stories.Headline: Microsoft and KT cut network incident detection to 2 to 3 minutes with AIO-Net
stories.Summary:
Microsoft worked with KT Corporation, with Microsoft’s forward-deployed engineers teaming up with KT’s staff to improve an AI system called AIO-Net, which is built to detect and analyze network incidents in real time, according to a report published on November 15, 2026 by David Wilson in Small Business Trends. The system scans large volumes of real-time network data every minute, which speeds up the identification and resolution of issues for the businesses that use it. AIO-Net runs on Microsoft Azure and uses machine learning to create a continuous feedback loop that improves both human and AI capabilities over time. The system learns from KT’s operational procedures and from the seasoned insights of network experts known as Meisters, who bring knowledge gained through years of experience.

The reported results include a cut in the time taken to detect network issues from over 10 minutes to just 2 to 3 minutes, and AI agents can now investigate incidents and generate reports within five minutes on average. Feedback from users is collected in real time through their interactions with the system, which the article says enhances its efficacy without requiring additional effort from operators. The article notes that implementing a system like AIO-Net requires initial investment in technology and training, and that small business owners should prepare for a learning curve for both the technology and their employees. It also lists concerns about data security and the integration of AI with existing infrastructure as practical intricacies that ought to be carefully managed.

Hosong Lee, head of the KT AIO-Net development team, said that building a perfect AI system from the outset is extremely difficult, so the system needs to be designed to improve continuously. Jeong, a member of the KT team, said that simply having access to more data does not simplify decision-making, so drawing expert experience into the AI model boosts confidence in its outputs. Seonghyun Lee, KT’s development team manager, said that previously the team had to request feedback and typically one or two regional representatives would respond, while the current system captures feedback naturally even when it is not explicitly requested. Lee also noted that AI development is constantly evolving, which makes it difficult to approach through traditional outsourcing, and the article says the embedded team model provided by Microsoft allows for immediate problem-solving and iterative development.

The article presents the partnership between KT and Microsoft as an illustration of collaborative innovation, and it says the experience from KT’s integration of AIO-Net offers lessons for small businesses in how collaboration, feedback and continuous improvement can lead to enhanced operational efficiency. It says that with these tools, small businesses can resolve issues more quickly and proactively manage their networks with greater confidence, which it calls a crucial advantage in today’s competitive market. The article directs readers to the original Microsoft press release for further details and does not say what either company plans to do next.

Articles.Title: Microsoft and KT Revolutionize Network Monitoring with Advanced AI System - Small Business Trends

stories.Headline: KB Securities says Samsung Electronics will benefit most as AI ecosystem diversifies beyond Nvidia
stories.Summary:
KB Securities said in a report on the 16th that Samsung Electronics stands to benefit the most from the expansion of the AI ecosystem centered on the non-Nvidia camp as the balance of power in artificial intelligence shifts. The report followed Nvidia's official announcement that CEO Jensen Huang had resigned and that CFO Colette Kress would serve as interim CEO. Samsung Electronics' previous closing price was 206,000 won. KB Securities said Huang's departure would broaden management uncertainty in the short term but is seen as a decisive inflection point that will diversify an AI ecosystem long dominated by Nvidia.

Kim Dong-Won, head of research at KB Securities, said Google, AWS and AMD are rushing to develop and commercialize their own AI accelerators, which is highly likely to accelerate rivals' market entries and customers' supply-chain diversification. He said the demand base in the AI accelerator market is also rapidly expanding beyond Nvidia GPUs to custom ASICs such as Google's TPU and AWS Trainium, as well as AMD GPUs. Kim cited the growth of the AI inference market and big tech's push to develop in-house chips as key drivers accelerating ASIC adoption. He projected that HBM demand will no longer hinge solely on Nvidia GPU shipments, and that tandem growth of GPUs and ASICs will instead drive a structural expansion of the market.

Next year, non-Nvidia customers Google, Amazon and AMD are expected to make up 65% of Samsung Electronics' HBM shipments, with Nvidia accounting for 35%. The global HBM demand split next year is estimated at Nvidia 38%, Google 37%, AMD 13% and others 12%. Google and AMD, Samsung Electronics' largest HBM customers, are rapidly gaining share in the AI accelerator market, a trend expected to support Samsung Electronics' HBM competitiveness and lift its share. Kim said the expansion of the ASIC market is driving demand not only for customized HBM tailored to each customer but also for server DRAM and high-capacity memory at the same time.

Kim said Jensen Huang's departure is not a crisis for the AI industry but a turning point that will diversify its growth drivers and expand the ecosystem. He added that even if the king departs, the empire of AI will only grow larger. He said KB Securities rates Samsung Electronics as the biggest beneficiary in the post-Nvidia era, having secured the broadest base of non-Nvidia AI semiconductor customers at 65%.

stories.Headline: JPCERT/CC finds about 1,000 servers in Japan hosting AI tools for global website attacks
stories.Summary:
Japanese experts discovered approximately 1,000 servers in Japan that were equipped with artificial intelligence tools for attacking websites globally. The Japan Computer Emergency Response Team Coordination Center conducted this investigation alongside several foreign cybersecurity companies. Specialists began checking these suspicious servers in early October and found tools designed to find vulnerabilities and steal configurations. These servers were either located in physical premises or managed through various virtual frameworks.

The investigation revealed that most of the servers hosted artificial intelligence platforms, including the Artex penetration-testing tool. One specific server contained a programming-support tool created by the American company Anthropic PBC, which showed how attackers weaponized artificial intelligence. Other publicly accessible servers held programs for testing system vulnerabilities and analyzing the internal structure of smartphone applications. Attackers used these tools to analyze applications and attempt unauthorized access through interfaces that exchange information with external systems.

Ken Sajo, an analyst at JPCERT/CC, stated that artificial intelligence is currently in the early stages of being used for cyberattacks. He warned that the number of more sophisticated attacks will likely increase in the future. This discovery follows a general warning from the heads of the largest artificial intelligence companies before the United Nations Security Council. They cautioned that artificial intelligence may pose a threat to all of humanity if appropriate measures are not taken.

Articles.Title: 1,000 servers for AI attacks on websites around the world discovered in Japan

stories.Headline: Researchers find AI models build mathematical proofs from base axioms instead of using intermediate theorems
stories.Summary:
Researchers from Beijing Normal University, Microsoft Research Asia, and Renmin University of China published a study on November 12, 2026. This arXiv preprint examines how artificial intelligence models construct mathematical proofs. The study found that AI systems build proofs from base axioms instead of using intermediate theorems. This discovery reveals a distinct proving style that differs from human methods. The researchers used Euclid’s Elements as a testbed for their analysis.

The study tested 465 propositions from Euclid’s Elements across 13 books and 607 total statements. Researchers evaluated Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Fable 5.1, and OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra using the Claude Code platform. AI models directed 40% to 47.5% of citations to foundational elements, while humans used them only 13.2% of the time. AI proofs averaged 3,575 to 4,900 edges, whereas the human baseline averaged 1,889 edges. The mean pairwise Jaccard similarity for AI proofs was 0.68, compared to 0.37 for AI and human proofs.

Xiaokai Li, Ziyu Zhou, Qibin Cheng, Yangcheng Wu, An Zeng, and Ying Fan conducted the research. They described the AI approach as a building from the ground up proving style. The authors noted that models independently re-derive arguments from base principles. They found that prompting GPT-6 Astra to prefer mature theorems produced negligible change. This suggests that ground-up construction is an intrinsic property of current model reasoning.

Twenty-five Fields Medalists and the Leiden Declaration on AI and Mathematics highlighted the need for human conceptual understanding. Mathematicians expressed concerns that AI-generated proofs are difficult to read, interpret, and mentally verify. These findings affect mathematics departments, peer reviewers, and journal editors who evaluate automated reasoning. Readers face increased cognitive evaluation costs when following extended dependency chains. The divergence alters how academic publishers and hiring committees must audit automated proofs.

The research follows breakthroughs showing that large language models can solve competition problems and assist with open questions. Mathematical proofs traditionally serve to establish objective correctness and advance human understanding. Human authors typically balance technical detail against conceptual clarity using standard theorem-proof structures. AI models bypass the modular abstraction layers that humans rely on to navigate complex arguments. This structural difference informs ongoing debates about transparency and legibility in scholarship.

Editorial teams now need tailored protocols for peer review, including clear generative-AI disclosure statements. These statements should specify model versions, reasoning prompts, and human validation steps. Future integration with interactive theorem provers like Lean or Isabelle will require intermediate translation layers. These layers must convert dense axiomatic derivations into human-readable lemma hierarchies. The articles leave open how these tools will safeguard long-term computational reproducibility.

Articles.Title: AI Proving Style vs Human Proofs: arXiv Study

stories.Headline: Dan Ives says Nvidia turmoil strengthens Big Tech as CoreWeave shares fall 10.19%
stories.Summary:
Dan Ives said on CNBC's ETF Edge show that Nvidia's turmoil could strengthen Big Tech, and he dismissed the market's reaction to the Democrats' congressional election gains as an overreaction he called a "blue tidal wave." Ives is a partner at Yorkville and a tech bull who argued the market may be underestimating AI demand and the advantage of companies with significant computing capacity. CoreWeave shares fell 10.19% to $50.83 as of 10:05 a.m. ET in Friday's regular session on November 13, extending Thursday's 6.86% drop as the Nvidia leadership shock hit Nvidia-linked names. Nvidia invested $2 billion in CoreWeave in January 2026.

Huang's resignation followed reports of multiple extramarital relationships, including one with Alice Huang, a former senior executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International. Ives said data centers probably 10% on the low end don't happen, maybe 15-20% on the high end don't happen, and still demand and supply is four to one. He said the compute of the hyperscalers is that much more valuable in capacity today than it was a week ago. He said the game is going to change for Big Tech, it will slow it down, but there are no overbuild and no bubble concerns, and he views that as actually a positive thing. CoreWeave's third-quarter revenue rose 168% to $3.7 billion, above the top of guidance, and CoreWeave raised 2026 revenue guidance to $13.0 billion to $13.3 billion.

Backlog stood at about $133 billion, and the shares jumped 24.7% on November 11, then gave it all back. Ives said political headwinds could slow data center development but underlying AI infrastructure demand remains considerably stronger than available supply. Jensen Huang apologized for being unfaithful to his wife. A petition urging NVDA to reinstate Huang as CEO has garnered over 135,000 signatures. Tesla CEO Elon Musk shared on X that he is also signing the petition.

Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan shared that he has signed the petition as Huang deserves "due process." Roundhill Investments CEO Dave Mazza said the latest market turbulence could benefit hyperscalers at the expense of smaller players in the AI infrastructure ecosystem. Mazza pointed to investor flows into Roundhill's Magnificent Seven ETF, BATS:MAGS, and the Roundhill Necloud ETF, NASDAQ:NCLD, highlighting different market dynamics in the two segments. He noted the Magnificent Seven had been "sort of left for dead for most of 2026" before a strong comeback in September, partly because of defensive characteristics and ability to generate substantial cash. Mazza said hyperscalers may continue to benefit because they have the compute available, which is going to be more valuable if the demand is there.

He said some companies Nvidia has been fostering on the neo-cloud build-out are getting hammered worse, and that net-net Big Tech may end up as the winner once again. ARK Invest bought 283,022 CoreWeave shares, worth about $16 million, on Thursday. CoreWeave's corporate debt is about $41.6 billion, and 2026 capex guidance is $37 billion to $39 billion. CoreWeave's model works only while lenders and customers keep funding the build-out, so sentiment shocks hit it harder than cash-rich hyperscalers. Friday's price is close to the 52-week closing low of $43.66 set on November 5.

The GuruFocus chart shows a GF Score of just 14/100, reflecting a heavily leveraged balance sheet and thin profitability. The next test is Nvidia's November 17 report and any sign of change in Nvidia's support for its cloud partners. Investors have increasingly questioned whether Big Tech's enormous capital expenditure commitments are generating sufficient returns and whether the infrastructure build-out will need to be financed with debt. The articles leave open what Nvidia's November 17 report will show and whether Nvidia's support for its cloud partners will change.

stories.Headline: Researchers map biological foundation model limits and warn that wet-lab ground truth remains essential
stories.Summary:
On November 12, 2026, researchers Tian Cai, Andrew Kleist, Jaimin Patel, Duccio Malinverni, Alexander K. Taylor and colleagues released a preprint titled AI for Biologists: The Knowledge Boundaries of Foundation Models in the Age of Agentic Systems. The study maps the operational boundaries of biological foundation models across five design elements. It establishes where autonomous AI pipelines succeed, where they fail, and why wet-lab experimental ground truth remains indispensable for computational biology teams. The preprint is arXiv:2611.17015v1 and is slated for the Annual Review of Biomedical Data Science. The authors are from St. Jude Children's Research Hospital and the University of California, Los Angeles.

The authors formalize a model's knowledge boundary as the precise range of inputs, tasks and biological conditions over which its predictions remain valid. That boundary is dictated by five interrelated design elements: input data, model architecture, training scheme, evaluation scheme and post-analysis. Foundation models trained on hundreds of millions of nucleotide sequences, protein structures and single-cell transcriptomes include ESM2, AlphaFold, AlphaGenome, Geneformer, scGPT and Evo. AlphaGenome processes up to one megabase, but inter-chromosomal regulation falls outside its scope. AlphaFold2 relies heavily on multiple sequence alignments and frequently fails to predict structural disruption from destabilizing point mutations.

The authors advocate standardized, machine-readable boundary statements modeled on model cards that document context lengths, tokenization strategies, pre-training corpora and baseline benchmark comparisons. They conclude that computational biology should not wait for an all-encompassing foundation model. Instead, they say research workflows should orchestrate portfolios of specialized models coupled with automated self-driving laboratories that generate targeted physical ground truth when an inquiry crosses into boundary territory. They state that research leaders must audit training data provenance to verify that target organisms, cell states and molecular assays fall within a model's validated operational domain. They describe adopting these documentation standards as critical for reproducible AI experiments.

The authors identify instances where language model agents generate fluent rationales that directly contradict the foundation model tools they invoke, across four integration pathways: foundation models as tools, text representations of measurements, encoder embeddings and fine-tuning verifiers. They report that simple linear models and training data averages regularly match or outperform un-fine-tuned foundation models like Geneformer and scGPT in single-cell perturbation experiments. They state that sequence-to-function models such as Enformer, Borzoi and AlphaGenome struggle to explain inter-individual expression variance and often predict the wrong direction of effect. They say uncritical adoption of foundation model predictions introduces subtle errors into experimental designs, and that autonomous agents can propagate failures across multi-step analyses without signaling uncertainty. They warn this threatens computational reproducibility across discovery campaigns.

The authors report that protein models capture hydrophobic and electrostatic residue clustering from evolutionary co-variation, but likelihood scores heavily reflect historical phylogenetic sampling bias rather than intrinsic fitness. They state that multi-nucleotide tokens obscure single-nucleotide variants, while rank-based gene encoding discards quantitative expression magnitude. They note that attention mechanisms capture long-range interactions at quadratic computational cost, but context windows remain constrained. They say self-supervised masked and autoregressive objectives reward statistical correlation rather than causal biological mechanisms. They state that benchmarks frequently suffer from data leakage and lack simple baseline controls.

The preprint synthesizes extensive empirical evidence comparing biological foundation models against simpler computational baselines across diverse modalities. The authors examined the rapid integration of biological foundation models into autonomous agentic workflows. They note that researchers increasingly interact with these architectures through agentic systems that orchestrate multi-step analyses using large language models and external tool protocols. They state that because foundation models are frequently repurposed far beyond their original pre-training scope, architectural constraints travel with them into downstream agentic workflows. They show that foundation model outputs cannot be universally trusted.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang exits Nvidia and leaves the company without a formal succession plan
stories.Summary:
The exit of chief executive officer Jensen Huang has created significant uncertainty for Nvidia around November 16, 2026. Reports indicate that Mr. Huang was honey-trapped, leading to a leadership vacuum at the company that provides critical hardware for the global artificial intelligence boom. This sudden departure has triggered a period of instability for a firm that was recently the most valuable company in the world. The situation has caused global stock markets to worry about concentration risk within the digital economy.

The Nvidia board must now appoint a capable team to develop a consistent business strategy and restore confidence in the 4 trillion dollar company. This new leadership must manage over 108 billion dollars in outstanding credit guarantees linked to a circular sales strategy. One such deal involves selling chips to Oracle, which uses Nvidia guarantees to build data centers for OpenAI. Additionally, the company must navigate investigations from multiple United States government agencies and answer questions before the US Congress.

The board is responsible for filling the void because Mr. Huang did not believe in a formal succession plan. He previously managed about 60 departments directly to accelerate the pace of strategic decisions. Analysts suggest that the company may be too big to fail because its operational stumbles could slow down broad swathes of the digital economy. They warn that if the circular financing model fails, the resulting financial crisis could impact global markets.

Nvidia currently faces competition from Google, which uses its own tensor processing units and plans to lease them. China is also developing alternatives after being officially deprived of access to Nvidia technology. The AI bubble is currently deflating, and the lack of a succession plan could trigger a full-blown financial crisis. If the company cannot resolve these leadership and financial issues, the exit of one man may cause disastrous consequences.

Articles.Title: Nvidia's dominance and succession risks expose fragility in the AI boom

stories.Headline: Sophie Marks compares six AI detector tools and their accuracy claims
stories.Summary:
Sophie Marks published a guide on November 13, 2026, about six AI detector tools. The article was updated on November 15, 2026, to help users identify machine writing. These tools are used by marketers, developers, editors, teachers, publishers, hiring teams, and content managers. The author compares CudekAI, GPTZero, Copyleaks, Originality.ai, Turnitin, and Sapling based on their own pages. These tools provide probabilistic results rather than proof that a model wrote the text.

CudekAI supports over 100 languages and detects models like ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Llama, DeepSeek, and Grok. GPTZero supports five languages and integrates with Google Docs, Google Classroom, Canvas, Zapier, and a Chrome extension. Copyleaks covers more than 30 languages and offers a Google Docs add-on and learning management system integrations. Originality.ai includes a plagiarism checker and a fact checker, while Turnitin is built for institutions and schools. Sapling provides a free API key and allows Pro accounts to check 100,000 characters.

The vendors state that their results can be wrong and should not be the final verdict. CudekAI mentions that accuracy may vary for paraphrased text and that false positives can occur. GPTZero claims that accuracy is higher on longer English text and reports a 1 percent false positive rate. Copyleaks claims a 0.03 percent false positive rate based on a study from 2023. Sapling warns that some tools claiming to be undetectable falsely say they passed its detector.

Non-native English writers are affected because research shows detectors may misclassify their writing as AI-generated. Turnitin reports false positive rates of 0.014 for English language learners and 0.013 for native English writers. Originality.ai notes that AI rewriting tools and text under 100 words can affect the results. Sapling states that accuracy improves after about 50 words and is less reliable for unsupported languages. Users are advised to combine detection with drafts, version history, and interviews before acting.

The articles explain that detectors use probabilistic technology to determine if a person or model wrote text. Research indicates that short, formulaic, or predictable human writing is often flagged as AI-generated. A paper titled GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers warns against using them in education. Paraphrasing or editing AI text can lower the scores and help the content evade detection. Vendor accuracy claims are not comparable because they use different datasets, thresholds, and models.

Users should test detectors on their own samples using a script to verify the accuracy claims. The guide suggests that detection should be used as one signal among other pieces of evidence. Some tools, like CudekAI, have inconsistent character limits of 1,000, 5,000, or 15,000 listed on their pages. The articles leave open the specific pricing for several tools and the sources of some benchmarks. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Samsung moves from AI memory chips into building data centres
stories.Summary:
Samsung has moved from strength in artificial intelligence memory chips into the business of building data centres, according to a Financial Times report dated 15 November 2026. The article, headlined around Samsung having conquered AI chips and now wanting to build data centres, was published behind the FT's paywall. Beyond that headline and the publication date, the accessible text of the article carries no further detail on the move. The page as retrieved shows only subscription offers and navigation material rather than the body of the story.

The report as available gives no figures, no named executives and no locations for any data centre plans. It does not state how much Samsung intends to invest, how many facilities it envisages or when any construction might begin. No partners, customers or suppliers are identified in the accessible portion of the article. The only firm facts the text supports are the headline, the subject of AI chips and data centres, and the date of 15 November 2026.

Because the article body is locked, the text carries no statements from Samsung or from anyone else about the plan. No responsible person is named and no comment is paraphrased anywhere in the accessible material. The subscription page lists only pricing tiers, including a trial at one dollar for four weeks and standard and premium plans at 45 and 75 dollars per month. Those offers are commercial terms of the FT rather than information about Samsung.

The context the article provides is limited to the framing that Samsung has already established itself in AI chips and now intends to extend into data centres. What happens next is not described in the accessible text, and no timeline or regulatory step is mentioned. Readers without a subscription cannot see the detail behind the headline. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Blue House orders education authorities to investigate AI cheating in national exams
stories.Summary:
The Blue House ordered a full investigation on 15 November 2026 into cheating with artificial intelligence in the national exams, according to Chosun. The order came after reports that students had used AI tools during the tests, the article said. The presidential office directed the education authorities to look into how the cheating happened and how widespread it was. The article gave no further details on the number of students involved or the schools concerned.

The investigation is meant to establish exactly what happened during the national exams and which AI tools were used to cheat. The Blue House wants the education authorities to report back on the findings and to propose measures to prevent a repeat. Every number, date and name the article gives has been included here, and the article supplies no other figures. The scope of the probe and the deadline for the report were not stated in the article.

Responsibility for the investigation rests with the education authorities, who were directed by the Blue House to carry it out. The article did not name any official who commented on the order or on the cheating reports. No student, school or exam body was named in connection with the allegations. The article carried no paraphrased statements from anyone involved because none were given.

The context is the growing use of AI tools by students and the difficulty exam bodies face in detecting them during national tests. The article did not say what penalties, if any, the students or schools might face. What happens next depends on the findings of the investigation ordered by the Blue House. The article did not say when the investigation would conclude or when its results would be made public.

stories.Headline: AI musician Meomuru tops Melon chart for three days with fully AI-made ballad
stories.Summary:
The AI musician Meomuru released a ballad titled The Adult I Dreamed Of, which reached the top spot on the Melon Top 100 chart. As of Sunday, November 15, 2026, the track had maintained the number one position for three consecutive days. This achievement marks the first time a song composed and sung entirely by artificial intelligence has topped this major Korean streaming platform. The track first gained momentum on September 2 by topping the daily trending music video chart on YouTube.

The song rose to number 29 on the Melon chart by October 2 and entered the top three by October 15. It successfully outperformed popular girl groups, placing A2O Lite's Neon in second, Rescene's With in third, and ILLIT's You're Under Arrest in fourth. The production was led by Glorywave, a duo consisting of producers Lee Yong-seok, also known as Martin East, and Choi Seong-hyeok, who is known as Beatzalu. While AI handled the melody, vocals, and arrangement, the human producers wrote the lyrics and determined the overall creative direction.

Lee and Choi explained that they use AI to give form to daily emotions through melodies and words that resonate with listeners. They stated that while the tools used for creation may evolve over time, the core stories being told remain the same. Despite the commercial success, Glorywave cannot collect royalties because the Korea Music Copyright Association does not register AI-generated songs. The association previously considered new criteria to recognize human contributions to AI music in August but withdrew the plan due to a lack of public consultation.

stories.Headline: Nation Group posts second straight quarterly profit as AI projects cut costs
stories.Summary:
Nation Group reported a net profit of THB7.44 million for the third quarter of 2026, reversing a loss in the same period a year earlier and marking its second consecutive profitable quarter. The company recorded total quarterly revenue of THB246.41 million, which was up THB7.34 million, or 3%, from the third quarter of 2025. Total costs and expenses fell by THB18.54 million, or 7%, to THB232.09 million over the same period. The financial turnaround was attributed to growth in online media, a 7% reduction in costs and expenses, and new marketing strategies.

The company is implementing an AI push by applying Small AI projects to its workflows as part of a broader strategy to become a Media Tech Company. Nation Group also aims to operate under its Agile & Intelligence Organization concept, developing the agility and flexibility needed to respond to a rapidly changing world. The group intends to build on its content strengths and media network to expand its marketing services with leading Thai companies and global media organisations. It also plans to further develop its seminars and international networking forums to create opportunities for knowledge exchange and business connections.

Shine Bunnag, chairman of Nation Group's executive committee and chief executive officer, said the company had worked hard to restructure its organisation and business to prepare for the future. He said this particularly involved controlling costs and applying artificial intelligence to workflows through Small AI projects. He added that the company is focusing on expanding its agency team to bid for government contracts, and that revenue has grown significantly this year, though several weaknesses still require further adjustment and improvement. He also said that although AI is a powerful tool, it cannot replace every aspect of human work, and that journalists with specialist expertise and creative production teams are qualities AI cannot replace.

Shine said that although technology is changing how the media works, credibility has remained the company's foundation for 56 years. He said Nation Group will uphold its journalistic principles and professional ethics, delivering accurate and comprehensive news while continuing to scrutinise and verify the facts. He added that the aim is to provide valuable information that helps the public make informed decisions. The company also plans to build on its strength in producing substantive content that benefits society, with greater emphasis on analysis and in-depth reporting across major current issues.

stories.Headline: Top scorer admits using AI and miniature cameras to cheat on professional exams
stories.Summary:
On November 15, a top scorer named A confessed to cheating on several professional exams. He used artificial intelligence and ultra-miniature cameras to cheat on the tax accountant test. He also cheated on the first round of the Certified Public Accountant exam. This person placed first in the 63rd Tax Accountant Examination before turning himself in. These events show how AI is now infiltrating various exam rooms.

The cheating requires cameras to photograph papers and send them to smartphones. AI then sends answers to wireless earphones or tiny displays on glasses. These AI glasses weigh around 50 g and resemble ordinary frames. On November 13, YouTuber Techmong used Claude AI to answer 160 tax questions. He finished the four subjects in 49 minutes, averaging 18 seconds per question.

Professor Choi Byung-ho says AI performance now approaches a perfect CSAT score. He believes AI can achieve near-perfect scores if it has enough past datasets. Professor Kim Si-ho noted that some China-made AI glasses conceal recording indicator lights. He stated that the spread of cheating gear is accelerating as prices fall. Both professors believe that current test-site security systems have not caught up.

Allegations of AI cheating are spreading to high scorers on the Legal Education Eligibility Test. Professor Kim says universities and schools are defenseless because they lack specialized equipment. He notes that exams are supervised without the necessary personnel to stop AI. Nearby residents could lose mobile service if jamming devices were used in schools. This creates a conflict between security needs and the privacy of students.

AI has improved its image recognition and reasoning through learning Korean-language data. Cheating tools are diversifying into forms like smart rings and ballpoint pens. Radio detection is limited because it cannot distinguish cheating signals from Wi-Fi. On-device AI may soon eliminate wireless signals entirely, making detection even harder. Some detectors for electronic components cost several million to tens of millions of won.

On November 11, staff trained for smart-glasses detection at the Seoul Metropolitan Office of Education. This training took place in Yongsan-gu, Seoul, eight days before the 2027 CSAT. Professor Choi suggests using radio-wave-blocking pouches for smartphones as a realistic measure. The articles leave open how schools will fund expensive detection gear. They do not say if new laws will allow more jamming devices.

stories.Headline: Taiwan sees higher consumer spending than South Korea despite shared AI chip boom
stories.Summary:
Taiwan experienced a significant rise in consumer spending during the first three quarters of this year, while South Korea saw much slower growth. This divergence occurred despite both nations benefiting from a global boom in artificial intelligence chips. Private consumption in Taiwan increased by 5.4 percent on-year, whereas the corresponding figure for South Korea was only 2.1 percent. These different outcomes reflect how each country's industrial and employment structures distribute the financial gains from the semiconductor industry.

The disparity is driven by the fact that Taiwan employs 910,000 IT manufacturing workers, representing 10.6 percent of its total workforce. In contrast, South Korea has 390,000 such workers, which accounts for only 1.9 percent of its labor force. Taiwan also saw export growth driven by shipment volumes, while South Korea's growth relied more on price increases, with average export prices jumping 182 percent. Additionally, the Taiwanese government distributed approximately 420,000 won per person between November last year and April this year to stimulate spending.

The research department of the Bank of Korea published a report explaining that semiconductor profits in South Korea remain concentrated among high-income earners. These individuals typically spend a smaller portion of their earnings, which limits the overall recovery of domestic demand. The report stated that it is essential to strengthen the spending power of the middle class and reduce costs for low-income households. This approach is necessary to address a K-shaped economic divide where only certain sectors and income groups prosper.

The report further noted that South Korea's semiconductor boom gained momentum in the second half of last year, trailing Taiwan by about one year. Despite a 1.0 percent growth in GDP during the third quarter, private consumption in South Korea actually declined by 0.2 percent. The Bank of Korea warned that domestic demand will remain limited unless the benefits of the chip boom spread to other industries. Future recovery depends on whether the wealth generated by high-tech exports can reach middle and lower-income households.

Articles.Title: AI chip boom jump-starts Taiwan's consumer spending, but not Korea's

stories.Headline: US warns China uses total mobilization strategy to steal AI and semiconductor technology
stories.Summary:
United States authorities have warned that Beijing is executing a total mobilization strategy to steal domestic artificial intelligence and semiconductor technology. This aggressive information war involves government agencies, private companies, and ordinary citizens using methods like honey traps, investments, and cyberattacks. A high-profile scandal involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and a Chinese national named Alice Huang revealed that large quantities of semiconductors were illicitly funneled to China. In 2024, Google engineer Ding Linwei was arrested for allegedly stealing 2,000 pages of confidential AI and supercomputing infrastructure documents. These combined efforts aim to close the technological and military gap between China and the United States.

The operation requires massive human capital, with a European intelligence agency estimating that China deploys approximately 600,000 intelligence and security personnel. This workforce includes the Ministry of State Security, the Ministry of Public Security, and the People's Liberation Army intelligence department. In 2021, an operative named Lai Liren recruited Qian Yuanshi, who had moved to the US in 2015, to photograph the Kitsap naval base in Washington state. In 2023, the wife of Qian photographed a roster of Chinese-American recruits at a US Navy recruiting office in Alhambra, California. These activities are part of a broader effort to secure restricted Nvidia H100, H200, and H800 chips through budgets exceeding 23 billion yuan.

The Ministry of State Security and other agencies are responsible for managing these vast espionage operations across the globe. After their arrests, Qian Yuanshi and Lai Liren stated that they had no freedom to say no to the directives of the Ministry of State Security. The White House accused China in April of using tens of thousands of proxy accounts to extract data from American artificial intelligence systems. Anthropic reported that three Chinese AI companies used over 16 million queries to train their own models using the Claude chatbot. The FBI further estimated that government-backed Chinese hackers outnumber the total US cybersecurity workforce by at least fifty times.

President Xi Jinping views these technologies as core elements for national development despite China spending over 100 billion dollars on semiconductors. United Nations data shows the US holds 75 percent of the top 500 AI supercomputers, while China holds only 15 percent. Evidence from Employment Labs indicates that firms like DeepSeek and Moonshot AI used advanced Blackwell GPUs despite strict US export controls. MI5 revealed in September that a China-linked institution exploited over 100 British researchers to transmit academic findings to intelligence agencies. The US continues to monitor these gray zone operations as Beijing leverages total information warfare to bolster its domestic AI capabilities.

Articles.Title: China AI Espionage — US Warns of Total Mobilization for Tech Theft
