stories.Headline: Ranmore's Sean Peche calls himself a bear on AI stocks as Microsoft forecasts $175 billion in capex
stories.Summary:
Sean Peche, founder and portfolio manager of Ranmore Fund Management, raised concerns about artificial intelligence-related stocks, pointing to substantial infrastructure investment by major technology companies and the possibility that market expectations have moved ahead of financial returns. He said he remains cautious about the sector despite the attention AI companies have received from investors. He said he is a bear for AI-related stocks. He said the large technology companies are spending an absolute fortune on AI capex and that investors need to be very careful. His comments followed recent declines in technology shares and renewed scrutiny of the financial commitments associated with artificial intelligence development.

Microsoft has forecast approximately $175 billion in capital expenditure for the 2026 calendar year, illustrating the scale of investment taking place across the industry. Such spending includes the development of data centres and the acquisition of computing equipment needed to support AI applications. Peche questioned whether future financial returns would be sufficient to support the current level of investment. His concerns reflect uncertainty about the timing and scale of revenue generation from AI services relative to the capital required to develop them. The Nasdaq Composite recorded its largest one-day decline since April 2025 during the previous week.

Peche highlighted the tendency of investors to assume that recent market trends will continue. He argued that past share price performance can influence expectations about future returns, even when underlying financial conditions change. He said history shows that is not always the case. He said Ranmore looks at the numbers, not the story, and that most people listen to the story, but the problem with falling for stories is knowing when you are wrong. He said you have got to exit these waves before they crash, and that in AI there is a big wave going on.

Bernstein said in a recent research note that it did not find the bearish argument on AI particularly compelling. The firm maintained a positive longer-term assessment while acknowledging that near-term market developments were difficult to predict. Companies associated with AI infrastructure were among those affected by the selling. The decline followed Democratic victories in the US midterm elections, which raised concerns among some investors about possible delays to data centre construction. Uncertainty surrounding project schedules added to existing questions about infrastructure expenditure and the financial performance of companies supplying the AI industry.

Meta and Alphabet recorded negative free cash flow during the third quarter, according to the report. The report also stated that Meta, Alphabet and Amazon had suspended share buybacks while increasing their use of debt and equity financing. These developments indicate that infrastructure investment is influencing capital allocation decisions among large technology businesses. Investors are assessing how spending commitments affect cash generation, financing requirements and the capacity to return capital to shareholders. The eventual financial returns from these investments remain an important consideration in evaluating AI-related equities.

The market movements illustrated how expectations about future development activity can influence technology stock valuations. Peche has focused on the risks associated with substantial capital expenditure and elevated expectations, while Bernstein continues to see longer-term investment potential. As companies report further financial results, capital expenditure, cash generation and returns on investment will provide additional information for evaluating the sector. The differing perspectives reflect uncertainty about how quickly companies will generate financial returns from their AI investments. The outlook for artificial intelligence-related stocks remains a subject of debate as major technology companies commit substantial capital to infrastructure development.

Articles.Title: AI Investment Spending Draws Scrutiny as Ranmore’s Sean Peche Questions Technology Stock Outlook

stories.Headline: GitHub adds REST API controls for repository AI Scan enablement
stories.Summary:
GitHub announced REST API controls for repository AI Scan on 13 November 2026, adding a public-preview way to manage enablement across organizations and repositories. The new repository_scan property accepts enabled or disabled. GitHub's REST reference documents GET and PATCH operations at /orgs/{org}/code-scanning/ai-scan and /repos/{owner}/{repo}/code-scanning/ai-scan. These endpoints read or change the setting, while the separate pr_scan property controls pull-request scanning. The change lets teams automate configuration, but enabling the setting does not launch an analysis.

For fine-grained access tokens, the reference specifies Administration write permission at organization level for organization updates and at repository level for repository updates. The November 13 announcement identifies organization owners and security managers as the people who manage the organization setting, with repository administrators able to opt individual repositories out. GitHub says repositories inherit an enabled organization setting and can opt out individually. An organization that disables repository AI Scan prevents its repositories from opting in. Enterprise owners must allow AI Scan through enterprise policy, and an attempt to enable it against that policy returns HTTP 422.

A request can update pr_scan and repository_scan together. If either change is blocked, GitHub says the API returns 422 and leaves both settings unchanged. For institutional automation, that means a rejected combined request cannot be treated as a partial rollout. The repository-backlog documentation lists public organization repositories as eligible, while private or internal organization repositories require GitHub Code Security or GitHub Advanced Security. A GitHub Copilot license is not required, and the November 13 announcement excludes GitHub Enterprise Server.

Users with repository write access still initiate scans manually, and each scan consumes Code Security AI credits. GitHub documents default-branch analysis and says scheduled scans and automatic scans on push are unsupported. Its scanner selects code within a time budget, does not examine every file exhaustively, and does not guarantee detection of every vulnerability. AI findings can also be inaccurate and require review. The institutional implication is a separation of responsibilities, since enterprise policy establishes whether the feature is allowed and organization and repository settings establish where it is enabled.

Execution and assessment establish whether a scan was performed and what happened to its findings, and a configuration inventory alone cannot establish the latter. For a research office coordinating with research software engineers, the new controls offer a way to manage settings across eligible repositories while retaining named responsibility for running scans and assessing alerts. The practical consequence of GitHub's stated limits is that scan findings belong alongside other source-code analysis and research software code review. An enabled flag is not evidence that a codebase is secure or that its scientific results are correct. This extends an existing feature, since GitHub introduced repository AI Scan in public preview on October 28.

That launch put repository findings alongside CodeQL alerts, and the new development is programmatic management of enablement rather than a new general-availability release of the scanner. The sources cited are the GitHub Changelog post "Manage AI Scan for repositories using the REST API" of 13 November 2026 and the GitHub Docs pages on REST API endpoints for code scanning and AI Scan for a repository's backlog, all checked 2026-11-14. The article is licensed under CC-BY 4.0 and was published by the CASRAI Editorial Board on 14 November 2026. The articles do not say when the public preview will end or when the controls will reach general availability. They also do not say how many organizations or repositories have enabled the setting.

stories.Headline: FBI warns that hackers weaponize ARTEX agentic AI framework to automate global intrusions
stories.Summary:
On November 13, 2026, the Federal Bureau of Investigation released a TLP:CLEAR FLASH report regarding the ARTEX autonomous penetration testing framework. This advisory warns that malicious cyber actors have weaponized the open-source, agentic platform to automate intrusions at machine speed. The FBI reports that these actors have used the tool since at least August 2026 to target organizations globally. The report identifies a variety of affected sectors, including financial services, government, technology, defense, semiconductor, energy, healthcare, manufacturing, telecommunications, and legal. These attacks move from initial reconnaissance through data exfiltration using large language model driven agents.

The framework requires external LLM providers, including frontier models like OpenAI GPT and Anthropic Claude, or Chinese models such as DeepSeek, GLM, Grok, and Kimi. The FBI notes that DeepSeek Flash family models are most prevalent due to low cost and a lack of observable guardrails. The developer, known as Autumn-27, released the Go-based code on GitHub in July 2026 and removed the repository on October 8, 2026. Despite this, the tool remains available through mirrors, community forks, archived copies, and a commercial version called ARTEX PRO. Researchers found over 1,600 publicly exposed ARTEX consoles in early November.

The FBI is responsible for the FLASH-20261113-001 report, which it issued through the Internet Crime Complaint Center. The agency stated that agentic offensive frameworks are now a mainstream threat rather than a research curiosity. It warned that the tool allows actors with minimal technical expertise to run complex, multi-target operations simultaneously. The FBI recommended that organizations inventory and shrink their external attack surfaces to mitigate risks. It also asked organizations to vet indicators of compromise before blocking them, as it does not endorse any commercial entity.

Microsoft reported that some intrusions progressed from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours, leaving defenders very little time to respond. The tool affected more than 2,250 downstream tenants of ConnectWise Cloud Backup, an activity Microsoft attributes to the China-state aligned actor Storm-0940. Financially motivated Chinese speakers targeted South Korean banks in early October, exfiltrating personal information from approximately 67,000 individuals. CrowdStrike reported ARTEX use against more than 200 organizations, including Japanese companies. Other affected areas include iOS application distribution infrastructure, which agents modified via exposed cloud credentials.

The FBI based its findings on reports from eleven sources, including Akamai, Google Threat Intelligence Group, Mandiant, Censys, CrowdStrike, Zscaler ThreatLabz, CERT-EU, and Check Point Research. The framework uses a planner agent to convert goals into intents, which are then executed by worker agents in a loop. It abstracts the attack lifecycle across six specialized sub-agents to automate enumeration and exploitation. The tool gained between 1,500 and 2,000 GitHub stars within ten weeks of its initial release. Other similar frameworks, such as PentAGI, have also been used by threat actors.

Organizations must now review every Microsoft 365 tenant where affected ConnectWise applications were authorized and keep those connections disabled. The FBI continues to track infrastructure, such as the host 38.244.50[.]120 and the domain xcai[.]pro, tied to South Korean financial attacks. It also monitors command and control infrastructure from a Storm-3358 campaign that was active as of November 6, 2026. The articles leave open how defenders can effectively coordinate responses when attack speeds compress the detection window. It remains unclear how many other localized variants of the tool are currently active in the wild.

stories.Headline: Uber registers autonomous AI agents in its AI Registry and enforces behavioral authorization at runtime
stories.Summary:
Uber Engineering published an article describing a Secure AI Framework that governs autonomous AI agents across their entire lifecycle, from pre-deployment through runtime enforcement to post-deployment continuous assurance, according to InfoQ on November 15, 2026. The company said traditional identity and API controls can determine whether a user or service may access a resource, but they cannot determine whether an agent's proposed action is appropriate given the user's request, the agent's intended purpose, its permissions, and the context of the interaction. Uber said this gap creates risks including prompt injection, tool and memory poisoning, goal hijacking, behavioral drift, and hallucination-driven actions. The framework was built to decide whether an agent's action is appropriate in context rather than only whether it is permitted.

At provisioning time, agents must be registered in the Uber AI Registry, which establishes identity, ownership, persona, permitted intents, constraints, dependencies, and risk classification, and this process is automated using Argus. Argus analyzes the agent's source code, prompts, configurations, dependencies, exposed endpoints, and tool-invocation paths to identify security weaknesses, and the same approach is enforced for MCP servers and tools the agents use. At runtime, the framework extends the traditional model of policy administration, policy decision, and policy enforcement with behavioral authorization, implemented through the AI Registry, AI guards, and Agent Guard runtime hooks. The AI Registry defines and manages agent policies, personas, intents, and constraints, AI Guards evaluate interactions and proposed actions against those policies, and Agent Guard runtime hooks invoke AI Guard at critical checkpoints and apply its verdict before an interaction or action is allowed to proceed.

After deployment, a Continuous Assurance layer relies on end-to-end observability, auditing, explainability, and replay, comprising a unified execution trace connecting agent actions, tool calls, and security decisions, plus recorded interactions that can be replayed whenever policies and guardrails are updated. Uber identified several challenges in implementing security controls in production, including balancing policy restrictiveness to avoid both excessive false positives and insufficient protection, minimizing runtime latency, reducing developer friction during framework setup, and moving beyond generic controls toward agent-specific policies, which Uber said made enforcement more contextual and precise. Commenting on LinkedIn, UN senior information technology officer Tristan G. said per-agent personas, intents, constraints, and calibration add the most value but come at a significant cost because the effort scales with the number of workflows. He also said the strongest control, restricting agents to explicit constraints, is least privilege rather than a new idea, and that the open question is how this works for agents you do not build, such as vendor or SaaS agents where you cannot insert your own enforcement hooks.

Uber said the least glamorous lesson, explicit intents and constraints per agent, was the one it rated most effective, because generic thresholds failed since every agent has a different purpose and risk profile, and it said the cost is flexibility, which it says is worth paying. Uber's Secure AI Framework is still evolving, with plans to expand its capabilities across all the areas outlined above, and the company said there is much more to the framework than can be covered in the summary, encouraging readers to consult the original article for a comprehensive overview. The InfoQ article appeared alongside other coverage, including a report that Google finds technical debt can derail coding agents through what it calls agent distraction, a report that LinkedIn replaced Argo CD with a custom GitOps engine for Kubernetes deployments, and a report that GitHub made agentic workflows generally available with isolation and budget controls. The articles do not say what specific expansions Uber plans or when they will arrive.

Articles.Title: Uber's Secure AI Framework Governs Autonomous AI Agents Across Their Lifecycle

stories.headline_source: Uber's Secure AI Framework Governs Autonomous AI Agents Across Their Lifecycle

stories.Headline: Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney criticizes Steam's AI disclosure label as unfair to developers
stories.Summary:
Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney criticized Valve's Steam storefront over its rule that developers must add a label when a game uses artificial intelligence, in comments reported by GamesBeat and covered by MP1st on November 14, 2026. Sweeney has been critical of Steam on social media in recent months, and this time he defended AI while attacking the disclosure requirement. His remarks came amid a growing debate about AI in the gaming industry. He said large-scale game development will be totally changed by AI and that teams which do not adopt it will be left behind and become uneconomical compared with their peers. Sweeney argued that one team may soon make a game four times more efficiently, and perhaps 10 times more efficiently, than another team making the same game, leaving no way to compete the old way.

He said no game developer has 75% to 95% profit margins that they can risk by not being as productive as possible. He rejected the idea that the label simply informs players, saying he does not buy it in the slightest, and argued that reviews already cover a game's quality, scope and entertainment value. He said AI can be used to make good games and bad games, and that tying AI to bad games is unfair to developers who use it well. Sweeney described the label as a guilt by association pattern that all developers need to push back on. He said a large resistance movement against AI seems focused on bullying developers into not adopting it by attacking individuals and review-bombing projects, and that he has been trying to make his views known to as many developers as possible.

He said the industry has to power through this and build games with maximum acceleration because it is a survival issue for all companies in the industry. He also said the label is absolutely being used by anti-AI advocates to undermine developers' reputations and the viability of their projects. The article says nearly 20% of games released on Steam in 2025 disclosed using generative AI, an 800% increase from the previous year. It also notes that Metal Gear Solid and Death Stranding creator Hideo Kojima has been both fascinated and cautious about artificial intelligence. The article asks whether players have a right to know how the games they buy are made and whether AI was used, and it does not say what Valve or Steam has done in response or what happens next.

Articles.Title: Epic Games CEO Sees Steam’s Policies as “Unfair to Developers Who Use AI to Make Good Games”

stories.Headline: Noah Sander launches Zionist Investor to pair AI property search with Israeli real estate experts
stories.Summary:
Noah Sander, a Canadian-born real estate agent who made aliyah and served in the IDF, launched Zionist Investor, a platform for international buyers of Israeli property, and it has been live for several months. He announced it in a ynetnews.com article dated 2026-11-14T06:00:00Z, writing that he had spent years helping overseas buyers and had shared his experience in columns on ynet. The platform combines AI-powered property searches with personalized guidance from Israeli real estate professionals. Sander wrote that buying property in Israel for foreigners remains far more complicated than it needs to be. He said he built the platform after asking why someone should have to speak with five different agents and visit ten different websites.

Zionist Investor lets prospective buyers browse Israeli residential developments, compare prices and locations, and explore properties on an interactive map. Its central feature is AIgent Z, an AI-powered real estate advisor that helps buyers compare Israeli cities, assess budgets and identify suitable properties. Sander gave the example of a buyer who insists on Tel Aviv but, after discussing budget, lifestyle and preferences, may find a nearby city connected by light rail offers a more suitable property at a significantly more attractive price point. He wrote that AIgent Z's knowledge, personality and conversational style were shaped by his years of client conversations and his approach to advising buyers. The platform pairs the AI with a real team of professionals on the ground in Israel who guide buyers through the entire purchase process.

Sander said he does not believe artificial intelligence should replace human expertise in real estate, calling buying property a high-trust industry. He said no amount of technology eliminates the importance of experience, judgment and accountability, and that experienced professionals still matter enormously when evaluating an opportunity, understanding a transaction, negotiating terms and navigating the purchase. He said the goal is not to remove the human element but to give buyers tools and knowledge to engage professionals from a position of understanding rather than a blank slate. He wrote that the challenge is not that people lack information but that they lack a clear, reliable way to make sense of it all in one place. He said clear information is crucial when making a major financial decision like buying property in Israel.

Sander wrote that a bad investment does not magically become a good one simply because it is located in Israel, and that prices, financing costs, location and long-term appreciation are essential considerations. He said that for many Jews around the world purchasing property in Israel carries an additional dimension, such as a connection to family history, a place for holidays, a future home for their children or a foothold in the Jewish homeland. He described buyers who arrive with spreadsheets and investment models applied in other countries, others with childhood memories of visiting Israel, some thinking about retirement, others making aliyah, and many who already live in Israel. He said there is no single reason to buy property in Israel and there should not be a one-size-fits-all approach. He wrote that he grew up in Canada, made aliyah, served in the IDF and built his life and career in Israel.

Sander wrote that he had approached the problem the way most real estate professionals do, one client conversation at a time, spending hours understanding a buyer's priorities, explaining neighborhood differences, identifying suitable properties and guiding them through the Israeli market. He said he still does that today and genuinely enjoys it. He wrote that technology has transformed how people travel, manage finances and make major purchasing decisions, yet discovering and evaluating real estate in Israel, particularly from abroad, remains surprisingly fragmented. He said he wanted to build something bringing together real opportunities, market knowledge, personalized guidance and professional expertise in one place, leveraging AI, rather than another website filled with listings and real estate jargon. He wrote that he and his team spent the past year building the platform.

Sander wrote that the platform's ambition is bigger than helping someone find their next property, and that they are building Zionist Investor to become the natural starting point for Jews around the world considering purchasing property in Israel. He said it is available for anyone to explore. He wrote that buyers can begin without scheduling an appointment just to ask their first questions, and that the platform is designed to help people figure out what they are looking for rather than requiring them to know before they start. He said the goal is to help people ask better questions and approach their property search with greater clarity. The article does not say what the platform costs, how many properties or developments it lists, or when it will expand beyond its current features.

Articles.Title: Buying property in Israel made easier: where AI meets human expertise

stories.Headline: P.E.I. RCMP say AI-generated child abuse material rises to a third of online investigations
stories.Summary:
Prince Edward Island RCMP say there has been a notable increase in child sex abuse material made using artificial intelligence across parts of the province. P.E.I. RCMP senior communications adviser Scott Ferris said in an email it is a safe estimate that one third of Island RCMP online child abuse investigations now involve AI-generated material. That estimate considers only areas under RCMP jurisdiction, which excludes Charlottetown, Summerside and Kensington. Internet watchdog reports indicate a trending global rise in AI-generated child sex abuse content, previously known as child pornography.

In St. John’s, N.L., this summer, a 17-year-old boy was charged with nearly 60 counts related to the creation and distribution of child sexual abuse material. Police allege he used AI tools to alter images of 19 minors and make them explicit. The 17-year-old boy, who was hit with 58 criminal charges, faces 19 counts of making child sexual exploitation material after allegedly using AI to digitally alter photos of teenage girls. In an email, Summerside police reported at least one instance where a suspect used AI-generated child sex abuse material in a sextortion attempt this year.

Const. Stephanie Myers with the Royal Newfoundland Constabulary told CBC News On the Go host Krissy Holmes the case is probably one of our first if not the first specifically involving AI being used to create child sexual exploitation material. Mauranne Ste-Marie, senior research analyst with the national RCMP’s sensitive and specialized investigative services unit, said in many cases AI-generated content is either produced to create material of a child that is in the family or the neighbourhood of that offender. She said it increases the demand for the material and normalizes the abuse. Ste-Marie said it is a stepping stone and one step closer to sexually abusing a child, and that after viewing material for a certain number of weeks or months it may not meet their needs anymore.

Jacques Marcoux, director of research for the Canadian Centre for Child Protection, said AI-generated or manipulated material is increasingly used in sextortion attempts. His organization operates Cybertip.ca, Canada’s national tip line for reporting online child abuse. Marcoux said that in lieu of being able to trick the child into giving them an intimate image, offenders will simply create one using AI, then threaten to release images online claiming they are real. P.E.I. RCMP media relations officer Gavin Moore said there were 26 reported instances of sextortion last year in Island areas under RCMP jurisdiction, and noted reporting rates are typically very low for this type of crime.

Certain generative AI models, which are ultimately trained on images of real people, can create abusive images or videos either in the likeness of a specific person or by generating a non-existent, synthetic child from scratch. Some offenders also use AI-powered nudify tools to create explicit deepfakes, realistic fake images or videos of a victim. Mainstream generative AI models like ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude have strict safeguards in place that are designed to block the generation of any child abuse material, and confirmed violations are supposedly then reported to law enforcement. To circumvent these controls, offenders often rely on freely available open-source software to generate abusive media offline, where it is far harder to detect, and since these models are typically used without an internet connection, any exploitative content they produce can be incredibly difficult for police to track.

Under the criminal code, AI-generated child abuse is treated the same as authentic abuse material, and altering or generating explicit media with AI through written prompts can constitute making child sexual abuse material. In April 2023, 17-year-old Harry Burke from Fortune Bridge, P.E.I., took his own life hours after telling his parents he had been victimized by a sextortion scam. Ste-Marie said every time you post a picture or a video of yourself or your children there is a risk it could be used by someone with bad intentions, and one recommendation is to take precautions like covering a child’s face in photos. She said your child is never responsible for the creation of that type of content, even if they posted images online and they feel like it was their fault, and they have the right to post and to share without thinking that someone will use it against them.

Articles.Title: Rise in AI-generated child sex abuse fuels real-life risk, police and experts warn

stories.Headline: Malaysia probes Megaspeed unit over possible illegal re-export of AI chips
stories.Summary:
Malaysia's trade ministry announced on 13 November 2026 that it is probing a company called Speedmatrix regarding the movement of AI chips. This company is the Malaysian unit of Megaspeed, which is based in Singapore, and is currently under official investigation. The ministry is checking if advanced AI chips imported by the unit were later re-exported to other countries illegally. This probe is being conducted together with the customs department to see if the shipments complied with Malaysian law. The investigation follows reports that high performance chips linked to an Nvidia case may have been diverted from Malaysia.

Speedmatrix is a tenant at data centres in Malaysia and can bring AI chips into the country without a permit. However, since July 2025, any entity that wants to export, re-export, transship, or transit US AI chips must obtain permits. Giving customs false information about these items is a serious offence, and the ministry is checking for such violations. The ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry, known as MITI, is working closely with authorities in Singapore and the US. MITI is also considering stronger controls where necessary to prevent the illegal movement of these high performance semiconductor chips.

MITI stated that Speedmatrix has never been cleared of wrongdoing and that official visits to its facilities were regular monitoring. The ministry said it is working with the customs department to establish if any chips were re-exported to other countries. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said there is no indication that AI chips linked to Megaspeed were shipped out of Malaysia. He added that Malaysia has received no request for assistance from Singapore or the US but will collaborate on probes. Ibrahim stated that the government wants to make sure the rules are being followed regarding the movement of these chips.

Singapore is also investigating Megaspeed because servers containing chips were exported through Singapore to Malaysia but suspected of going elsewhere. Singaporean authorities barred Alice Huang from re-entering the country in February for giving investigators inaccurate information about her Megaspeed role. A US senator alleged that the firm may have been used to get around US controls on advanced semiconductor chips. The US alleges that Alice Huang spied for China, although China denies this and Singapore says she was not investigated. The Nvidia scandal has reportedly wiped almost half a trillion dollars off the market capitalization of the American chip giant.

Megaspeed is under scrutiny over ties between former executive Alice Huang and Jensen Huang, who was the chief executive of Nvidia. Jensen Huang resigned over an affair with Alice Huang, who is a Chinese national and a suspected spy for China. Megaspeed is accused of steering Nvidia AI chips to China despite US export rules designed to slow Beijing's AI development. The reports describe the chips generally as advanced or high performance, but they do not identify the specific chip model. None of the reports states that a re-export from Malaysia has been established, as the checking is still underway.

Megaspeed stated on its website that it takes its US compliance obligations extremely seriously but did not comment on the MITI statement. The next confirmable developments include the outcome of the customs check and any official assistance requests from Singapore or the US. It remains open whether the US Commerce Department will release official text regarding remote access through third country data centres. The articles leave open whether Malaysia will actually announce a change to its permit regime to strengthen its current controls. No statement has been provided by Nvidia regarding the probe into the re-export of chips through the Speedmatrix unit.

Articles.Title: Malaysia Probes Whether Megaspeed Unit Re-exported AI Chips

stories.Headline: Visa warns AI shopping agents can be fooled by counterfeit merchants as Adobe forecasts AI retail traffic to rise 130%
stories.Summary:
Adobe forecasts that AI-driven traffic to US retail sites will rise 130% year over year this season, November 1 to December 31, and 159% on Thanksgiving. It expects a record $275.1 billion in US online spending. Amazon renamed Rufus as Alexa for Shopping on May 13, 2026. Its Buy for Me button lets Amazon buy an item from another merchant's website for you. Prime members can ask it to auto-buy an item when it hits a target price.

Google's agentic checkout in Search and AI Mode can buy from eligible US merchants with Google Pay. Google says it always asks permission first and buys only after you confirm the purchase and shipping details. Meta's Muse agent, launched in September, picks products and proceeds to checkout with your approval. Amazon notifies you after the order is placed and gives you a free 24-hour cancellation window. Scamwise users report a new fake store roughly every three minutes, according to its October holiday report.

In the US, the Fair Credit Billing Act lets you dispute credit card charges for things you didn't accept or weren't delivered as agreed, as the FTC explains. Regulation Z section 1026.13 gives you 60 days from the first statement showing the error to send your dispute. Debit cards fall under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act and its Regulation E. Its definition of unauthorized excludes transfers made by someone you gave access to, unless you told your bank that access was withdrawn. Per the FTC, the most you might owe for unauthorized credit card charges is $50, and for a debit card it can reach $500 if you report late.

Visa has warned that AI shopping agents can be deceived by sophisticated counterfeit merchants engineered specifically to exploit them. In October, Inc. reported Visa repeating that warning for the holiday season. Savi Security's Scamwise holiday report, published October 20, says a new fake store is reported roughly every three minutes, about 500 a day. Fake holiday-themed stores reported to it grew fivefold in the previous 60 days. Nearly 40% were less than 90 days old when first reported, and 85% were gone within two weeks.

The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security put the core idea in one line in its online shopping guidance: treat AI-generated recommendations as guidance, not assurances of legitimacy. Fortune reported in April that Amex pledged to protect cardmembers from erroneous transactions made by agents registered with Amex. In September, six banks, including Bank of America, Capital One, ING and NatWest, published shared principles for trusted agentic commerce. Fox Business reported that their paper flags agents requesting customers' card details and entering them directly into websites as one of the risks. A study from Columbia Law School's Center for Law and the Economy, reported by Reuters in July, tested Amazon's Alexa for Shopping and Walmart's Sparky.

The study found the assistants can often detect when Made in USA product labels are false, yet those labels stayed in front of shoppers. The Alliance for American Manufacturing has since asked the FTC to open an inquiry into AI shopping assistants. Scamwise found an impossible discount in one in four scam stores. The Scamwise report says fake delivery texts, order confirmations, and refund scams spike after big shopping days. In the US, report scams to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov, and in Canada, report to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre.

Articles.Title: Before You Let AI Do Your Holiday Shopping: 7 Rules From a Security Expert

stories.Headline: SMIC reports profit surge as China accelerates development of independent AI industry
stories.Summary:
Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corp reported a 123.4 percent year-on-year increase in net profit for the third quarter of 2026. This financial growth occurred as Jensen Huang resigned as the chief executive officer of Nvidia, sparking debates about American technology policy. These events highlight a broader trend where growing market demand is providing stronger commercial returns for the Chinese semiconductor industry. The domestic AI sector is now operating from a firmer industrial foundation than it possessed several years ago.

The current situation requires Chinese technology companies to adapt their computing systems to a growing range of homegrown processors. SMIC invested 258.4 million dollars into research and development during the third quarter alone to support this transition. Companies such as Huawei and Cambricon are expanding their market presence to create a self-sustaining AI computing ecosystem. This shift reduces the vulnerability of the industry to external restrictions and decreases the overall dependence on American technology.

The Global Times suggests that the resignation of Jensen Huang may weaken the influence of commercial interests in Washington. They argue that national security concerns are now dominating US technology policy over the commercial arguments previously made by chip companies. The publication claims that tightening export controls has actually accelerated Chinese efforts to build an independent AI industry. They believe that further US restrictions could prompt other Asian economies to diversify their supply chains away from American technology.

The US government is reportedly considering requiring permits for global AI chip sales from companies like Nvidia and AMD. Such measures may lead to greater scrutiny for chip and data center industries across Southeast Asia. If these policies are implemented, US chipmakers might be among the first to bear the costs due to intertwined supply chains. China intends to continue gathering pace in AI development regardless of the political tug-of-war in Washington.

Articles.Title: GT Voice: US chip curb debate cannot stymie China's AI progress - Global Times

stories.headline_source: GT Voice: US chip curb debate cannot stymie China's AI progress

stories.Headline: Voters reject data center measures in 40 of 41 local ballots across 10 states
stories.Summary:
Voters rejected AI data centers in dozens of communities in the 2026 midterm elections, with data centers on the ballot both directly and indirectly. A total of 41 local ballot initiatives concerning data centers in 10 states were up for a vote. All but one resulted in measures to restrict or limit their development. In Ohio’s race for a U.S. Senate seat, Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown hammered incumbent Jon Husted for his past support of data centers. In Texas, Gina Hinojosa made Republican Gov. Greg Abbott’s track record of supporting tax breaks for data centers a focal point of her winning campaign.

Her victory marked a historic break with decades of Republican control in the state, and as governor-elect she immediately reaffirmed her campaign pledge to pursue legislation protecting Texans from data centers. According to NBC exit poll data, 56% of voters felt that data centers were a major or even a crucial factor in influencing their congressional vote. For Black voters, the share was even higher, at 68%. The margins for the restrictions were large, averaging 49 percentage points. The one restrictive local measure that failed to pass was in Harwood, North Dakota, population around 800.

Barbara A. Trish is a professor of political science, with a Ph.D. from The Ohio State University, who studies political parties, electoral politics and technology. Her forthcoming book, “Democratic Intelligence: Navigating Electoral Politics in an AI World,” examines how the adoption of this technology is reshaping established practices and power dynamics in campaigns. She writes that the widespread pushback against data centers is now part of the narrative explaining the dramatic results of the 2026 midterms. She writes that the seeds of this argument were in place before the election, picking up on unusual alliances that marked the data center opposition. She writes that it matters little whether the data center electoral narrative is accurate, and that so far the reported evidence is limited.

The Annenberg Public Policy Center asked Americans in mid-2026 whether they support or oppose having data centers in their communities, and opposition was stronger among Democrats, at 69%, than Republicans, at 54%, but it crossed party lines. Communities as disparate as deeply red Edgewater, Florida, and solidly blue Alhambra, California, voted to prohibit them. Of the 56% of voters who said data centers played a “major” or “crucial” role in their vote, approximately two-thirds were Democrats and one-third Republicans. In cities and counties, zoning fights are drawing environmentalists, voters reeling under high electricity costs, local-control advocates and farmers concerned that data centers eat up land. President Donald Trump pushed back, suggesting that data center opponents want their communities to be “backwards and poor.”

Several weeks before Election Day, the House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act by a 417-3 vote, and the bill would require states to consider adopting a policy that data centers pay for the upgrades necessary to meet their high electricity needs. The three nay House votes were from progressives who felt the bill’s measures, which would be voluntary, didn’t go far enough to protect consumers. Similar concerns killed the Senate version. Data centers are key components in artificial intelligence infrastructure, housing the computing resources used to train AI models, and these massive facilities guzzle energy and water and are very noisy. Many Americans argue that their costs, in terms of land use, higher utility bills and environmental degradation, outweigh the benefits.

Brookings Institution scholars anticipate that the newly elected Congress will take up the issue again, this time with a directive to states to establish mandatory, not voluntary, requirements. Trish writes that as the 2028 presidential primaries come into focus, many Democratic and Republican hopefuls should be expected to emphasize their support for data center restrictions and bans as they throw their hats into the ring. She writes that we need to know where losing candidates stood on data centers, not just the winners. She writes that despite a 98% success rate across the 41 local ballot measures, it’s hard to gauge how much resistance there is to the more than 600 proposed data centers that are slated to be built. She cites Elon Musk’s post on Nov. 4 on X, his social media platform, that “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” and the sell-off of data center-related stocks the next day.

Articles.Title: Opinion: Voters rejected AI data centers in dozens of communities as 2026 blue wave crested

stories.Headline: Jane King hosts Bloomberg show on sovereign AI and fusion energy
stories.Summary:
New to The Street Show #780 premieres tonight, Saturday, November 14, 2026, at 6:30 p.m. ET on Bloomberg Television as sponsored programming. Jane King hosts conversations on sovereign AI, fusion energy, global private credit and partner-led streaming infrastructure. The show airs across the United States, Latin America, the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) and Southeast Asia. Guests include Ralf R. Debbas of Robo.ai Inc. (NASDAQ:AIIO), Dr. Jasem Al Mansoori of ALIF Holding, Mansoor Ali Khan of Neurovia AI, Brent Nelson of American Fusion Inc. (OTCQB:AMFN), Bilal Adam of Stewards Investment Capital and William "Bill" Mobley of FreeCast, Inc. (NASDAQ:CAST).

In a three-executive panel, Jane King asks where Robo.ai fits in the AI investment cycle. Debbas describes Robo.ai as a UAE-based, Nasdaq-listed group connecting regional technology with global market reach. Its main operating businesses are Neurovia AI, focused on visual data efficiency, ALIF Holding, which brings industrial integration, manufacturing and execution, and Quantum Core Capital (QC Capital), which contributes operating revenue and is developing AI applications including AI-generated video and content creation. In a company demonstration shown on air, a 12.15 GB 4K video file was reduced to 421 MB, a reduction of more than 96%, and actual results depend on deployment conditions and use-case validation.

Debbas said the ambition is to help build sovereign AI capabilities within the UAE itself and the wider region, technology that can be deployed, supported and developed locally. Al Mansoori, whose ALIF Holding is Robo.ai's Abu Dhabi-based industrial group, draws on more than 30 years at the UAE Ministry of Interior and said this experience taught him the importance of reliable solutions and strong local support. Khan notes that the large majority of the world's data is visual and unstructured, and said the goal is to address the main costs of AI, storage, compute, transmission and power, and make AI more affordable and sustainable. Nelson said an independent third-party reviewer recently completed an on-site evaluation of the Texatron™ aneutronic fusion engine, with a final report expected later this month, and that the draft highlights look good so far.

Nelson, who added the CEO title in late October, says his priorities for the next six months include closing on the company's North Texas "Ranch" facility, which American Fusion expects by Thanksgiving, and developing the property. The company is also moving from its temporary facility into new lab and office space and plans to build its own testing bunker at the Ranch, and Nelson said the Texatron is still operating and testing daily and the data is getting better. Adam, a chartered accountant from South Africa with a background in investment banking, describes building a business with activities spanning South Africa, Mauritius, the United States and Monaco, and discusses a relationship with Nasdaq-listed Stewards, Inc. (NASDAQ:SWRD), a U.S.-based diversified financial platform led by President and CEO Shaun Quin that provides financing to small businesses across the United States. Stewards Investment Capital is affiliated with, but separate from, Stewards, Inc., and Adam highlights telecommunications tower investments aimed at expanding connectivity and financial inclusion in rural African communities.

Mobley explains that FreeCast is not another streaming service but provides software infrastructure letting telecom companies, wireless carriers, internet providers, satellite companies and membership organizations launch their own branded entertainment hubs, offering free television, premium subscriptions, sports, advertising and commerce. Mobley said partners bring the customers and FreeCast brings the media and monetization technology, and he walks through PEAC, the company's metric for partner-enabled addressable customers, which measures potential distribution reach through enterprise agreements and does not represent active users, paying subscribers or confirmed revenue. Mobley said FreeCast does not need Netflix to lose for it to succeed and wants more content and more services participating in its marketplaces. The broadcast also covers SafeSpace Global Corporation (OTCID:SSGC), T-REX Acquisition Corp. (OTCQB:TRXA), Big Sky Industrial (NASDAQ:BSIN) and Acurx Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (NASDAQ:ACXP), whose lead drug ibezapolstat has the FDA agreeing to consider a future application based on two planned trials, Pathfinder and Aspire.

Following the broadcast, every segment will be distributed across the New to The Street TV and NewsOut YouTube channels, which together have more than 6.6 million subscribers. New to The Street's Meet The Companies tour brings presenting companies face to face with family offices, accredited investors and high-net-worth individuals in three cities in 2027, with New York on Thursday, January 7, 2027, at The Hudson Yards Penthouse, 455 Tenth Avenue PH, New York, NY 10018, the week before the Needham Growth Conference, with a cocktail reception on Wednesday, January 6, Atlantic City on Thursday, January 28, 2027, and Las Vegas on June 17-18, 2027. Each event hosts up to 20 presenting companies, with 20-minute slots that include a 15-minute presentation and Q&A, and for Atlantic City and Las Vegas presenters New to The Street pays for your stay. Founded in 2009, New to The Street is a sponsored and syndicated business television platform co-founded and led by CEO Vince Caruso that has worked with more than 200 public companies.

stories.Headline: Moe Asnani proposes converting old Arizona cannabis farms into mini data centers
stories.Summary:
Moe Asnani, the former owner of two D2 Dispensaries in Tucson, has set his sights on converting old cannabis farms into mini data centers, according to an Arizona Public Media report. The idea comes as cannabis growers in the US face falling prices, rising costs and increased competition. In Arizona, cannabis sales peaked in 2024, with an oversupply of marijuana pushing prices down. As a result, some growers are considering selling their cultivation facilities or finding new uses for them. Asnani believes these facilities could be repurposed to support the growing demand for computing power.

Asnani told Arizona Public Media that a lot more cannabis is grown in Arizona than Arizonans use, and that many people are getting out of the business, like himself, at least on the cultivation side. He said these facilities can potentially be repurposed to be mini data center nodes. Indoor cannabis farms already require substantial amounts of electricity and water to support lighting, climate control and plant growth. His proposal is based on converting existing buildings rather than constructing entirely new facilities, an approach known as adaptive reuse. The proposed mini data centers would be smaller than large facilities such as the Project Blue data center being built near the Tucson fairgrounds.

Asnani's former company, D2, estimated that its 18,000-square-foot cultivation facility used around 1.7 million gallons of water in 2024. For comparison, Project Blue could use up to 31 million gallons of water annually. Existing infrastructure does not automatically make a cannabis farm suitable for a data center, and operators would still need to assess power capacity, cooling systems, internet connectivity and other requirements. Tucson City Council member Paul Cunningham said he is willing to explore the possibility of converting former cannabis facilities into data centers. Cunningham said data centers are dirty words and everybody knows that, and that no one wants to build a brand new data center anywhere.

Cunningham said that if there are buildings that were using that amount of water and that amount of energy already in their previous function and it can be done without being invasive, he is OK with exploring that option. Asnani believes smaller data centers could help create what he calls sovereign AI, allowing users to control their own data processing rather than relying entirely on large technology companies. He said the whole idea is if you create these smaller nodes where people control their own data, where they are not at the mercy of other people's updates, that is kind of where the idea came in, because he believes in decentralization. The concept could appeal to organizations looking for more local control over their computing infrastructure. However, smaller data centers are not automatically more secure than larger ones, and experts say cybersecurity depends on network safeguards and the people managing the systems.

They state that Cunningham said he is willing to explore the possibility, and that Asnani believes smaller data centers could help create sovereign AI.

stories.Headline: Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO amid scandals and suspected spying
stories.Summary:
Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on November 12, 2026, following a series of scandals. He left the world's first five trillion dollar company amid reports of inappropriate romantic relationships. These events occurred during a volatile couple of weeks for the dominant artificial intelligence trade. The situation involved suspected spying and a sex scandal involving the former chief executive. US authorities suspect one of his romantic partners was a Chinese asset.

The company shed about 500 billion US dollars in market value during one week. Nvidia stock dropped 14 per cent at the open before closing down 4 per cent. Its price to forward earnings ratio is now around 11 after a 15 per cent swoon. The S&P 500 index is down 4 per cent from its peak last month. AI and Big Tech stocks account for roughly 35 per cent of that index.

One insider told the Financial Times that Huang was viewed as a god to be worshipped. The author states that placing immense power in flat corporate structures is a mistake. This failure shows that billionaires are fallible mortals who hold too much global wealth. The author suggests that the current stock prices may be cheap as chips. The text notes that the AI concept has not collapsed in on itself.

Retail investors rushed to buy the stock on November 10 and November 12. Vanda Research reported that opening inflows on November 12 were 40 times bigger than usual. US midterm elections in early November showed a backlash against the power of billionaires. Bond market buyers are affected because they cannot load up on individual themes. These buyers are struggling to digest borrowing for various data centre projects.

The AI trade is characterized by mind bending levels of concentration at every level. Stock markets in the US and South Korea are extremely top heavy with tech stocks. Bond markets are reaching the limits of what they can absorb from Big Tech. This has caused the taps for cheap borrowed money to squeeze shut. Global markets have faced larger tests since the Covid 19 pandemic.

Jensen Huang now faces a grilling in Congress over his relationship with a suspected asset. The S&P 500 remains caught between rising interest rates and strong AI excitement. Markets may remain resilient unless another ugly twist occurs in the Nvidia soap opera. The articles leave open whether the Nvidia scandal will get worse before it improves. It remains unclear if robots will eventually steal jobs or laser people in half.

Articles.Title: AI believers hold the line after Nvidia ructions - The Business Times

stories.Headline: European Parliament votes to regulate AI in democratic processes and plans an AI observatory
stories.Summary:
The European Parliament voted to regulate artificial intelligence in democratic processes on Thursday, November 13, 2026. Members of the European Parliament passed a resolution regarding the institutional aspects of AI and European integration. The final vote count was 405 in favor, 133 against, and 60 abstentions. This action seeks to ensure oversight and compliance with the fundamental values of the European Union. MEPs assessed the opportunities and concerns of using AI in public administration and democratic processes.

The resolution requires that AI use within EU institutions remains human-centered and subject to human oversight. It proposes a budget-neutral administrative unit called the European Parliament AI observatory to support parliamentary committees. The text calls for a reform of European electoral law and new rights in the Charter of Fundamental Rights. These new rights include algorithmic transparency and the protection of personal identity and likeness. The EU also seeks an international agreement on security and societal risks modeled on nuclear non-proliferation.

Rapporteur Manolis Kefalogiannis of the EPP from Greece was responsible for the report on these institutional aspects. He stated that AI advances in leaps rather than linearly, so Europe must take the lead in shaping it. He paraphrased Abraham Lincoln to say that AI should be by, for, and with humans. This approach ensures that AI does not become the last invention that humans ever need to create. He believes the European Union must lead the way in managing these technological advancements.

MEPs argue that AI can assist with evidence-based policymaking and the evaluation of EU law. However, they state that AI must never replace human political responsibility or result in purely automated decisions. The resolution notes that AI increasingly shapes public discourse, electoral processes, political communication, and decision-making. These changes affect the institutional balance of the Union and the fundamental rights of its citizens. The members believe that safeguards must be built without hampering competitiveness or innovation.

The articles state that European AI tools should be prioritized to ensure strategic autonomy across the AI value chain. The EU intends to scale up European technology to reduce dependence on non-European AI systems. This background emphasizes the transformative potential of AI in supporting the lawmaking processes of the European Union. The Parliament views AI as a tool for simplifying and evaluating existing EU laws. This effort is part of a broader strategy to maintain European values in a digital age.

Next, the proposed AI observatory will perform ex post evaluations of AI-related legislation for the Parliament. It will also analyze how AI impacts democratic processes and the institutional balance of the Union. The EU will seek a leading role in establishing the proposed international agreement on AI security. The articles leave open how the budget-neutral observatory will be funded and staffed. They also do not specify the exact timeline for reforming the European electoral law.

stories.Headline: Applied Materials forecasts first-quarter revenue above estimates due to AI chip demand
stories.Summary:
Applied Materials announced on November 12 that its fiscal first-quarter revenue is expected to exceed Wall Street estimates. This growth is driven by chipmakers who are increasing their spending to meet the massive demand for artificial intelligence chips and memory. The company reported that its fourth-quarter adjusted profit reached US$4.16 per share, which surpassed the average analyst prediction of US$4.05. Its stock has already increased by approximately 48% throughout 2026 as a result of these market trends.

The company forecasts fiscal first-quarter revenue of about US$11.1 billion, plus or minus US$500 million, beating the LSEG estimate of US$10.89 billion. Fourth-quarter Semiconductor Systems revenue rose 64% to US$8 billion, while sales in China grew 35% to US$2.64 billion despite representing 25% of total revenue. Applied Materials is also working with Apple at its Austin, Texas, facility to increase the domestic production of chipmaking equipment. These figures highlight a significant surge in the acquisition of tools for wafer fabrication processes.

Chief executive Gary Dickerson stated that 2027 could be another record year for both the company and the broader market. He noted that demand for wafer fab equipment should rise by more than 30% and that customers are requesting tools sooner. Bob O’Donnell, the chief analyst at TECHnalysis Research, observed that current market metrics show demand remains very strong. He added that foundries and chipmakers are currently purchasing as much equipment as they possibly can to keep up.

stories.Headline: Nvidia investigates Jensen Huang after allegations of ties to Chinese intelligence agent
stories.Summary:
Allegations emerged on November 11, 2026, that Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman named Alice Huang. This woman was a former executive at the Singaporean cloud computing firm Megaspeed and is reportedly linked to intelligence services in Beijing. The scandal has prompted the board of Nvidia to investigate if their leader was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. Meanwhile, Singapore police are investigating Megaspeed for suspected breaches of domestic laws regarding the illegal transfer of restricted technology.

The situation may require the United States to implement tougher enforcement of export restrictions on advanced artificial intelligence chips. Washington might focus more closely on neocloud companies in Southeast Asia, specifically in trading hubs like Singapore and Malaysia. This follows a recent case where four individuals and four companies in Singapore faced fraud charges over servers shipped to Malaysia. Additionally, Malaysian customs seized 30 servers containing advanced AI chips worth about 12.1 million US dollars last month.

Alex Capri from the National University of Singapore Business School believes a major crackdown on cloud computing companies is coming. He stated that these services have acted as a loophole allowing global companies to rent computing power without buying chips. Jay Goldberg of Seaport Research Partners suggested that rivals like AMD, Broadcom, and Huawei could benefit from this fallout. He noted that AMD and Broadcom have relatively limited exposure to China compared to the current market leader.

The United States and China remain at odds over critical technologies and the movement of sensitive semiconductors. While the US eased some licensing policies in January, Beijing still requires approval for Nvidia chip imports to promote domestic alternatives. Capri believes this scandal will serve as fuel for the fire regarding China's push for chip self-sufficiency. Nvidia shares fell more than 5 per cent on Tuesday as the company faces this period of leadership uncertainty.

stories.Headline: Algernon Yau warns Hong Kong to prepare for a potential global AI slowdown
stories.Summary:
Secretary for Commerce and Economic Development Algernon Yau warned on Sunday, November 15, 2026, that the global development of artificial intelligence might experience a slowdown. This caution follows a period of significant economic growth, as Hong Kong exports surged by nearly 65 percent in September compared to the previous year. This increase represents the fastest monthly year-on-year growth the city has seen in more than four decades. Yau believes the region must remain vigilant because the current upward trend is heavily driven by AI advancements.

To maintain its status as an international trade centre, Hong Kong must adjust its strategies and expand its trade network. The city needs to pay close attention to global trends because different countries hold varying views on how AI should advance. These external influences could cause the current boom to subside, requiring the SAR to seek new opportunities. Yau also mentioned the upcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen as a way to build a regional community.

Speaking on a Commercial Radio programme, Yau explained that the global landscape is constantly evolving and subject to external pressures. He stated that the nation hopes economies within the Asia-Pacific region can cooperate to achieve mutual development. The minister emphasized that the city must be prepared for shifts in technology to ensure long-term economic stability. By monitoring international trends, Hong Kong can better navigate the potential decline of the artificial intelligence boom.

stories.Headline: KAIST researchers develop visual speech recognition that turns lip movements into text
stories.Summary:
A research team from the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology developed a visual speech recognition technology on November 15, 2026. Led by Professor Yong-Man Ro of the School of Electrical Engineering, the team created a system that converts lip movements into text without audio signals. This new method identifies clear lip shapes first and uses them as clues to decode ambiguous words based on the surrounding context. By moving away from reading sentences from left to right, the system reduces errors caused by similar lip movements.

The process requires a diffusion large language model that repeatedly restores blank spaces in sentences starting from high confidence positions. The training involved two stages to link lip movements with text and to learn various sentence lengths. During testing with a public evaluation dataset of 433 hours of video, the technology recorded a word error rate of 19.4%. This specific metric indicates the frequency of incorrectly converted, omitted, or unnecessarily inserted words compared to the original sentence.

Professor Yong-Man Ro stated that flexibly adjusting the order of word generation can overcome the limitations of visual ambiguity. He explained that this foundation will allow the technology to be used reliably in industrial fields and various real life devices. The team believes the system can assist the deaf and hard of hearing or workers in noisy industrial settings. Future applications include creating communication aids that convey silent lip movements as text in environments where sound is difficult to hear.

stories.Headline: KAIST team led by Noh Yong-man develops lip-reading AI that cuts word error rate to 19.4%
stories.Summary:
KAIST announced on the 15th that a research team led by Professor Noh Yong-man of the School of Electrical Engineering developed a technology improving the accuracy of visual speech recognition, which converts spoken words into text by analyzing lip movements. The team used a diffusion large language model, which repeatedly fills in blanks in a sentence, to decode ambiguous lip movements by leveraging surrounding context. Conventional AI models generate sentences sequentially from the first word, so an incorrect word at the beginning propagates errors through the rest of the sentence. The team changed this approach from reading in order from the beginning to reading from the most certain parts first. The system first identifies words whose lip movements are clearly distinguishable, then uses those words as clues to decode the remaining parts.

The team trained the AI on the 433-hour lip-reading video dataset LRS3, and it achieved a word error rate of 19.4%, the lowest error rate reported among previous studies using LRS3 as a training dataset with reference sentences provided. Word error rate is the proportion of words incorrectly recognized, omitted, or unnecessarily added when the AI's output is compared with the reference sentence. The team split AI learning into two stages, teaching it to associate lip movements in the video with corresponding text content and to model sentence length. When decoding speech, the AI estimated several possible sentence lengths based on video duration and selected the most reliable sentence. The team received the Outstanding Paper Award at the international conference Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing 2026.

Professor Noh said the study is significant in that it demonstrates how flexibly controlling the order in which AI generates words alone can overcome fundamental limitations of speech recognition with visual ambiguity. He said the team aims to establish a reliable physical AI foundation that can be used across diverse devices in everyday life and industrial settings. Postdoctoral Researcher Yeo Jeong-hoon is the first author. Humans find it difficult to understand speech using only lip movements without hearing the sound, because there are words whose sounds differ but whose lip movements look similar. The research team's approach is similar to solving a puzzle by first fitting the pieces with clear shapes and then filling in the surrounding pieces.

The technology is expected to be used as a communication tool, such as converting speech to text in noisy environments or supporting communication for people who are deaf or hard of hearing. It could be developed into devices that understand workers' speech in noisy industrial sites or assist conversations among people who are deaf or hard of hearing. The research team plans to reduce the size and computational cost of the AI model so it can be deployed on various devices. Enabling real-time AI operation on wearable devices or robots without an internet connection is their next challenge. The articles do not state when the research began or how long the project took.

More to follow.

stories.Headline: KAIST researchers led by Ro Yong-man develop AI that reads lips without sound to convert speech into text
stories.Summary:
Researchers at KAIST developed an artificial intelligence system that reads lip movements without sound on Sunday, November 15, 2026. A team led by Professor Ro Yong-man of the School of Electrical Engineering created this technology to convert visible speech into text. The system uses a diffusion large language model to identify clear words first and then interprets ambiguous ones using surrounding context. This approach allows the AI to overcome visual ambiguity by placing recognizable pieces of a sentence like a puzzle.

The framework, called DLLM-VSR, achieved a word error rate of 19.4 percent using the LRS3 dataset which contains 433 hours of video. This result was the lowest among methods trained solely with that specific labeled dataset. The researchers also implemented a two-stage training method to align lip movements with text and predict sentence lengths. This work received an Outstanding Paper Award at the EMNLP 2026 international conference on natural language processing. The project was supported by the Institute of Information & Communications Technology Planning & Evaluation and the 2026 Jang Young-sil Fellowship Program.

Professor Ro Yong-man, the corresponding author, stated that flexible word generation helps solve the fundamental challenges of visual speech recognition. He explained that the team hopes this technology will provide a foundation for physical AI systems used in industrial settings and everyday life. Postdoctoral researcher Yeo Jeong-hun served as the first author, while doctoral researchers Kim Chae-won and Rha Hyeong-seop acted as co-authors. They believe the system could eventually be integrated into communication aids for people who are deaf or hard of hearing.

The technology may also be useful in noisy industrial environments where traditional speech recognition fails to distinguish voices from background noise. Because the system has only been tested on research datasets, its effectiveness in clinical settings or daily conversations remains unproven. The team now plans to reduce the computational requirements and the size of the model. This will allow the AI to operate in real time on robots or wearable devices without needing an internet connection.

stories.Headline: Google launches two specialized TPU chips and challenges NVIDIA's general-purpose roadmap
stories.Summary:
Google released two new TPU chips, the TPU 8tx and the TPU 8i Max, according to a 36Kr article dated 13 November 2026. Google designed the chips itself, and the article said the launch challenged NVIDIA's general-purpose chip roadmap. The 8tx is sold to government agencies and regulated industries and features chip-level data encryption. The 8i Max packages two chips in the same enclosure and focuses on ultra-long context processing. Amin Vahdat, head of Google's chip business, told Bloomberg that "the future belongs to specialization."

Google usually launched a new AI processor every two years, but that rhythm was disrupted in 2026. Vahdat said four TPU products will each be optimized for different needs. The 8tx works with AMD CPUs to encrypt data at the chip level, bypassing the usual step of decrypting data in memory before processing. The 8i Max integrates two TPUs in the same package, raising both computing power and memory capacity. Vahdat said that capability matters for drug R&D and mathematical computing and is also critical for programming applications.

Vahdat said Google could build one general-purpose chip for the whole market or launch different specialized versions, and that the latter approach lets it "actually create more value for our customers." He said the 8tx lets data be processed without first being decrypted in memory, part of Google's cooperation with AMD. He said the 8i Max's combined computing power and memory are important for drug R&D, mathematical computing and programming. He also said the TPU team gets early access to Google's latest Gemini model, which is used to improve chip energy efficiency and detect software vulnerabilities. He said AI is reducing the probability of design flaws that can cause billions of dollars in losses.

Oracle's senior vice president of cloud infrastructure, Karan Batta, said that as AI workloads become increasingly complex, customers need more choices. Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Mandeep Singh said TPUs cost about 30% less than NVIDIA GPUs while remaining competitive in throughput, though Google's TPU business margin is not that high. Counterpoint Research vice president Neil Shah said developers' time, code and project experience in CUDA are sunk costs that cannot be migrated. Jump Trading chief technology officer Alex Davies said the firm has thousands of TPUs, mainly to train models assisting trading research, but still mainly uses NVIDIA chips for model training, and only a small number of employees are particularly fond of TPUs.

Google TPUs have attracted Apple, Meta and Oracle, and in October Oracle announced that from next year its cloud customers could use Google TPUs for the first time, where they could previously choose only NVIDIA and AMD products. According to a recent regulatory filing, Anthropic has an option to buy up to $150 billion worth of TPUs between 2028 and 2031, and Bloomberg previously reported that OpenAI also plans to buy TPUs. Google wrote in its financial report that all currently available TPUs have already been booked by customers. Google cooperates with Broadcom on chip design and production coordination, signed an agreement with Broadcom competitor Marvell in recent months, and MediaTek is reported to be supporting the TPU business. A startup called Tenspresso, founded by two former TPU engineers, is developing its first chip aimed directly at the 8i Max's market, with design at least another year from completion.

Bloomberg Intelligence estimates that by 2028 Google's TPU-related sales of chips, software and hardware will exceed $135 billion, against an expected $12 billion this year, a figure that excludes revenue from customers using TPUs through Google Cloud. The same research says opposition to data center construction may cut the $1.4 trillion tech companies expected to invest in 2027 by 5% to 7%, spending that covers chips, network equipment, land and other materials. The article said market concerns about a possible slowdown in AI infrastructure investment are weighing on tech stocks, and the Democratic Party's victory in the US midterm elections has brought new uncertainties to data center projects. More than a decade ago Google developed TPUs to reduce its purchases of NVIDIA GPUs. The article said the competition is not about whose chips are faster but about who can make developers modify fewer lines of code.

stories.Headline: Tanisha Bansal leads a free AI agents masterclass on 28 November 2026
stories.Summary:
ET TechGig is holding a free live online masterclass titled AI Agents: From Demo to Real-World Deployment on 28 November 2026 at 4:00 PM, lasting 75 minutes, according to an announcement published on 15 November 2026. The session will be led by Tanisha Bansal, an AI and Technology Professional at Accenture Strategy & Consulting, whose expertise covers Generative AI, agentic systems, RAG, MCP, enterprise integrations, workflow automation, cloud technologies and AI evaluation. The class is aimed at AI and Machine Learning Engineers, Software Developers, Application Engineers, Cloud and Solution Architects, Generative AI Practitioners, Engineering Managers, Technical Leads and Enterprise Technology Professionals. It will include a 15-minute live Q&A in which participants can put questions to the speaker.

The masterclass follows a practical, architecture-first approach across six areas, starting with why AI demonstrations often struggle in real enterprise environments and moving through enterprise AI architecture built from models, RAG, MCP, tool calling and orchestration. It will show how an agent can interpret user intent, retrieve information, validate business rules, execute approved actions and verify outcomes through a worked example, and it will cover guardrails, security, evaluation, observability and human-in-the-loop approvals. The session also addresses measuring AI implementation through completed workflows and tangible business outcomes rather than the quality of generated responses, and it offers a structured framework for moving prototypes toward production. Registration is free.

The article frames the class around a gap it describes between agents that perform well in demonstrations and those that work reliably in real enterprise settings, saying successful implementation requires more than connecting a large language model to a tool. It says developers must handle security, permissions, validation, failure recovery and human approvals, and that the difference between an impressive demo and a dependable solution lies in how these components are engineered. The article states that professionals who understand how to build secure, reliable and production-ready AI agents will have an important advantage as organisations adopt autonomous workflows. It gives no further details on what follows the session beyond registration being open.
